# P r e f a c e .

---

Just a few words to recommend a book that has been little read until now and, as I believe, has been unjustly disparaged! This writing, which constitutes only a small part of a large work consisting of nine quarto <term>quarto: a printing format where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves (eight pages), resulting in a medium-sized book</term> volumes, appears here in translation because it deserves to become better known for its remarkable content. I wished that a book which sheds so much light on antiquity <note>original: "Alterthum" — here referring to the study of the ancient world</note>—one that at present is found only in large book collections <note>referring to private or institutional libraries</note>—might be read by more people, its content examined, and judged more by one's own insights than by those of others.

I am far from approving of this writing in its entire content, or regarding it as a complete explanation of the secrets of antiquity <note>original: "Alterthum"</note>. I myself am by no means satisfied with many of the author's explanations, and especially with his manner of explaining the **Labors of Hercules** <term>Labors of Hercules: A series of twelve difficult feats carried out by the hero Hercules in Greek mythology, often interpreted allegorically in older scholarship</term>. I therefore do not wish to impose my judgment on anyone, and even less to decide whether the author's mode of presentation is the only true one. Everyone may judge for themselves as they please. Even if some proofs are too weak, some conjectures too daring, and many etymologies <term>etymology: the study of word origins; here referring to the author's potentially strained linguistic arguments</term> undeniably too forced; this criticism applies more to individual parts than to the **main subject** of this writing. Whoever demands here that a writer treat such a subject, the meaning

Nowhere do the writers who sought to explain mythology <note>original: "Fabellehre"</note> provide the reason for this union. They allowed themselves to be carried away far too much by the passion for devising systems to have precisely investigated the facts, which they mostly overlooked. Furthermore, their principles were very convenient; for everything that did not agree with their systems, or what they could not explain, was either corrupted and distorted, or absurd.

In the conviction that with such principles nothing could be discovered or explained, I have chosen the opposite path. I gathered facts together and compared them: and this is the source from which the many discoveries I am making public have flowed—discoveries which shed so much light and offer the greatest utility regarding antiquity and the origin of knowledge.

It is specifically to this method that one must owe the interpretation of these three Oriental <note>or Eastern</note> allegories, which form an inseparable whole, and whose reunification confirms the truth of the accounts of **Diodorus** and **Sanchoniatho**.

<summary>The author continues a mythological genealogy involving Thoth and Hercules, criticizing previous scholars for prioritizing rigid theoretical systems over historical facts. He argues that his comparative method reveals the underlying truth within the interconnected allegories of ancient Phoenician and Egyptian historians.</summary>
<keywords>Thoth, Mercury Trismegistus, Uranus, Hercules, Sanchoniatho, Diodorus Siculus, mythology, historical method, Oriental allegories, antiquity</keywords>

--- Page 25 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding three specific "Oriental" allegories. The catchword "Diese" from the previous page correctly transitions into the opening sentence here.</meta>

These three allegories are the stories of **Saturn**, who is the same person as **Osiris**, of **Thoth** or **Mercury**, and of the 12 labors of **Hercules**.

Closely connected to one another, they form a whole, where all individual parts mutually explain each other and are made for one another.

**Saturn**, the devourer of children <note>Referring to the myth of Saturn/Cronus swallowing his offspring to prevent being overthrown</note>, opens the procession with his scythe; he is followed by the messenger of the gods, **Mercury**, with his caduceus <note>original: "Schlangenstabe," literally "snake-staff"</note>: and the entire scene is concluded by the lion-conqueror, **Hercules**, victorious in twelve battles with his club, as he burns himself on a funeral pyre and ascends to heaven.

If one observes these pictures in this very order, and overlooks none of the symbols <note>original: "Sinnbilder"</note> by which they are characterized, they appear to be what they truly are: very ingeniously devised and most fitting allegories, as they depict the most necessary arts with the greatest truth.

Thus, the story of **Saturn** is an allegorical tale of the invention of agriculture <term>Ackerbau: the cultivation of land for crops</term>, which had to lay the foundation for states and wealth, and lead to the measurement of time.

**Mercury** will offer us an allegory about the invention of astronomy and the calendar, according to which the farmer guides himself in his field work.

And in the story and the 12 labors of **Hercules**, we will see the plowing of the earth and the distribution of rural tasks for every month of the year.

<summary>The author identifies three key mythological figures—Saturn, Mercury, and Hercules—as allegories for the development of human civilization, specifically agriculture, astronomy, and the seasonal calendar.</summary>
<keywords>Saturn, Osiris, Thoth, Mercury, Hercules, allegory, agriculture, astronomy, calendar, twelve labors, mythology</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that mythological figures are allegorical representations of agricultural and scientific progress. These three persons are thus just as closely connected in nature as they are in mythology <note>original: "Fabellehre," the study of myths or fables</note>, and the latter is transformed from a nonsensical tale or distorted history into a monument to the genius and spirit of its inventors, and a proof of their delicate feeling for the most useful and interesting subjects.

I will begin with the previously incomprehensible passage by **Sanchuniathon** <note>original: "Sanchoniaton"; a Phoenician author believed to have lived before the Trojan War, whose writings on mythology were preserved by Philo of Byblos</note>; the facts themselves, upon which I will base my explanation, I will borrow from those writers who, due to their great antiquity, were best positioned to know the original traditions.

If one accepts the explanation I have just given, then this passage by **Sanchuniathon**—which is entirely unexplainable as literal history and so strikingly absurd that one might rather conclude its author was insane, a passage which has until now been a true torture to all its interpreters since none knew how to understand it—this passage, I say, then appears so clear, so inviting, and so appropriate to the spirit of antiquity <term>Alterthum: the period of ancient history, specifically the classical civilizations of the Mediterranean and Near East</term> and the natural order, that one must admit: once explained in this way, any other explanation becomes unnecessary.

The following is the main idea of these three allegories, the rough sketch of these three paintings surviving from antiquity, which were painted upon the sacred walls of the temples for public benefit and instruction.

Why have these subjects been celebrated by poets and preserved by historians? Why did the wise Egyptians, the Greeks, and others depict them on the walls of their temples in colors that have been preserved for millennia—at least in Egypt? And if these subjects are merely ridiculous fables and tasteless tales of abominable and revolting events, why do all the arts vie for the glory of contributing something to their preservation and beautification? It is simply because they only *seem* absurd; in fact, they instruct humanity under the guise of a pleasant pastime, and beneath this allegorical veil, they introduce them to the most useful truths.

Since the lawgivers <note>The author refers to "Gesetzgeber," ancient civilizers who used myth and ritual to establish social order and moral codes.</note>, who were at once poets and masters of music, wished to make their instruction enduring and suited to the comprehension of all people, they had to give it more charm and omit everything that might weary the attention. Therefore, they translated it into actions and paintings, and from this come the sacred images and poems in which these images are described in a manner that is as allegorical as it is picturesque.

These allegories, which were intelligible at the time of their creation, necessarily became increasingly obscure the more one lost sight of their origin and mistook them for corrupted history. From this arise the apparent absurdities and immense difficulties which immediately

The reader will become very clearly aware of this if he follows me attentively in the explanation of these three present allegories. All obscurity will vanish; he will then be all the more convinced the further he reads.

It cannot be anything but gratifying for him to see mythology <note>original: "Fabellehre," referring to the systematic study or body of myths</note> transformed into a vivid painting of truth, and to see that which previously seemed extremely obscure explained in a very rational manner. — Should it not bring him joy when, contrary to his expectations, in the very place where he believed he saw only senseless and contradictory fictions, he suddenly makes the pleasant and surprising discovery that the subject of these fables is the immortalization of the sciences and arts, and especially of agriculture; — of agriculture, that excellent art so highly esteemed by the ancient world and so greatly praised even in their fables and songs? An art without which no state, no population, and no science can exist! Without it, humans, like wild animals, would wander through vast deserts and consume the same food as they; whereas, on the contrary, with the help of agriculture, the human race progresses unhindered toward perfection <note>In this Enlightenment context, "perfection" refers to the full realization of human social and intellectual potential.</note>. The earth glistens and overflows with goods of every kind; where previously there were only wildernesses and marshes, numerous herds now graze and play, entire empires arise and climb to the highest peak of glory, and the sciences and arts increase and multiply alongside enjoyment and abundance.

## VII. Saturn’s Allies, etc.

The allies of Ilus <note>Ilus is the Phoenician name for the god the Greeks called Cronus and the Romans called Saturn</note> were called Elohim <note>original: "ΕΛΩΕΙΜ", the Hebrew word for "gods"</note>, meaning they were the "Cronians," or those who lived in the time of Cronus. <margin>5) Or Saturnians.</margin>

Cronus stabbed his son Sadid with his own sword because he held him in suspicion; by thus taking the life of the boy with his own hand, he became the murderer of his own blood.

Likewise, he also cut off the head of his own daughter, an act which left all the gods stunned by Cronus’s state of mind.

## X. Saturn as the Vanquisher of Uranus.

In the thirty-second year of his power and reign, **Ilus** <note>original: "Ἴλος"; a Phoenician name for the god El</note>, also known as **Cronus**, lay in wait for his father **Uranus** in an inland, mountainous region <margin>(†) Not in a great plain, nor in a type of valley, as the *Universal History* and **Fourmont** <note>Claude Étienne Fourmont (1703–1745), a French scholar who translated ancient Phoenician fragments</note> have translated.</margin> and, having captured him, he cut off his genitals near some springs and rivers.

When Uranus had breathed his last, he was deified <note>original: "ἀφιερώθη"; literally "consecrated" or made sacred</note>. His blood dripped into the waters of the nearby springs and rivers, and to this very day, that location is still pointed out.

These are the famous deeds of **Cronus**, and such are the venerable aspects of the life under Cronus which the Greeks celebrate; they are those who call this era the **Golden Age**...

## XI. Saturn kills his son.

During a time of great famine and pestilence <note>original Greek: "Λοιμοῦ δὲ γενομένου καὶ φθορᾶς" (When a pestilence and destruction occurred)</note>, Cronus offered up his only son as a whole burnt offering to his father Uranus; he circumcised himself and compelled his entire army <note>original Greek: "συμμάχους" (allies)</note> to do the very same.

Not long after, he deified another son who had just died, named Muth, whom he had by Rhea. This is the same one whom the Greeks (*) call <term>Thanatos</term> <note>The personification of Death</note> and the Phoenicians call Pluto (12).

Following these events, Cronus gave the city of Byblos to the goddess Baaltis (also known as Dione); Berytos <note>modern Beirut</note> he gave to Poseidon, the Cabiri <note>a group of enigmatic chthonic deities</note>, the Agrotae (13), and the Fishermen, who consecrated the remains of Pontus <note>a personification of the sea</note> at Berytos.

The symbol meant that Cronus saw while sleeping and slept while waking; and similarly with the wings, that resting he flew, and flying he rested. # Preliminary Remarks.

## §. 1.

### Regarding the hitherto incomprehensible monument, and why it was incomprehensible.

This is the nature of this strange, ancient monument, which has come down to us from the dimmest antiquity. Everything—even the enigmatic turn of phrase that prevails within it, the exalted persons who are its heroes, the nature of their actions (especially those attributed to Saturn <note>The Roman equivalent of the Greek Titan Cronus</note>, which make him an inexplicable being), the impossibility of finding a family that fits all the characterizing traits mentioned in this monument, the absurdities with which it is filled (which make it so difficult to determine whether it is a history, a fable, or the work of a mad writer), the conflicting opinions of scholars regarding its authenticity, its various interpretations, its correspondence with the most important subjects of history and mythology <term>mythology: translated from 'Fabellehre', referring to the study of ancient myths and legends</term>, and the obscurity itself—all this has made this fragment famous and alluring.

### §. 1.

## Concerning the hitherto incomprehensible monument, and why it was incomprehensible.

This is the nature of this strange, ancient monument, which has come down to us from the dimmest antiquity. Everything—even the enigmatic phrasing that prevails within it, the exalted figures who are its heroes, the nature of their actions (especially those attributed to Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Greek Cronus, often identified in these texts with a Phoenician deity like El</note>, which make him an inexplicable being), the impossibility of finding a family that fits the characterizing traits mentioned by this monument, the absurdities with which it is filled (making it so difficult to determine whether it is a history, a fable, or the work of a mad writer), the conflicting opinions of scholars regarding its authenticity, the various interpretations of it, its agreement with the most important subjects of history and mythology, even the obscurity itself—all of this has made this fragment famous and alluring.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Phoenician fragments preserved by Eusebius. It specifically addresses the transmission history—from Sanchoniathon's original Phoenician text to Philo of Byblos's Greek translation—and the profound difficulties scholars face in interpreting these surviving remnants without the original context.</meta>

which contains the history of the ten generations, has been brought down to us.

Eusebius borrowed both fragments from the translation by Philo, a Phoenician from Byblos, who had translated into the Greek language the history written by his countryman Sanchoniathon in his native tongue across eight books.

Unfortunately, the Phoenician original and its translation are no longer in existence, and we must rely solely on the fragments copied by Eusebius.

This loss is all the more keenly felt because this fragment is extremely difficult to understand; furthermore, all hope of determining its meaning is lost, as it cannot be understood in and of itself. We lack both the individual parts and the work as a whole, which would allow us to compare the former and thereby deduce the author’s intent.

To achieve this, it would be necessary to guess from the fragment itself the spirit in which it was written and to seek out, by blind chance, the connections it might have had to Eastern antiquity <note>Refers to the ancient civilizations of the Near East, particularly those of the Levant and Mesopotamia</note>. Such an effort was entirely uncertain and lacked any success; for how could one judge the value of a translation in the absence of the original text? Let us not wonder, then, if this monument was never understood! The reason lay in the ambiguous and absurd sense of the translation, and in an explanation that remained imperfect and entirely unsuited to the whole.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the loss of the original Phoenician texts to the author's proposal of a new, "natural" interpretive framework. It begins to establish the historical context of Sanchoniathon, citing the testimonies of ancient scholars like Eusebius and Porphyry regarding his origins and his sources of information.</meta>

### §. 2.

## New, Clear, and Natural Interpretation of the Fragment 
## of Sanchoniathon.

This shall not prevent me from attempting an explanation that none of my predecessors have chanced upon. It is natural and simple; it flows from the subject matter itself and is entirely appropriate to the spirit of antiquity. It confirms our opinions on the origin of the sciences and arts, and thereby opens a vast field for a more precise knowledge of the ancient world and its allegorical spirit; it affords us a completely new view, quite unsuspected until this hour. Mythology receives an entirely new form: a new order rises up from the wreckage and ruins of antiquity; this is as simple and pleasant as antiquity previously seemed inexplicable and absurd.

### §. 3.

## Fatherland and Era of Sanchoniathon.

Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop often called the "Father of Church History" for his work recording the early centuries of Christianity.</note> asserts that Sanchoniathon was a native of Berytus <note>modern-day Beirut, Lebanon</note>, a Phoenician city, and I shall have occasion to expand further on this during the explanation of this fragment. Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Phoenician Neoplatonic philosopher who was often critical of Christianity.</note>, who was himself a Phoenician, adds: “that this writer

> "...history was found to be very faithful; Sanchoniathon and Abiba <note>Abibalus, the King of Tyre and father of King Hiram, a contemporary of David and Solomon according to later records</note> 
> had, as one could be convinced by the list of Phoenician 
> kings, lived around the time of Moses; the 
> former [Sanchoniathon], however, had borrowed his history partly from the records 
> of city archives, and partly from the records carefully 
> preserved in the archives of the temples."

If one could grant credence to this report, then the era in which Sanchoniathon lived would indeed be very well known. The god Jevo <note>original: "Jevo"</note> would be the "Jeve" of the Hebrews (known today as Jehovah), and his priest "Jerombaal" would be the Hebrew judge with the surname "Jerubbaal"—that is, Gideon. However, through an error of the translator, he has been quite incorrectly assigned the title of a priest, as the translator did not realize that the word for "priest" (*) also signifies a prince and a sovereign leader. This same error was also committed in the translation of the Bible, where the children of David are given the title of "priests" instead of "princes," and the fathers-in-law of Joseph and Moses are called "Priests" of Heliopolis and Midian.

It is certainly true that, in those days, a man often united the dignity of a prince and a priest within himself; however, this does not justify a translator who distorts a word so much that, through his translation, it carries a far more restricted meaning than it possessed in the original language.

---

(*) The author likely has the Hebrew word *kohen* <note>original: "כהן"</note> in mind here. It is also quite certain that this word does not always signify a priest, but generally a leader—both spiritual and secular—and consequently can just as easily mean a state official, as seen for example in 2 Samuel 8:18. <note>original: "A. d. H." - Editor's Note</note>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Sanchoniathon’s identity, moving from the etymology of his name to a scholarly debate over the authenticity of the surviving fragments of his work. The name Sanchoniathon, as strange as it may seem, is not foreign to Phoenicia. The suffix *on* is common in the Orient, and one even finds in the Hebrew books a person named *San*, the son of *Chonias*. These two names joined together form the name of our author, which must be written San-Choniat-on.

### § 4.
## On the Authenticity of this Fragment.

Despite all these circumstances accompanying the historical narrative of Sanchoniathon, which seem too natural to be mere fictions, the opinions of scholars regarding his authenticity are quite diverse. Although it appears that those who rejected this historical record did so more because of its obscurity than for any other more substantial reason, I will, without siding with one party or another, present to the reader a summary of all the various opinions.

<meta>This page continues the argument for the authenticity of the Phoenician writer Sanchoniathon, asserting that the Greek fragments we possess must be based on a genuine ancient source rather than being a later forgery by Porphyry or Philo. Regardless of who the author of this fragment may be, one must still regard the Greek text as a translation of an originally Phoenician work collected by **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who preserved many fragments of ancient history that would otherwise be lost.</note>. The translation is full of Phoenician words that the translator was unable to express through Greek words; we shall observe in the following pages that every ambiguity stems solely from the fact that the Phoenician words used by the original author possessed various meanings. Furthermore, the work as a whole is too distinct from Greek ideas and too consistent with the foundational concepts of the East for **Porphyry** or any other scholar of his time to have invented it.

## Section 6.
### The Perspective From Which This Fragment Must Be Judged.

One should not be surprised if these scholars, despite their erudition, failed in their efforts to explain this fragment <note>Referring to the surviving portions of Sanchuniathon’s Phoenician History</note>. They certainly would have found the truth if erudition alone had been sufficient; however, they followed a method that necessarily led them further away from it. Since insurmountable difficulties appeared to them at every step, they sought to rescue themselves through the most erroneous and tasteless etymologies, and through unsustainable propositions

Abbé"</note> Mignot, which is intended for the *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres* <note>original: "Memoires de l'Acad. des Insc. et Belles Lett."</note>; I know this one only by name. For my part, I adhere strictly to the allegorical sense, which, however, must always be based on nature. The matter would thus be sufficiently prepared, and the public in a position to pass a final judgment on it.

...to help; one might say that everything seemed right to them, provided it created a mere illusion for themselves and their readers.

Everyone wishes to see a historical narrative in this monument <note>Referring to the written records of Sanchuniathon’s Phoenician history</note>. They took Eljon <note>A Phoenician deity whose name means "the Most High," often equated with the Greek Zeus</note>, Uranus, Saturn, and so on, to be a succession of kings from one and the same family; their only struggle was to discover the place and time of their reigns, and which historical persons might be designated by these names. But where could one find a family whose history was so fantastical and unnatural? How could one give these fables a historical appearance and transform them into a series of rational facts?

We shall therefore choose a completely opposite path, one more firmly grounded in reason and ancient customs. We will not have to explain a historical narrative, but rather an ingeniously devised <term>allegory</term> <note>A story where characters and events represent deeper symbolic meanings, often related to nature or philosophy</note> which is connected to Eastern mythology <note>original: "morgenländischen Fabellehre"</note>, the mother of Roman and Greek mythology. In this view, Uranus was unfaithful to his wife only in an allegorical sense, and Saturn’s revolting cruelties will be nothing more than pleasant riddles, beneath which lie hidden the facts that truly deserve to be passed down to us.

Our predecessors on this path would have realized this as well, had they been less preoccupied with various prejudices; had they looked more closely at the spirit of the ancients, at the nature of fables, at all that their <term>cosmogonies</term> <note>Accounts or theories regarding the origin of the universe</note> and <term>theogonies</term> <note>Accounts of the origins and genealogies of the gods</note> represent, and at the similarity of this fragment with a considerable part of anti-

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that Phoenician myths should be read as philosophical allegories rather than literal histories of ancient kings. ...of antiquity and to the words of the fragment itself: ”that **Thabion’s son**, having presented everything in **allegories**, combined them with physical ideas and natural phenomena, and left them to those who celebrated the **orgies** <note>In this historical context, "orgies" (from the Greek *orgia*) refers to sacred rites or secret religious ceremonies, not the modern secular meaning</note>, and to the priests who presided over the **mysteries**,” <note>original: "Mysterien" — secret religious cults of the ancient world</note> they would have been more attentive. Finally, if they had carefully weighed all the peculiar expressions of the writer they intended to explain, regardless of any preconceived system, and considered the various meanings they might hold—comparing them especially with the spirit of the **Phoenician language** (which one must never lose sight of, and to which the translation at hand must always be traced back)—things would have been different.

This fragment would then have presented itself quite differently to their searching eyes; they would have perceived that the history contained within—the story of **Cronus** <note>The Greek name for the Titan who ruled during the Golden Age</note> or **Saturn**, and his wars against his father **Uranus**—was never a history of mortal men who became gods. One is utterly deceived when trying to find historical events therein; these occurrences relate to Saturn only insofar as he is regarded as all-devouring **Time**. This would naturally have led them to the **allegory**, as the contemplation of time could lead to the idea of Saturn. Yet, it was irrational to link the concept of Time with a specific man named Saturn, making him the "God of Time" rather than a representation of a completely different part of the world or a distinct physical property.

<meta>This page continues the argument that ancient myths are not literal histories but sophisticated allegories. The previous page ended mid-sentence with "m-", and the catchword "hende" indicates the full word was "machende" (making). The author is transitioning from discussing Saturn as a personification of Time to Saturn as the inventor of agriculture.</meta>

Had they subsequently also considered the **symbols** <note>original: "Sinnbilder" — emblematic images or icons used to represent abstract ideas</note> attributed to the God of Time, **Saturn**, they would have seen that these were not derived from Time itself. Instead, they were taken from their resemblance to another object whose cycles coincide with those of Time, which serves as a measure for it, gives it a new significance, and inevitably made the most vivid impression on humanity. This object is the **harvest**.

In the most ancient times, when Time was first armed with the **reaper’s scythe**, symbols were drawn from the harvest. Initially, everything that would later be applied to Time itself had to be said first about the harvest and the reaper. Thus, the **allegory** <term>Allegory: a story or image where characters and events symbolize deeper moral or natural truths</term> of Saturn viewed as Time could only be an imitation—an extension—of the allegory of Saturn as the inventor of **agriculture**. These two allegories are inseparable, for Time (or the years) and the harvests keep the same pace, and both "devour" all living things. <note>The author is reinterpreting the gruesome myth of Saturn devouring his children as a natural metaphor: just as the harvest marks the end of a season's growth, time eventually consumes everything it brings forth.</note>

Indeed, in every mythology, we find the God of Time, Saturn, presented as the inventor of agriculture. The fact that the harvest is the preeminent measure of time naturally led to his transformation into the God of Time.

This story of Saturn, which seems so absurd and strange—so much so that no commentator could offer any reason for it—is therefore an ingenious and beautiful allegory of the invention of one of the first arts: an art without which neither populous societies nor flour- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("blü-"), likely "blühende" or "flourishing."</note>

What an impression such a speech must have made upon the listeners! And how those societies who remained in a wild state must have been astonished when, during their roamings, they suddenly beheld a spectacle of which they had no prior concept; when they saw vast fields where one could perceive neither thorn hedges, nor useless trees, nor unhealthy stagnant waters; where everything—a regular division of the land, a variety of objects, the beauty of the verdant countryside, and fruits of every kind—rendered the view enchanting; where numerous herds leaped about as a sign of the abundance in which they lived; where their owners, no longer forced into a wandering and miserable way of life, had settled firmly in such places and built pleasant dwellings, and saw themselves surrounded by a large family whose joyful and cheerful appearance proclaimed their happiness, while the field echoed with the sound of instruments mingling with the songs of the workers and the bleating of lambs.

Indeed, the introduction of agriculture <term>Ackerbau</term> <note>farming and the cultivation of the soil</note> must have constituted a remarkable epoch <note>a significant historical turning point</note> for all time in the history of the human race. It was destined to be immortalized through the rural festivals to which it gave rise; it had to provide the poets with material for their verses, and the greatly varied tasks of farming must have provided inspiration for paintings <note>original: "Gemählden" – referring here to vivid artistic descriptions or visual depictions</note>. This invention therefore had to become personified in their language, and through its contradictions, the most ingenious yet simultaneously difficult to fathom allegories <note>symbolic stories where characters represent abstract ideas</note> must have arisen, as soon as one failed to transport oneself back into the times that produced them.

## Article I.

### Of the first four persons of Sanchuniathon, Elion and his family.

Sanchuniathon’s monument <term>Denkmal</term> <note>The author uses "monument" to refer to the ancient written records attributed to the Phoenician priest Sanchuniathon, whose work survives only in fragments quoted by later writers.</note> begins in the following manner:

> ” Elion <note>original: "Eljon"; a Semitic term for "the Most High."</note>, or the Most High, and his spouse Beruth,
> ” who lived in the region of Byblos, sired
> ” Epigeus or Autochthon <note>original: "Epigius oder Avtochton." "Autochthon" is Greek for "sprung from the earth itself."</note>, who was subsequently
> ” named Uranus, and from him the element above us,
> ” because of its excellent beauty, received the name Ura-
> ” nus (Heaven.) <note>original: "Uranus (Himmel.)"</note>

> ” From these same parents Uranus also had a
> ” sister named Ge <note>The Greek word for "Earth."</note>, and because of her beauty,
> ” her name was bestowed upon the Earth.

The knowledge of a beginner in the Greek and Oriental languages should suffice to recognize this passage at first glance as completely allegorical; and to see that its author had no intention at all of writing the genealogy of mere mortals.

How great, therefore, must have been the preconceived delusion of the scholars who wished to explain it, if the light that shines forth from the union of these names could no longer make an impression on them; we should not wonder, then, that since they absolutely did not want to see, but rather diligently sought to view this beautiful allegory from a completely false perspective, they have made such a masterpiece of obscurity and absurdity <term>Albernheit</term> out of it.

We do not even exclude the translator himself. His translation, which is half-Phoenician and half-Greek, proves that he did not always understand the true meaning of the author, and that he was not always able to maintain the ambiguity inherent in the allegory, consequently diminishing its beauty and its impact.

Fortunately, he left many Phoenician words standing, through which one can always find the thread of the allegory again; it would not be very difficult to restore them through a new translation into a single language, and thereby restore the original work to its former perfection.

Elion is no human being; everything—his name, the translation by Philo himself, and the children attributed to him—reveals this.

->§. 1.<-

**Helion**, (20) the name for the most noble of the Oriental <note>In this context, "Oriental" refers to the cultures of the ancient Near East, such as the Phoenicians, Hebrews, and Arabs.</note> deities, comes from the Sun; and this, through its sublimity and as the source of light, unites the very properties that were perceived in the deity.

**Philo** <note>Philo of Byblos (c. 64–141 AD), the Greek-speaking scholar who claimed to translate Sanchuniathon's lost Phoenician history.</note>, who could not express this word with any Greek word that suited it, left it as it was, and explained it using the Greek word **Hypsistus** or **Hupsiste** <note>original Greek: *Hypsistos* (Ὕψιστος)</note>, which means the "All-Highest," and which was formed from the root word **Hyp** or **Hup** <note>referring to the Greek prefixes *hypo-* or *hyper-* indicating height or placement above</note> meaning "exalted."

He translated it very well, and one therefore does not read the history of a human being, but rather God Himself is the subject here.

->§. 2.<-

But he has a wife named **Beruth**. This too is strictly true, though only in an allegorical sense, and nothing can be proven more easily. To this end, one only needs to look at the true value of this word in Phoenician and in all other Oriental languages.

**Beruth** is a feminine noun, which is formed from the noun **Bar** or **Ber**, which means *creator* (and from which the Hebrew verb **Bara** <term>Bara <note>original Hebrew: ברא (to create)</note></term> *to create* is derived). It therefore expresses Creation. This is inseparable from the Almighty, for through her everything that exists has been brought forth. This difference is sometimes almost imperceptible. Here it consists in the fact that one must regard human names as words that signify beings who were never human.

Because of this, a distortion in history can easily arise from carelessness and error, and we will become aware of a large number of such mistakes in the course of our investigation.

### §. 5.

If this passage is therefore only allegorical, and begins with the account of creation: it proves that the first Phoenician philosophers were not atheists, and that they expressed themselves on this matter just like the **Chaldeans**, the **Egyptians**, and **Hebrews**; indeed, it is also of the greatest importance because of its agreement with ancient traditions of creation.

It also prepares us for great things, especially in the allegorical style, as the ancients always made a beginning with the creation of the universe whenever they wished to depict <note>original German: mahlen — literally "to paint," but here used as "to describe" or "to depict"</note> sublime and truly poetic subjects.

### §. 6.

But do we not encounter insurmountable obstacles at the very first step? **Eljon** <note>A name meaning "The Most High," appearing in both Phoenician and Hebrew contexts</note>, our author continues, was killed by wild animals: He must therefore surely be a human being, for how else could he be killed? Yes, for those who suspect no allegory here, and who associate a definite and literal meaning with an ambiguous phrase, he is indeed only a man.

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument from the previous section, where he questioned how a figure reportedly killed by wild animals could be worshipped as a god. Certainly this figure of speech is an allegory, for this is revealed by the words added by our author:
> "and immediately *Eljon* <note>The Most High</note> was invoked as God
> "by his children."

No dead person, however—especially a man whom wild animals have just torn to pieces—would be elevated to a god; it is impossible to expect the strength required for the preservation of one’s own people and all goods necessary for life from one who could not even defend his own life.

It is the Most High alone whom his children worship divinely, whom they regard as their father and their God, and to whose service they dedicate themselves forever.

The phrasing used for this transition must, therefore, be thoroughly ambiguous and capable of various interpretations, depending on whether it is taken in a historical or an allegorical sense, making *Eljon* either a god or a man.

To convince ourselves further of this, we wish to translate the Greek phrase back into Phoenician or Hebrew—which are essentially the same, as both languages do not differ from each other—and through this, we obtain these words:

->Eljon rested from his work<-
<note>original Hebrew/transliteration: Eljon Schabbatha mi - melachtho / עליון שבת מי מלאכתו</note>

the analysis of which will show the true meaning, and how that meaning was necessarily distorted in the Greek translation.

*Schabbatha* is the verb *to rest*; it originates from the word *Sabbath*, which in relation to days signifies a day of rest.

--- Page 70 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s linguistic deconstruction of a Phoenician myth. Having previously established that "Eljon" (The Most High) was said to have "rested from his work," the author now explains how the specific words used in that phrase were prone to mistranslation, leading later Greek readers to believe Eljon was a mortal man who died, rather than a god who finished creation.</meta>

But **R e s t** is an ambiguous expression, and is capable of both a literal and a figurative meaning; historically, one can take it as an interruption of ordinary labor, and allegorically for death, which ends all labor. This is likewise found in the French language in the following phrases: *one rests on a bed, on the turf; and one rests in the tomb.* <note>original French: "on repose sur un lit, sur le gazon; et l'on repose dans la tombe."</note>

The one expresses a **recovery** <note>original French: "se delasser"</note> and the other a **state of being dead** <note>original French: "être mort"</note>; and if a foreigner errs in the choice of these different meanings, he will surely say: one died on the turf, and one recovered in the grave.

As soon as **Eljon** <note>The Most High</note> was turned into a human being, it was also natural that the word was taken in the latter sense, and people said: Eljon had ceased to live, was dead, was no more.

The following word **Mi** is just as ambiguous. It is a preposition which unites within itself the double sense of the French *De* <note>meaning "of" or "from"</note>, which corresponds sometimes to the Genitive, sometimes to the Ablative cases used by the Latins, or to the French preposition *Par* <note>meaning "by" or "through"</note>. To avoid this ambiguity, the Italians created two different words, *di* and *de*. One can, consequently, translate **Mi** as "from" or "by," and the context alone must determine the choice.

Now follows the word **Melachth** in the *plural*. This too is ambiguous; for in the simple sense it means "labors" or "works," but in the allegorical sense it means "companions of labor," such as the animals that [help] humans in their rural—

<summary>The author explains how linguistic ambiguity in the words for "rest," "from," and "work" allowed a theological statement about God's Sabbath to be misinterpreted as a historical account of a man's death. He uses French and Italian grammar as analogies to show how easily a translator can choose the wrong meaning of a word.</summary>

--- Page 71 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s linguistic analysis of the word "Melachth," focusing on its plural form and the suffix "o." The previous page established that "Mi" can mean "from" or "by," setting the stage for the current discussion on how "Melachth-o" (his works/animals) was misinterpreted by Greek translators.</meta>

...[human] labors, the true human labors, for which they were destined upon their very entry into the world, to provide assistance.

The final syllable is **O**, which is the *hu* <note>original Greek: "hu" — here referring to the third-person pronoun or breathing</note> of the Greeks, and the French *soi* <note>meaning "himself" or "his own"</note>.

We have here, then, a phrase that has a double meaning:

1) If one considers **Eljon** <note>The Most High</note> as God, it means: **Eljon rested from his labors;**

2) If, however, one takes him merely for a common man, it expresses: **Eljon was killed by his animals.** <note>The author is demonstrating how the same root word for "work" or "labor" could be mistranslated as "beasts of burden" or "animals."</note>

But that he must be regarded here as God, we shall prove, and **Sanchuniathon** <note>a legendary Phoenician author whose works survive only in fragments quoted by others</note> says so himself. He was, therefore, not killed by his animals; rather, this meaning arose only from an error by the Greek translator. Those scholars who relied upon that translation, without comparing it with the spirit of the Phoenician language, necessarily missed Sanchuniathon’s true meaning.

Now that this phrase has been restored to its original language, it becomes perfectly identical to the historical description left behind by **Moses**, with which he concludes his narrative of the Creation—the beginning of which we have already seen above. (1)

->**God . . . rested from his work.**<-
->**אלהים שבת מי מלאכתו**<-

...the assertions just expressed could be reconciled. 
> "They lived," it is said, "in the region of Byblos;" 

now, Byblos was a Phoenician city, not far from Berytus <note>Modern-day Beirut</note>. This was bound to confuse the reader or listener most of all, persuading them that an allegory was the last thing to be sought here; "certainly," he therefore says, "these were human persons." But never was a more incorrect conclusion drawn, as we shall soon see, and as the following will increasingly prove. One should not immediately be perplexed by the use of the name Byblos. This name was chosen as the dwelling of Eljon <note>The "Most High" god in Phoenician mythology, often equated with the Hebrew *Elyon*</note> above all others because it suited the overall allegory perfectly.

Byblos is composed of two words: **By** and **Blos**. The first, which is pronounced **By** and **Bou** in Greek, and **Bau** and **Bi** in all Northern languages, signifies a dwelling, a residence, or even a physical presence.

The second part is again composed: first, of the Greek suffix **os**, which does not belong to the essence of the word, and second, of the Near Eastern <note>original: *morgenländischen*</note> root word **Bel**, **Belos**, or **Belus**, which signifies light and the sun.

Byblos is thus not the Phoenician city of this name here, but the City of the Sun, the abode of light, the actual dwelling of the Most High. This name was therefore very well chosen to carry a specific meaning within this allegory.

## Article II.
### Concerning Uranus and Ge; likewise regarding their marriage and their children.

->§. 1.<-

Uranus succeeded his father and took his sister as his wife. We have just seen that this prince is the Heavens, and his sister is the Earth <note>The name Ge is the Greek word for Earth, often personified as the goddess Gaia</note>, therefore both are allegorical figures; consequently, their marriage itself is also nothing more than an allegory.

But one could only call the Heavens the husband of the Earth, and conversely call the Earth his wife, in the sense that one intended to signify the fertility that the Earth must owe to the Heavens.

From the Heavens come the rain and the warmth necessary for making the Earth fertile. Without the Heavens, she would be condemned to eternal barrenness; she would produce nothing; she would not be covered with greenery and flowers in the spring; she would bear no fruit in autumn; she would not be able to call herself the Mother of Mankind. It would be in vain to depict her with towers upon her head <note>This refers to the "mural crown," a common attribute in ancient art for goddesses like Cybele or Rhea, symbolizing their role as protectors of cities</note> and with a pomegranate in her hand <note>A symbol of fertility and many-seeded abundance</note>.

<meta>This page continues the author’s linguistic analysis of Phoenician mythological names. **Atlas** is derived from the root word <term>Thla <note>original Hebrew: תלא; meaning to hang, bear, or lift up</note></term>, which expresses bearing or bringing forth, and corresponds with the Greek <term>Tao <note>original: Ταω</note></term> or <term>Tlao <note>original: Τλαῶ; to bear or endure</note></term>.

**Dagon** means grain or corn in Hebrew and Phoenician <note>original: דגן (Dagan)</note>. The Greek translator himself agrees with this; for a little further down he says: **Dagon** is that which the Greeks call **Siton** <note>original: Σιτῶν; a Greek term for a provider of grain or a granary official</note>. This word, however, is a surname for **Ceres** <note>the Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter</note>, designating a field or a place with grain, and originates from the Middle Eastern word <term>Sede <note>original: שדה (Sadeh); meaning field or plain</note></term>, which means exactly the same thing.

**Bethyl** <note>referring to Betylos</note> or the **Virgin** might therefore be the surname of **Ge** <note>the personification of the Earth</note>, who brings forth grain through the assistance of **Uranus** <note>the Heavens or Sky</note> alone, without any cultivation.

Indeed, as one sees in **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman natural philosopher</note>, (1) the ancients called that earth where no plow had yet come "virgin earth." The same also happened among the Greeks, who give unworked earth the name **Parthenia**, which was also the name for unmarried women; and this word, of which no etymologist has yet known the origin, is very expressive. It consists of the root word **Par** or **Parth**, which means **fruit** (2), and from the negation **En** or **Ain**, and thus literally expresses something which has not yet given fruit.

The phrase "to plow the earth," on the other hand, was called a violation of the earth, a robbery of its virginity—expressions which are very common among the ancients.

In this way, humans can get by everywhere with a small number of root words, drawing the names of almost all existing things from within themselves. With a series of only a few expressions, they can portray a multitude of objects, all of which are connected to one another through their analogical resemblance to those in the sequence.

One will perhaps find a contradiction between the title of "Virgin" and "Spouse of Uranus" <note>the personification of the Sky or Heavens</note>; however, she is a virgin for the very reason that she has no husband other than Uranus. She is his spouse because she brings forth fruit only through him; yet she is also still a virgin because her womb has not yet been torn by iron and the plow.

The contradiction lay only in the expressions used, and this was precisely the beauty of this allegory.

From this double relationship, it also followed that **Isis** (or universal Nature, the Earth from which all things arise), **Cybele**, **Vesta**, **Ceres**, and the **Syrian Venus**, were considered virgins in an allegorical sense because they brought forth life without human assistance; but because they were also the mothers and nourishers of all creatures,

The former was called by the Latins the **virgin earth** (**virgin earth** <note>original French: "Terre Vierge"</note>), while the latter was called **Mother Earth** (**Mother Earth** <note>original French: "Terre-mère"</note>), or ***Terra*** <note>Latin: "Earth" or "land," often referring to the physical element.</note> and ***Tellus*** <note>Latin: The personified goddess of the earth or the productive soil.</note>.

This distinction we make between **Hertha** and **Adama** is no mere pretense of the commentators, who often attribute subtleties and beauties to their text of which the author never thought. **Moses** himself never confuses these two words with one another and always uses them only according to the sense he had attached to them.

As long as he intended only to recount that God had created the earth, he always made use of the word **Arth** or **Herth** <note>The author uses these forms to represent the Hebrew word "Eretz" (ארץ), linking it to Germanic roots like "Earth."</note>. Here, too, he used it in this very sense. But as soon as he wished to designate the earth cultivated by man, he made use of the word **Adama**.

Consequently, these two Hebrew names for the earth are not, as has been believed until now, equivalent; therefore, in this regard, the Hebrew dictionaries require correction.

The terrible infidelities against the Earth and her children were the irregularity of the harvests, back when humans had to live only on the products spontaneously brought forth by the Earth. This led to the scarcity and famine which always followed, laying in the grave those who could not alleviate their misery through hunting or fishing. The meager nature of these products—which, due to their mediocrity, sufficed for only a few people—meant that societies which had nothing more lived, as it were, only a vegetative life <note>original: "Pflanzenleben" — literally a "plant-life," referring to a state of mere survival or subsistence without intellectual or social growth</note>, and always formed only small, poor, and powerless little tribes.

If man had always had to live only on such products, he would have had almost no advantage over the animals. Placed in the necessity of always struggling with them for his food, he would have become only a much wilder animal, and would never have been able to call himself lord and king of the Earth. Everything—that abundance which is the source of nations and the strength of empires; the various arts <note>term: "Künste" — in this historical context, "arts" refers to all human skills and technologies, including agriculture, crafts, and industry, not just the fine arts</note> which enliven humanity and which multiply the comforts and pleasures of life by increasing the means to satisfy desires; that effort through which man educates himself, organizes himself, and rises toward the most sublime knowledge—

### § 2.
### The History of Saturn: Merely an Allegory of Agriculture.

Cronus or Saturn is an allegorical person, and this expressive name—so capable of creating a deception—serves at the same time to leave us with the impression of the most important and useful discovery of mankind, namely field-cultivation or agriculture <term>Ackerbau: the practice of farming, including soil cultivation and crop production</term>, under the guise of a foolish fable or a fairy tale.

What has been said so far prepares us for the discovery of this art; the scythe with which Ge or Hertha <note>Ge is the Greek personification of the Earth; Hertha (often associated with Nerthus) is an ancient Germanic earth goddess. The author treats them as equivalents.</note> arms her son announces to us its actual existence, and everything that follows is only a development and confirmation of this art.

But how could it have happened that the history of the invention of agriculture was not discovered earlier in the history of Saturn, since his name was so closely linked to the name of this art—which was placed in his century—and since he also bore all its symbols?

We should not be surprised at this at all, for these symbols subsequently served a different purpose.

The reaper Saturn was at the same time Time itself, which, armed with its scythe, harvested mankind. Indeed, there reigns in the ancient allegories such beauty and such fertility that they not only correspond perfectly and in the literal and strict sense with the main subject, but can also be applied—by analogy and extension—to other subordinate subjects which bear great similarities to the main subject.

One must never lose sight of this when studying antiquity and its allegories; that vacillation <note>original: "Wankelmuth," referring here to the inconsistent or indecisive nature of historical interpretations</note> in their explanation was merely a consequence of the ignorance of this usage. ### §. 3.
## Explanation of the various names of Saturn.

**Ilus** signifies **strength** or **power** in the Oriental languages <note>The author refers to Semitic linguistic roots, such as the Hebrew 'El' (God/Might).</note>. This word therefore became the name of the Deity who is exalted above all others (1); it became the name of the oak, which surpasses all other trees in strength and durability; it became the name of the husbandman <term>husbandman: an archaic term for a farmer or tiller of the soil</term>, who secures his livelihood through skill, and under whose hands wealth and power sprout forth; and finally, we shall also see this word, in this same sense, transform into the name of the founder of **Ilium** or **Troy**.

**Cronus** is an Oriental word which, in its literal sense, means a **horn** (*corne*), but figuratively signifies **power, strength, greatness, and dominion**. From this comes the name of the husbandman, for which no better name could have been chosen; he alone possesses reliable property and has riches which, because the earth is their foundation, are all the more lasting. Various leaders of powerful societies also bore this name, such as **Cranaus** among the Athenians and **Caranus** among the Macedonians. It is even very probable that the word **crown** (*couronne*), common to so many ancient and modern languages, flowed from this same source.

We should not be astonished that among the ancients, the **horn** (*corne*) became a symbol of power and dominion. The horn is a symbol of a plowing animal <note>The ox was the primary draft animal; its horns represented the physical force required to break the earth.</note>. States founded upon agriculture could find no

**Saturn** is also a very fitting name for the inventor of agriculture, whether one considers it as a Latin or an originally Oriental <note>In the 18th and 19th centuries, "Oriental" was a broad term for the cultures and languages of the Near East, including Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic.</note> word. As a Latin word—derived from *Sat* <note>The Latin root for "sowing" or "planting"</note>—**Saturn** signifies a father who promotes emergence, who produces; a husbandman; a fertile source of wealth.

As an Oriental word, it designates a king, a protector, one who covers or hides (1). Yet among these meanings, there is not a single one that does not suit **Saturn** or **Cronus**, or align with his allegorical history; he has also been made into a king, but only a king who must flee to **Latium** to secure himself against the undertakings of **Jupiter**.

Indeed, **Latium**—or the land where the husbandman hides his grain so that it may develop and bring forth new wealth—is the only secure <note>The catchword "Zufluchts-" suggests the next page begins with "Zufluchtsort," meaning "place of refuge."</note>

place of refuge for the husbandman against Jove, the King of the Air. <note>In this allegory, Jove (Jupiter) represents the stormy sky or atmosphere, while Saturn represents the earth-bound activity of planting.</note>

The word *Latium* was very well chosen for this allegory, for it comes from the root word *Lat*, which unites within itself the double meaning of the noun *Lat*—land or earth—and the verb *latere* <note>Latin: "to lie hidden"</note>—to hide.

One should not be surprised that the name of a husbandman was derived from this circumstance, which seems to be the most insignificant; however, it must appear strange to us that a person who does not have enough grain to live still deprives himself of a portion of it in order to hide it in the womb of the earth.

Yet even now, one sees the farmer, even in the most barren year, and no matter how much his harvest has suffered through floods and storms, deprive himself of what is necessary to sow his fields again and comfort himself with the hope of a happier year.

Saturn was also called *Kiun* <note>original: כיון; a name for Saturn mentioned in the Hebrew Bible</note> or *Khevan* by the Egyptians and the people of the Orient.

This name was also very well chosen, as it is a member of the same family to which the verb *Kun* <note>original: כון; to establish, prepare, or plant</note>—which means to plant or to assist in emergence—and the word *Kne* <note>original: כנה; a shoot, plant, or root</note>—which designates a germ, a plant, and a root—belong.

# Article IV.
## Saturn's Advisors.

Sanchuniathon <note>original: "Sanchoniaton"; a semi-legendary Phoenician author whose works survived through later Greek summaries</note> assembles Saturn's council from only two famous persons; namely from 

**Athena** or **Minerva**, from whom Athens takes its name, and from 

**Hermes**, the **Thoth** of the Egyptians, or **Mercury**.

Upon their advice, Saturn has a sword and an iron lance made; Hermes, who also serves as his secretary, meanwhile unites Saturn's friends to stand by him against the Heavens. In compensation, Saturn grants Egypt to the former and the Attic territory to the latter.

->§. 1.<-

### Athena.

It is not without reason that these two persons have been drawn into this allegory of Saturn; they were essentially necessary: Hermes and Athena are inseparable throughout all of mythology; from this also stem the ancient monuments where Hermes is depicted leaning upon Athena (1) or Minerva, and from this come the Herma-Athenae <term>composite statues consisting of a pillar topped with the heads or symbols of both Hermes and Athena, representing the union of eloquence and wisdom</term> or statues which represent the union of these two deities.

1) Among others, on a beautiful stone by Bellori <note>Giovanni Pietro Bellori (1613–1696), an influential Italian biographer and antiquarian</note> in the *Cabinet de la Chausse* <note>Michel Ange de la Chausse, a French scholar and collector in Rome</note>. Page 27.

Athena or Minerva presided over wisdom. The wise man does nothing without her assistance. Minerva, wisdom itself, could alone guide humanity to the invention of agriculture and to all the beneficial effects which sprang forth from it in abundance; we also encounter this goddess again in the history of Osiris, who plays the same role in Egypt as Cronus <note>The Titan who ruled during the Golden Age, often identified with Saturn</note> does in Phoenicia.

One can call Athena a daughter of Cronus or Saturn (viewed as a symbol of time), since only age and long experience grant wisdom.

<margin>a) Pausanias, *Description of the Athenian Territory*.</margin>
One must not be surprised to see the name of the city of Athens in this Oriental <note>original: "morgenländischen"; literally "of the morning land," referring to the Near East</note> narrative; it is also found in the history of Osiris. The word originates from the Orient and is very cleverly used for the decoration of an allegory, and simultaneously for the designation of Minerva as the protector of the Athenians. The names of their city, their first kings, and their deities, etc., were Oriental. When Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer</note> places a prince named Porphyrion in this region before Cecrops <note>The mythical founder and first king of Athens</note>, who built a temple to Venus Urania (a) <note>original: "Venus Urania"; the "Celestial Venus," representing heavenly or spiritual love</note> there, he does not contradict us; for Venus Urania is an Oriental deity, and Porphyrion is the translation of *Malach* <note>original: "Malach"; likely referring to the Semitic root *MLK*, meaning "king"</note>, a name for Oriental kings, just as the Phoenician Malchus translated his name into Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius"; a reference to the philosopher Porphyry (c. 234 – c. 305 AD). His name Malchus (king) was translated into the Greek Porphyrios, meaning "clothed in royal purple"</note>, the name under which he is solely known.

One is rather astonished to see a person, of whom one usually formed such great ideas, here only as a secretary or as a counselor to Saturn, and indeed as a giver of such inhuman advice. ### §. 3.
### On the tools that Saturn invented.

Through the counsel of Athena and Hermes <note>Athena (the goddess of wisdom) and Hermes (the messenger god, identified here with Mercury and Thoth) are presented as the intellectual architects behind the physical inventions of Saturn.</note>, Saturn invented two iron instruments, to which Philo <note>Philo of Byblos, a writer who claimed to translate the works of the Phoenician priest Sanchuniathon.</note>—following the English and French translators—gave the names of a sword and a spear.

However, they translated them this way only according to their own plan, and the reason for such unfaithful translations is usually this: that translators do not always perceive, or cannot perceive, the true sense of the author they intend to translate.

Just as the Greek word *harpé* <note>original: "harpé" (ἅρπη). In Greek mythology, this is the curved blade or sickle used by Cronus/Saturn to castrate Uranus, and later by Perseus to behead Medusa.</note> was rendered as "sword," so too could the second word have been translated as "ship" or "vessel," for it means that as well.

Yet, passing over all the specific objects to which these words have been applied, let us consider only the nature of the objects indicated by their meaning; through this, we will immediately be able to recognize the true sense in which we must understand them here.

The first word does not mean a sword or any kind of blade in general; rather, it is a blade in the shape of a scythe, for "scythe" <note>original: "Sense"</note> is its literal and proper meaning.

### §. 3.
### Of the Tools Which Saturn Invents.

Through the counsel of Athena and Hermes, Saturn invented two iron instruments, to which Philo <note>Likely Philo of Byblos, who wrote a Phoenician history based on the works of Sanchuniathon.</note>—according to the English and French translators—assigned the names of a **sword** and a **spear**.

They have, however, translated them only in accordance with their own plan <note>Meaning they translated them to fit a military or heroic narrative rather than a technical or agricultural one.</note>, and the reason for such unfaithful translations is mostly this: that translators do not always perceive, or cannot perceive, the true sense of the writer they wish to translate.

Yet, just as the Greek word *harpe* <note>original: *harpē* (ἅρπη). While it can mean a curved sword, in the context of Saturn/Kronos, it traditionally refers to the sickle used in the myth of Uranus.</note> has been given as "sword," so too could the second have been translated as a **ship** or vessel, for it means that as well.

But, bypassing all the specific objects to which these words have been applied, we wish only to consider the nature of those objects indicated by their meaning; through this, we will immediately be able to see the true sense in which we must take them here.

The first word does not signify a sword or a rapier in general; rather, it is a blade in the shape of a scythe, for "scythe" is its proper and literal meaning.

Therefore, it should have been translated as **scythe** and not **sword**.

If the second [term] signifies both a spear and a vessel, this arises from the word's extensive meaning, in that it evokes the idea of any object that cuts through or splits as it advances. Here, the two instruments with which Saturn arms himself are perfectly distinguished; for one cuts from the side and the other splits straight ahead.

But what kind of tools would a Saturn or a plowman carry, if not the **scythe** and the **plowshare**? **Scythe** is indeed also the proper meaning of the word *harpe* <note>original: *harpē* (ἅρπη). While it can mean a curved sword or sickle, the author argues here for its agricultural function.</note>, and in fact a kind of saber, just as the plowshare is also the root meaning of the word *Dory* <note>original: *dory* (δόρυ). The plowshare splits the earth in the same way that a ship furrows the surface of the water.

These words could therefore not have been better chosen; and if our modern translators have erred, they have erred no more than Philo <note>Referring to Philo of Byblos, the purported translator of Sanchuniathon’s Phoenician history.</note>, who has the Most High, or **Elyon** <note>original: *Eljon* (עֶלְיוֹן). This was also, in all ages, the origin of great houses, and even the origin of the patrician <note>original: *patriotischen*. People usually imagine their leaders as men without heritage or wealth, who united under Romulus to enrich themselves and form a state, and they view the title of **Patrician** as a mark of distinction invented by this prince. However, one is entirely mistaken in this; the patrician families owed their privileges only to their own arms—to those arms with which they had acquired property and through which, after previously clearing entirely desolate stretches of land, they had attained great wealth. Far from enclosing themselves within the walls of Romulus's city, they instead continued to spend their lives on their country estates, where they enjoyed the advantages of masters and rulers. Through this, they necessarily ruled over that mass of people who had no lands and who placed themselves under their protection in the city. This city had been built by these families so that it might become the center of their union and the place of their general assemblies; consequently, it also became a respectable sanctuary <note>original: *Freystatt*. # Article V.

## On the Wives of Cronus.

> "Meanwhile," says our author, "Uranus,
> "who was constantly in flight, sent his
> "daughter Astarte against Cronus, along with her two sisters Rhea and
> "Dione, so that they might destroy him through some trickery;
> "but Cronus took them prisoner and married them.
> "Upon receiving news of this, Uranus sent Eimarmene <note>A personification of fate or destiny.</note> and Hora <note>A personification of a season or a specific time.</note> against him
> "with an army; but Cronus wins their love as well, and
> "keeps them with him also."

Here, therefore, Cronus marries five wives, all of whom come to him from Uranus. These must necessarily be five allegorical persons, a fact of which we shall immediately convince ourselves.

### §. 1.

### Rhea and her seven sons.

Rhea, who is named after Astarte in Sanchuniathon <note>A Phoenician author whose historical-mythological works are preserved through fragments in later Greek writings.</note>, is nevertheless the most prominent wife of Saturn <note>The Roman equivalent of the Greek Cronus.</note>, who gives him seven sons, while he receives only daughters from Astarte. According to Greek mythology <note>original: *Fabellehre*.</note>, Rhea is not only his wife, but he has no others besides her. This is also the case in Egyptian mythology, according to Plutarch's <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46–119 AD).</note> report. The other wives attributed to him by the Phoenicians are therefore so only in a

...more extensive sense, and thus all the more allegorical. This distinction will not be without utility.

Mythologists have very correctly noted that Rhea was the Earth, and that she was more than one generation younger than Ge <note>original: *Ge*; the Greek personification of the primal Earth.</note>, the mother of Saturn. Here we have the Earth personified twice: first under the name Ge as the mother of Saturn, and later also under the name Rhea as his wife. From where does this double usage, this strange confusion, arise? One asks the mythologists in vain; but through our principles, everything is clarified in the simplest and most satisfying way.

Ge, the wife of Uranus and mother of Saturn, is, as we already know, the Earth as she came from the hands of nature, bringing forth her fruits by herself without any cultivation. Rhea, the wife of Saturn, will therefore be the cultivated Earth, improved by man, which thereby becomes his own and, in a sense, his spouse, whom he adorns, never leaves, and fertilizes annually.

Similarly, Moses <note>original: *Moyses*.</note>, after having said (as we already know) that Hertha <note>Likely used here to refer to the Earth in a general sense, though "Hertha" or "Nerthus" is specifically a Germanic earth goddess.</note> was formed by the deity, adds: Noah became the husband of the *Adama* <note>original: *Adama*; the Hebrew word for ground or soil.</note>, if we translate this phrase literally or in the allegorical sense it offers. In fact, it only expresses that he became a man of the earth, or a husbandman <note>original: *Ackersmann*; literally a man of the fields or a farmer.</note>.

Among the Romans as well we find this very same thing; they called the uncultivated earth *Terra* and the cultivated earth *Tellus*. These words derive from two root words that correspond to these different meanings.

## Of the Seven Sons of Rhea.

She bore **Cronus** <note>In Greek mythology, the leader of the first generation of Titans; the author treats Cronus and Saturn as interchangeable figures representing time or agricultural cycles.</note> seven sons, the youngest of whom was sanctified immediately upon his birth. Until now, it has not been possible to discover who these seven sons of Rhea were, and particularly not who the one was that was sanctified at birth; however, as soon as one pays attention to the use of allegorical numbers—or those made sacred through symbolic language—this can be discovered at once.

These seven sons are the seven suns or days of the week; they are the sons of Saturn and Rhea. They were arranged according to the needs of agriculture: the first six days are the working days, and the seventh is the day of rest <note>The Sabbath</note>, which was sanctified immediately after its "birth." We shall soon see how they are contrasted with the seven daughters of **Astarte** <note>A major Levantine goddess associated with fertility and war, often linked with the planet Venus.</note> and Saturn.

Everything here is so bright and clear that no further explanation is required; moreover, it perfectly accords with the spirit of antiquity, which always regarded the number seven as pre-eminently sacred.

We do not overlook the fact that the name "Seven" <note>The author suggests a linguistic link between the word for the number and the concept of completion or holiness, common in ancient Near Eastern etymology.</note> originates from the fact that it was sanctified, and with it this specific number was complete, and because one rested on the seventh day; for this very root had been chosen to express all gradations. These allegories of the seventh son of Saturn, who was sanctified immediately upon his birth, present us with a very remarkable fact; namely, that the seventh day was observed not only by the Hebrews, but also by the Phoenicians themselves. Consequently, such a practice must have been common even before Moses, already in the times of the ancient patriarchs, and therefore must have been shared among various <term>Oriental: a historical term used here to refer to the cultures of the Near East or Levant</term> nations, as had already been suspected. Thus, Moses only renewed this institution among the Hebrews by reintroducing this festival for purposes which they viewed from an entirely unique perspective.

The seventh day of the week was also already held sacred by the Chinese in the most ancient times:
> "The ancient kings," they say (1), such as Chin-nong <note>A legendary ruler of China, also known as Shennong</note>, a successor of Fohi <note>Fu Xi, the first of the Three Sovereigns of ancient China</note>, "had the house doors closed on the seventh day, which was called the Great Day; on this day all business was suspended, and the courts pronounced no judgment."

They call this the old calendar.

The seventh day was also sacred to the Arabs long before Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, in honor of Venus Uriana. This compelled that legislator, who could not destroy this custom or did not wish to abolish it, merely to purify it by dedicating this day—Friday <note>original: "Freytag (Vendredi)"</note>—to the worship of the Supreme Deity.

Saint Augustine (2) has preserved for us a passage from Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> concerning Rhea <note>The mother of the gods in Greek mythology, often associated with Saturn</note>, which completely agrees with our assertions stated above, and which we therefore must not overlook.

## Astarte and Her Seven Daughters.

This daughter of *Uranus* <note>The Greek personification of the sky</note> plays a very significant role here. Various passages also speak of her, characterizing her and making recognizable the allegorical essence that was intended to be portrayed through her.

1) She is the eldest daughter of *Uranus*.
2) She bears *Saturn* seven daughters.
3) She has the epithet "the Great."
4) With the consent of *Saturn*, she rules over the land.
5) As a sign of her sovereignty, she places a bull's head upon her head.
6) On her journey through the world, she finds a star that had just fallen from the heavens; she kills it <note>The OCR reads 'tödtet' (kills), though in the original myth of Sanchuniathon, Astarte is said to have 'consecrated' (German: 'weihet') the fallen star in Tyre</note> and dedicates it at *Tyre*.
7) Although she is a daughter of *Uranus*, she is nevertheless not called the sister of *Cronus*.
8) The *Phoenicians* consider her—as the translator adds—to be the same person as *Aphrodite* <note>The Greek goddess of love; the ancients frequently identified her with the Phoenician Astarte</note>.

Her name does not derive from *Astaroth* (flock of sheep), as *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century biblical scholar known for his work on sacred geography</note> thought, being led astray by the error of the preceding argument.

## §. 2.

### Astarte and her seven daughters.

This daughter of <term>Uranus</term> <note>The personification of the sky</note> plays a very significant role here. Various passages also speak of her, characterizing her and making recognizable the allegorical nature that the authors intended to depict through her.

1) She is the eldest daughter of <term>Uranus</term>.
2) She bore <term>Saturn</term> <note>The Roman name for Cronus, the Titan of time</note> seven daughters.
3) She bears the epithet **the Great**.
4) With <term>Saturn’s</term> consent, she governs the land.
5) As a sign of her sovereignty, she places a bull’s head upon her own head <note>Likely an allegory for the crescent moon resembling horns</note>.
6) During her journey through the world, she finds a star that had just fallen from heaven; she kills it <note>original: "tödtet ihn"; in many versions of this Phoenician myth, she is said to have "consecrated" the fallen star/meteorite</note> and dedicates it at <term>Tyre</term> <note>A major Phoenician port city</note>.
7) Although she is a daughter of <term>Uranus</term>, she is nevertheless not called the sister of <term>Cronus</term>.
8) The Phoenicians consider her, the translator adds, to be the same person as <term>Aphrodite</term> <note>The Greek goddess of love and beauty</note>.

#### Regarding the first seven characteristics.

Astarte is not <term>Rachel</term> <note>The biblical matriarch</note>, as Mr. <term>Fourmont</term> <note>Étienne Fourmont (1683–1745), a French scholar who attempted to link Greek myths to Hebrew patriarchs</note> believed. Her name does not derive from <term>Astaroth</term> (meaning "flock of sheep") <note>original: "Schaafheerde"; a reference to the Hebrew word 'ashtarot</note>, as <term>Bochart</term> <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> thought, a conclusion he was led to by the error of the aforementioned scholar.
