It is composed of two <term>Oriental</term> <note>A historical term used here to refer to ancient Near Eastern languages like Persian and Arabic</note> words: first, from **Star** or **Astar**, which means star (<note>original: "Astre"</note>), and is a Persian, Indian, Arabic, and Latin word, etc., originating from the root **St**, meaning immovable or everlasting; and second, from **The**, which means perfect and has become the name of God in many languages.

This name, therefore, designates a goddess of the stars; and as such, <term>Astarte</term> <note>A major Phoenician goddess often identified with the Moon or Venus</note> is indeed the Queen of Heaven or the Moon. She is the eldest daughter of <term>Uranus</term> <note>The personification of the Sky</note> because she rules over the celestial bodies and is their queen.

She bears the epithet "the Great" because she is the largest celestial body that shines for us at night, and to which one attributes boundless power over nature.

She gives <term>Cronus</term> <note>The Titan associated with Time</note> seven daughters, who were called **Titanides**, **Artemides**, or **Dianas**. But who are these seven daughters, set in opposition to the seven sons of <term>Rhea</term> <note>The mother of the Olympian gods</note>, if they are not the seven moons <note>Likely referring to the phases of the moon</note> or the seven nights of the week? All these names also signify this in the original language from which they have come down to us through the Greeks and Romans.

**Titan** means "light of the earth" or "venerable light" in the original language.

**Artemis**, the only Greek name for <term>Diana</term> <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon</note>, is composed of **Ar** or **Art** (earth), **Tem** (law or rule—from which <term>Themis</term>, the goddess of justice, was derived), and **Is** (time). Thus, Artemis signifies such a,

*Diana* is derived from the root word *Di*, meaning "day"; from this also comes the French expression *to beat the Diana* <note>original: "battre la Diane," a military drum call or signal sounded at daybreak</note>, used to indicate the waking of the army at the break of day—a turn of phrase that was already in use during the reign of the House of *Valois* <note>A royal house of France that ruled from 1328 to 1589</note>.

This goddess was therefore the ruler of heaven and earth in the <term>Orient</term> <note>A historical term for the lands of the Near East, such as Phoenicia and Mesopotamia</note>, and her symbols were derived from this role.

Likewise, in the story of *Osiris* <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and fertility</note>, *Mercury* <note>The author likely identifies the Egyptian god Thoth with the Roman Mercury</note> places the same sign of sovereignty upon the head of *Isis* instead of a crown.

This Queen of the Heavens is also represented by the half-moon in all our calendars.

1) This derivation is all the more certain because it leaves the two original syllables *Ar* and *Tem*, from which this name is composed, intact, and at the same time leads to an essential idea. She is a daughter of Uranus <note>The personification of the sky in Greek mythology</note>, yet it is not said that she is a sister of Cronus <note>The leader of the first generation of Titans; the author suggests this family tree is symbolic rather than literal</note>: This expression, being too far removed from the truth, was only suited to create an error, and it was therefore entirely bypassed; a new proof that here only an allegory is to be sought.

## Of the last among the eight characteristics of Astarte.

But what does the last characteristic of Astarte signify—that star which falls from heaven and which she kills? An expression so foolish in appearance, which has puzzled all commentators. It is an error, said Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French scholar known for his vast knowledge of ancient geography and biblical animals</note>: according to him, that which Astarte kills and hallows in Tyre <note>An ancient and powerful Phoenician city-state</note> is an eagle.

But would it have been something so remarkable if Astarte had killed an eagle and sacrificed it upon the altars at Tyre; and would this event have deserved to be handed down to posterity? It may well be that the Tyrians, who carried an eagle in their coat of arms, had devised a similar origin for this custom out of jest, but that is certainly not the subject here. The Phoenician writer did not place the word "star" here instead of "eagle"; here, the discussion is reliably about heavenly stars, and that is not at all surprising since he is speaking of the moon. this celestial body truly kills the stars, because they vanish before its radiance; this expression is the specific word by which their disappearance is indicated; the Western word has no other meaning; *to fall or perish* <note>original Latin: 'accidere'</note> means to kill, and the *Occident* <note>The West, where the sun sets</note> refers to the being, or the time, which kills, because it is there that the sun and all the stars disappear. But how does the moon kill the stars? Our writer instructs us on this through the word *Tyr*, which here is not the name of the famous city *Tyre*, but an Oriental word that means radiance, glow, or the moonlight before which all stars are extinguished; however, because this word was also used to designate *Tyre* and Syria—צור *Syr* or *Tsyr* <note>original Hebrew: צור, the root for the city of Tyre, meaning a rock or sharp edge</note>—this gave rise to the error, into which one could all too easily fall if one did not consider the text as an allegory.

Now it is no longer surprising when the translator says that the star, after its death, was consecrated or dedicated to *Tyr*; for the word which means to dedicate to a good use <note>original French: 'consacrer à un bon usage'</note> also means to dedicate to an evil use <note>original French: 'consacrer à un usage mauvais'</note>, or to darken and ruin. Could one express it any better than: *Astarte*, in her heavenly course, compelled the stars darkened by her radiance to disappear?

From the stories of *Mercury* and *Orion*, we shall see that this expression "to kill" has also been used in other allegories, and indeed in this same sense as here.

## Cities which take their name from Astarte.

We further note that the name Astarte dates back to the greyest antiquity. Even in the time of Abraham, one sees cities of this name among the Canaanites. ### §. 3.

The third wife, according to our author, was **Dione**, another daughter of Uranus, who in Greek mythology married Jupiter and became the mother of Venus, or Love; consequently, an allegorical marriage lies hidden here as well. **Dione** originates from an Eastern word <note>original: "morgenländischen Worte"; the author is likely attempting to link the Greek name Dione to a Semitic root meaning abundance or sufficiency.</note> which signifies "Abundance." Abundance is, in truth, a daughter of Heaven, a wife of Saturn, and a mother of Venus.

She is a daughter of Heaven because without its assistance there can be no harvest; she is a wife of Saturn <note>Saturn was the Roman god of agriculture and time, often identified with the Greek Cronus.</note> because the husbandman <term>husbandman: a farmer or person who cultivates the land</term>, by virtue of his labor, lives alongside her; and finally, she is called a mother of Venus and of Love because marriages cannot be happy, nor can people even think of them, until they live in a pleasant and decent abundance and are in a position to support a family.

### §. 4.

#### Eimarmene and Hora.

**Cronus** also brings **Eimarmene** and **Hora** to his side, who are just as much allegorical personae as the previous figures; they signify **Fortune** and **Beauty** <note>In Greek, *Eimarmene* usually refers to destiny or fate, while *Hora* can refer to a specific time, a season, or the personification of beauty and order.</note>. One can even translate the latter word as **Seasons**.

The ruler of a land does indeed secure his fortune; he enriches himself and makes himself great and distinguished through the foodstuffs he produces and through the goods whose growth he continually helps to promote.

The seasons always accompany him, for he must arrange all his labors according to the seasons, which support and protect his work.

# Article VI.

## Saturn’s Children.

**B**esides the seven Titanesses or Artemises, and the seven sons whom *Saturn* had by *Rhea*, our author attributes many other children to him, who are likewise allegorical and perfectly suited to the theme of agriculture.

### 1) Three sons, whom Saturn had in Peraea.

> ”He had three sons in *Peraea*; one was named, like
> ”himself, *Cronus*, the second *Belus*, and the third *Apollo*.”

Critics have been completely bewildered by this genealogy and this region. Even the undaunted *Fourmont* <note>Claude Fourmont (1690–1745) was a French scholar known for his attempts to reconcile ancient mythology with biblical history.</note> felt some trepidation toward it; consequently, after admitting he had cause for anxiety here, he sought to extricate himself from the embarrassment by asserting that *Apollo* is *Horus*, and that *Horus* is the *Korah* <note>original: "Core des Moyses"; likely referring to the biblical figure Korah from the Book of Numbers.</note> of *Moses*. As for the brothers, he passes over them in silence. We will therefore make an attempt to see if a better explanation can be provided.

*Peraea* in the Eastern language פרה <note>original: "פרה" (parah); a Hebrew root meaning to bear fruit or be fruitful.</note> signifies growth, production, and fertility. It is the true land of the husbandman <term>husbandman: a farmer or person who cultivates the land</term>; a fact which *Blackwell* <note>Thomas Blackwell (1701–1757) was a Scottish scholar who wrote "Letters Concerning Mythology."</note> recognized very well in his letters on mythology, and he therefore explains *Peraea* as meaning "Fertility."

It is likewise certain that *Bel* and *Apollo*, who belong among the sons of *Saturn*, refer to the sun...

## 2) Sadid.

If any trait in Saturn’s history suggests that it is merely an allegorical fabric, it was his cruel behavior toward his brother, his father, and his children. Here we have one whom he himself kills: "Cronus," says the narrator, "slays his son **Sadid** with his own iron." <note>original: "Eisen" (iron); this refers to the sickle or scythe, the traditional implement of Saturn/Cronus, used here as an allegory for harvesting or tilling.</note>

This name fits quite well with that of Saturn, and with the Eastern words **Sade**, meaning a field, and **Sadad**, meaning to harrow <term>harrow: an agricultural tool used to break up clods of earth and smooth the soil</term>, or to tear the clods of earth apart.

### 3) Monogenes or his Only One.

Soon after and during a time of famine and mortality, he sacrifices his only son to his father Uranus.

What a contradiction if everything is taken historically! We have just counted twenty sons of Saturn, and now there is talk of only one single son again. Considered as history, this narrative is pure nonsense; but as an allegory, it is ingenious.

Who then is this only son of the husbandman, this son whom he sacrifices at a time of famine and mortality?

Without a doubt, it is his harvest. This is unique, as one never has more than one at a time; it is a child of the husbandman, the spouse of Rhea, because it would not exist without him; it is the fruit of his diligence, over whose childhood he has watched with the greatest care. Meanwhile, in a time of famine, he cuts the life-thread of his son without pity, and this is also entirely true, since Saturn and all other people would have to die of hunger without the new harvest, because the previous harvest has already been consumed. This our writer calls at the same time a circumcision <note>original: "Beschneidung"; the author likely draws a parallel between the ritual of circumcision and the "cutting" or harvesting of the grain.</note>, since

### 4) M u t h.

Saturn's history is like the seven-headed Hydra; for with the removal of one difficulty, a thousand new ones always arise. Here is yet another son of Saturn—and indeed he is at least the twenty-first—but he is dead, and his father has sanctified him after his death. What an incomprehensible father! Toward his dead children he is full of tenderness, and toward those still living he is unjust and cruel. What are we to do with this one here? He is called Muth, we are told, and *Muth* <note>original: "מות"; in Phoenician and Hebrew, this term signifies death.</note> signifies death in the Phoenician language; but death was no child of Saturn, and what does it mean to "sanctify death after his death"?

There is thus also an ambiguity here in the expressions. Muth is the threshed, ground grain that has been transformed into flour; from this comes the name Tham-Muz <note>Tham-Muz: more commonly known as Tammuz, a deity associated with the cycle of life, death, and the rebirth of vegetation.</note>, under which the festival of Adonis was celebrated, and the month that followed the harvest, in which this festival was held, was also named the same. Muth was therefore only sanctified after his death because one could not eat the grain or offer it to the gods as cakes until it no longer existed as grain, but had been broken, ground, kneaded, and transformed into an entirely new form.

(1) But is it not truly the most perfect fruit of all? Nature does indeed produce wondrous fruits; but to create those that surpass all others, she required the arm of man; only under his hands and through his labor does she allow the most useful and pleasant forms to sprout forth.

Certain Carthaginian deities also bore the name **Abaddir**, as Saint **Augustine** (2) reports, and their priests were called **Euc-caddiren**.

The stone which **Saturn** took instead of **Jove** <note>Jove is another name for Jupiter. In Greek and Roman myth, Saturn/Cronus swallowed a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, believing it was his son Jupiter, who was thus saved.</note>, and which was called a **Betyl** <note>term: Betyl; from the Phoenician/Hebrew "Bethel" (House of God). One must not wonder, however, that the stones which **Saturn** took for an excellent meal were given the name **Abaddir** (excellent fruit); nor that deities who undoubtedly presided over the products of the earth, and who were worshipped at **Carthage**, were called **Abaddirs**.

### 5) Persephone.

This is the name of a daughter of Saturn. According to our author, she stands as a maiden, which is also true in the Pythagorean sense <note>The Pythagoreans often used "virginity" to describe certain numbers or cosmic principles that remained pure or indivisible within their mathematical-philosophical system.</note>.

Persephone is an Oriental <note>In this historical context, "Oriental" refers to the Near East, specifically Phoenician, Hebrew, or Syrian origins.</note> name which, according to the opinion of all experts in Oriental languages, means *hidden fruit*. It is, therefore, the seed—the grain—which the farmer encloses in the earth like his own child, so that it might bring forth new fruit.

Scholars also agree that the Latins knew Persephone by the name **Proserpine**; and this daughter of **Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter.</note>, whom **Pluto** had abducted while she was amusing herself by picking flowers, was also—in the opinion of the philosophers of antiquity—the preserved power of plants, or that specific force by which they take firm root in the womb of the earth and develop; meanwhile, **Pluto** represents the winter sun. Thus, when the grain is buried in the earth, **Proserpine** truly appears to be dead, without life, having descended into **Tartarus** <note>term: Tartarus; in Greek mythology, a deep abyss used as a dungeon for the Titans and the wicked; here used as a metaphor for the cold, dark soil where the seed lies dormant.</note>, and to have been carried off by **Pluto**.

For this very reason, the festival of the abduction of **Proserpine** was celebrated on the second of October; it appears, as the ancients also clearly recognized, to be a sowing festival. Therefore, the philosopher **Sallust** <note>Likely referring to Sallustius, a 4th-century Neoplatonist who wrote "On the Gods and the World," which provides allegorical interpretations of myths.</note> contrasts it with the pleasant festivals held at the time of the spring equinox. These indicated **Proserpine’s** return and the expulsion of winter.

It is indeed true that, even according to **Sallust**, the festival of **Proserpine** in October was simultaneously the festival of the descent of spirits into **Tartarus**; however, this only proves that along with the physical reason for this festival, a...

...connected it with a completely moral one. In truth, because of their similarity, both merged very naturally with one another; and just as the grain hidden in the earth then became the symbol of the bodies buried therein, so too did the new sprouting of this grain become a hopeful omen of a future life for the deceased.

Because of this connection between Persephone or Proserpina and the Husbandman or Saturn, the Romans also called her—as the Proconsul Capella reports (1)—**Centessima** <note>original: "Centessima"; Latin for "the hundredfold."</note>, she who gives back a hundredfold. This is a name which, according to Fulgentius <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Latin writer of late antiquity known for allegorical interpretations of mythology.</note>, is the literal translation of her Greek name **Hecate**, which comes from the word <term>hekaton</term> <note>original: Εκατον</note>, meaning *hundred*; and which, he continues, was rightly given to her because among various ancient peoples, the sown grain already bore hundredfold fruits.

# Article VII.

## On the Supposed Brothers of Saturn: Betyl, Dagon, and Atlas.

It is remarkable that all the words which Philo <note>Philo of Byblos, who claimed to translate the Phoenician history of Sanchuniathon.</note> mistook for so many brothers of Saturn or Ilus, actually fit this allegorical work; however, this also clearly proves that he either did not understand their meaning, or pretended not to understand it.

### I) On the Betyls.

The term **Betyls** <note>original: "Betylen"</note>, which means "animated stones," would be highly absurd if one were to take it literally; it is, however, a figurative expression, the development of which we shall see shortly.

These **Betyls** are indeed stones, and in this narrative, they are likely spoken of only as an allusion to the supposed son of Uranus, **Betyl**, who was mentioned above and who seems to be summoned once more. For Uranus is presented both as their inventor and as the father of the supposed Betyl.

Nevertheless, these words are quite different. The one appearing earlier was **Betyl**, and these stones are **Baitylen**. Thus, upon close observation of the orthography of Eastern <note>original: "morgenländischer"; literally "morning-land," a common historical German term for the Orient or the Near East.</note> words, one discovers a great difference. In the first word, **Betyl** or **Betul**, which...

The **Betyls** <note>original: "Betylen"</note> were thus stones dedicated to divine service, intended to preserve the memory of remarkable events in which the protection of the gods was especially taken into consideration.

These stones represented the gods themselves; they were their vivid likeness, and therefore literally **animated** or **living stones**. Under this name, statues were actually known to the ancients. The Greeks called them **animated images** <note>original: "Eikones empsykhoi"</note>. Virgil lets the bronze breathe and gives life to the marble when he sings:

Philo therefore did not invent the word **Betyl**. The Phoenicians used this expression to designate statues and sacred stones. In the works of **Photius** (2), **Asclepiades** stated that when he was on Mount Lebanon near **Heliopolis** <note>meaning "City of the Sun," the ancient name for Baalbek</note>, he had seen a great number of Betyls there; he also relates many wonderful things about them, and **Isidore** saw such things after him as well.

Whatever the cause of this similarity may be, it remains very strange.

### 3) **Atlas**.

**Saturn**, on the advice of **Mercury**, throws his brother **Atlas** into a pit because of a mere suspicion and buries him there.

Are these the heroes of <term>paganism</term> <note>The author uses this term to refer to the ancient polytheistic religions of Greece and Rome</note>, of whom such crimes are told as coldly as if one were speaking of the greatest virtues! For a mere suspicion, the reason for which one does not even care to state, one brother is said to have buried another alive! This is supposed to have happened on the advice of his wisest counselor; and yet one is still supposed to take this for actual history! One is expected to wish it were true, even though those who tell such stories themselves say that everything has been turned into allegories! That is to adopt a completely groundless and absurd system without any reflection.

<meta>This page continues the rationalist interpretation of Greek and Near Eastern mythology, specifically focusing on the figure of Atlas. The previous page established that the "burial" of Atlas was not a literal execution but a symbolic representation of agricultural practices.</meta>

Atlas is not a literal brother of Saturn; no living being or human person was actually buried in a deep pit by **Mercury**. Instead, these stories refer to matters related to agriculture. The name **Atla** <note>The author is likely connecting the name to Phoenician or Hebrew roots related to "bearing" or "carrying," a common practice in 18th-century mythography</note> means to produce or to bear, as we already know. If he is called a brother of Saturn, it is only in an allegorical <note>German: *räthselhaften*, literally "riddling" or "enigmatic"</note> sense. Such phrasing was intended to lead the listener astray—unless they could immediately perceive that grain is only called a "brother" of Saturn because both owe their existence to the Earth.

Or more accurately, the epithet "Brother of Saturn" was quite inappropriately given to Atlas, as well as to **Betyl** and **Dagon** <note>Dagon was a major Levantine deity, often associated by early scholars with either fish or grain (Hebrew: *dagan*); Betyl refers to *baetylus*, sacred stones often associated with the divine in the ancient Near East</note>.

**Atlas** does not represent sown grain—which is always a small amount—but rather the harvested crop and a great quantity of corn, which many ancient and modern peoples lay down in well-covered pits for preservation.

In the early stages of agriculture, it was necessary to handle grain in this manner, as the conveniences later developed for storing and protecting grain against frost and other harsh weather did not yet exist.

Atlas was therefore said to be "buried" due to a "suspicion"; namely, it was suspected <note>The author is playing on the mythological claim that Mercury buried Atlas out of suspicion/distrust, reinterpreting "suspicion" as the "presumption" or "technical requirement" for keeping grain fresh</note> that the grain could not be preserved in any other way than by this method of storage.

This custom still prevails among the Arabs and African Moors. "I have," says **Shaw** (1) <note>Thomas Shaw (1694–1751), an English traveler and clergyman whose work *Travels or Observations relating to several parts of Barbary and the Levant* was a standard reference for North African customs</note>, "seen 200 to 300 subterranean caves side by side, which they call *Mattamores* <note>original: "Mattamores"; from the Arabic *matmura*, referring to an underground silo or granary</note>, and the smallest

## Concerning the concubine of Uranus, whom Cronus or Saturn took prisoner: she was pregnant and gave birth to Demaroon.

If any part of this history seems entirely contrary to the perspective from which we view it, and appears quite impossible to explain allegorically, it is certainly this one; all the more so because our writer—who identifies this concubine of Uranus, captured by Cronus <note>In Phoenician mythology, Cronus (Saturn) captures a concubine of his father Uranus and gives her to Dagon</note>—says nothing further about the son that might shed light on the mother, but merely reports that he was named **Demaroon**. In the meantime, the explanation of these two allegorical characters will require little effort, yet will form a beautiful whole with our previously stated assertions.

The farmer or husbandman requires, besides the earth, another less fertile element for his labors, without which the earth would produce nothing. This element is **water**, which undoubtedly promotes the abundance and beauty of earthly products. Among all waters, however, the water from the **heavens**—or in allegorical language, the **water of Uranus**—is the most fertile and beneficial for plants. However, this element is not the primary wife of Uranus; rather, it is **Ge** <note>The Greek word for Earth; Gaea</note> whom he fertilizes, and consequently, in this same allegorical style of writing, water is merely his concubine. We shall soon see how expressively the ancients indicated the fertilizing power of water and under what symbol they represented it. Therefore, when Moses <note>original: "Moyses"</note> [describes] the fertility of the virgin...

This water is collected by the **husbandman** or **Cronus** <note>In this context, Cronus represents the archetypal farmer or the principle of time and agriculture</note> in water reservoirs, from which he distributes it by means of canals to all his lands; however, the Oriental word that expresses "canals" is almost identical to the word for "concubine," for the one is called *Peleguth* <note>original: פלגות Peleguth, likely referring to the Hebrew word for divisions or streams</note> and the other *Pellegesh* <note>original: פילגש Pellegesh, the Hebrew term for a concubine or secondary wife</note>. Perhaps there was a play on the similarity of these two words, although this is not at all necessary for our explanation.

But who is **Demaroon**, the son of this concubine? He is certainly the fertility that results from irrigation and rain, for his name, composed of the root words *De* and *Mar*, expresses exactly this. The Hebrew *Di* <note>original: די Di</note> or *Dei* undoubtedly means abundance, and the other can indicate a "lord" or the "slope of a mountain." These two latter meanings evoke the shared concept of great elevation or dominion. Whether one chooses one sense or the other, this name will always mean the "head" or the "source of abundance," or the "abundance of the hills"; for the mountains are the husbandman’s best water reservoirs.

He is the father of **Melicertes**, an epithet of **Hercules** in the East. Melicertes, however, signifies a "lord of the city," and rightly so: for are cities and empires anything other than the daughters of abundance?

## Section 3.
# Saturn’s Gods.

Saturn, or Cronus, was not the god of the land; rather, he himself worshiped others. "At the same time," says our writer <note>Likely referring to Sanchuniathon, the purported Phoenician author whose work was preserved by Eusebius.</note>, "Adod, the king of the gods, ruled the land along with Astarte and Jov Demaroon."

We already know that Astarte was the moon or the Egyptian Isis.

Who, then, is Adod? He is none other than the one and only sun, which is also what this name means in the Oriental language <note>The name Adad or Hadad is an ancient Semitic word for the storm or sun god.</note>.

One must wonder how anyone could doubt this for even a moment and see in him Ham, Cush, Nimrod, or others <note>The author is criticizing "Euhemerism," the practice of interpreting mythological gods as deified historical people from the Bible.</note>. Meanwhile, Fourmont (1) said he was a Syrian god—certainly a great favor! <note>Étienne Fourmont (1683–1745) was a French scholar of oriental languages; the author's tone here is slightly sarcastic.</note>

Who else but the sun <note>original: "le soleil"</note>, the king of the gods or stars, the Belus of the Chaldeans; who else but the moon <note>original: "la lune"</note>, or Belisame and Astarte, the Queen of Heaven; who else but these stars—whose orbits form the years, and according to whose will the husbandman must arrange all his labors if they are to be applied at the right time and accompanied by success—rule the land or the kingdom of the husbandman, or Saturn? But above all is still Jov Demaroon, and this too is true. Jov is the most sublime god, the Jovis <note>Jupiter</note> of the Latins, the Jehovah of the Hebrews; he is preeminently the Being, the Only One, who

This is a truth with which people of all eras were permeated, and which the author of these fragments also recognized. This fragment is therefore not the catechism of an atheist—an accusation that arose only because the text was not understood—but rather it is the catechism of a man entirely filled with respect and admiration for agriculture and with gratitude toward the deity who taught this art to humanity and, through it, spread blessings over their labors.

These scholars’ systems necessarily led them toward daring explanations; however, had they consulted antiquity more than the similarities to which their imaginations led them, they would certainly have seen just how far their imagination had led them astray.

To avoid being guilty of the same error, let us see what the ancients say about these figures. Through such a comparison, we must also learn about those things which our author only passes over briefly—assuming them to be well-known and therefore not worth developing further.

### 1) S y d y k .

Sydyk and the Cabiri <note>The Cabiri were a group of mysterious deities or "Great Gods" worshipped in ancient Greek and Phoenician mystery cults, often associated with protection at sea and metallurgy.</note> are entirely Phoenician or Oriental names. The same is also said to be the case with the name Asclepius or Aesculapius <note>The ancient god of medicine and healing.</note>, with the only difference being that the first two are still actually found in Oriental languages, while the latter can also be viewed as a name composed of two other languages.

Philo <note>Philo of Byblos, who claimed to have translated the Phoenician history of Sanchuniathon into Greek.</note> has translated the name Sydyk very well as **the Just** <note>original: "δίκαιος" (Dikaios).</note>. However, this person is neither Shem nor the father of Caleb, but rather the father of the Cabiri.

The latter word means "the Great" or "the Mighty," and is entirely synonymous with the Greek name of the Dioscuri <note>Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Zeus.</note> or "Sons of Jove"—that is, sons of the highest god.

### 2) Cabiri.

The seven Cabiri <note>Ancient deities of a mystery cult, often associated with metallurgy and protection at sea, but here interpreted as planetary spirits.</note>, sons of Sydyk or the highest God, are now nothing other than the seven planets, or the seven spirits <note>original: "Genien"</note> ruling over the planets, who govern the universe by means of them.

They are the sons of Sydyk, or the Just One, because he created them for their annual revolutions when he assembled the universe over which these heavenly spheres command.

### 2) Cabiri.

The seven **Cabiri**, sons of **Sydyk** or the supreme god, are now revealed to be nothing other than the seven planets, or the seven **genii** <note>Guardian spirits or divine intelligences.</note> ruling over the planets, who govern the universe by means of these celestial bodies.

Consequently, one was bound to be led astray, as the facts could not be reconciled at all with this unfounded opinion.

**Cabir** <note>From the Semitic root *kbr*, meaning "great" or "mighty."</note> was an epithet dedicated to the Great Gods, and there were several divisions of them.

In **Sanchuniathon** <note>original: "Sanchoniaton". A Phoenician author whose fragments, preserved by Eusebius, provide a foundation for Phoenician mythology.</note>, we find at least seven of them. Among the **Samothracians**, four are counted. The **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> recognized only two; and often only a single deity bore this name.

In Arabia, **Venus** was called **Cabar**; and at **Thebes** in **Boeotia**, **Ceres** was called **Cabira**. In the same way, **Jove** <note>Jupiter.</note> was also named thus by the **Etruscans**, as is proven by the inscription mentioned above in the section concerning **Rhea**.

In the **Orient**, this term was used to designate what the **Occident** <note>The West, specifically the Greco-Roman world.</note> called the **Great Gods**, of whom twelve were assumed; these twelve Great Gods, however, were the protectors of the twelve heavenly signs <note>The Zodiac.</note>, or the twelve months. **Venus** or **Astarte**, as well as **Ceres**, **Jove**, and the **Sun** were therefore rightly bestowed with the name **Cabiri**.

If one counted only two **Cabiri**, **Castor** and **Pollux**, of whom one was mortal and the other immortal, one in the underworld and the other in heaven, and allotted six months to each, then one understood them to represent the **Winter Sun** and the **Summer Sun**.

If, according to the Greeks, the **Cabiri** were sons of **Jove**, and according to the Phoenicians sons of **Sadyk**, they were also, according to the Egyptians, sons of **Vulcan**, as we know from **Herodotus**. The difference lies only in the words. **Vulcan**, or the god of fire, is called **Ptah** <note>original: "Phta". The Egyptian creator god associated with craftsmen and fire.</note> in the Egyptian language, which signifies one who rules all, like

We shall now see how he [the deity] evolved into a son of Sydyk <note>Sydyk or Sadyk is a Phoenician deity representing justice or "The Righteous One."</note> and became a god of the medical arts.

### 3) Asclepius or Aesculapius.

The story of Sydyk and the Cabiri <note>A group of enigmatic chthonic deities worshipped in Mystery cults, often associated with metallurgy and protection at sea.</note> seems to have a connection with the story of Saturn and agriculture only in relation to Aesculapius.

Meanwhile, it requires no small effort to perceive, from the little our author says, the perspective from which the story of Aesculapius unites with that of agriculture. Nevertheless, this similarity must have been very striking to the peoples of the East, as they felt compelled to unite this story here just as they did in the myth of Ceres and Proserpina <note>Better known by their Greek names, Demeter and Persephone. This myth explains the cycle of the seasons through the growth of grain.</note>, which also relates to agriculture. For according to the latter myth, Ascalaphus—who is certainly the same person as Asclepius—was responsible for Proserpina not being returned to her mother forever, because he reported seeing her eat six pomegranate seeds in Tartarus <note>The deepest part of the underworld. In mythology, eating the food of the dead bound Persephone to remain there for part of the year.</note>.

We shall, therefore, look around for another monument <note>Likely referring to a historical record, inscription, or artistic representation.</note> suitable for the clarification of this subject.

Now we know who belonged to the **Cabiri** <note>Mysterious deities of the ancient Near East and Greece, often associated with protection and the underworld.</note>, or to the eight great primordial gods of **Sabianism** <note>A term historically used to describe the religion of star-worshipers in the Middle East.</note>. <meta>This page continues the etymological and mythological exploration of the deity Esmunus, shifting from his role as the "Eighth" to his specific identification with the Egyptian calendar and the Dog Star (Sirius), explaining how his name and attributes evolved into the Greek figure Asclepius.</meta>

How then did this change occur? and how did the name **Asclepius** or **Aesculapius** itself arise? Answering these questions will now no longer be difficult. Two Egyptian cities bore the name **Esmunus**; one is **Achmin** <note>Modern Akhmim, an ancient city in Upper Egypt known for its temple remains.</note>, to which the Greeks gave the name **Panopolis** or City of the god **Pan**; and the other was called **Achmin**, a name which the Greeks translated as **Hermopolis** or **Mercury’s** city.

The Greeks here have therefore confused **Esmunus** or **Asclepius** with **Mercury**, and this error was likely caused by the fact that the Egyptians depicted **Esmunus** and **Mercury** with a shared symbol.

This symbol was a **dog's head**, by which both were distinguished from all other gods.

**Asclepius**, designated by a dog's head, would thus have derived his name from it; for then it would be composed of two words, **As** or **Es** <note>referring to the fire or light discussed on the previous page</note> and **Calab** <note>original: "Calab"; likely derived from the Hebrew/Semitic "keleb," meaning dog</note> **dog**; it would therefore mean a dog shining with light, and be the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius, whose rising heralded the Nile flood and the start of the Egyptian year.</note>, which opens the year for the Egyptians.

Here, therefore, the eighth **Cabirus** <note>The most significant of the primordial deities mentioned previously.</note>, the supreme god who is exalted above all fixed stars, was represented by the **Dog Star** or **Sirius**, the brightest fixed star, which precedes all others at the beginning of the Egyptian year.

Shortly thereafter, he was depicted with a dog by his side, and now, besides opening the year, he also became a being devoted to the hunt; we should therefore not be surprised that he was made into a hunter.

<meta>This page continues the etymological discussion regarding the deity Aesculapius. Macrobius <margin>8) *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 20.</margin> (8) depicts the concept held regarding Aesculapius and his similarities with the eight Cabiri <note>The Cabiri were a group of enigmatic, powerful deities honored in ancient mystery cults, often associated with the protection of sailors and the forces of nature.</note> in the following words very perfectly: "He is the healing power which descends from the sun upon mortal bodies and brings them back to life." <meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Aesculapius and the Cabiri to the primordial sea deity Pontus. ### 1) Pontus.

Although this genealogical register seems historical, it is nevertheless highly allegorical. Anyone with even a little knowledge of mythology <note>original: "Fabellehre"—the study of myths and fables.</note> knows that Nereus, Neptune, and Pontus were always considered sea gods.

The word **Pontus** means sea; from this comes the **Pontus Euxinus** <note>The ancient Greek name for the Black Sea.</note>, the Black Sea, and the **Hellespont**, or the "Sea of Helle" <note>In Greek mythology, Helle fell into this strait while fleeing on the back of the Golden Ram.</note>. This word, however, was only a surname and means **great** or **immeasurable**. The original word is **Pot**, meaning immeasurable, sublime, or venerable, which sounds like **Pont** when spoken through the nose <note>The author refers to a nasalized pronunciation common in many linguistic developments.</note>. The Greeks used only the root in its nasalized form, but in all its compound forms it became simple again. Thus they said:

->**Pot-Anos** for a river, that is, a "great water," and<-
->**Pot-Nios** venerable, that is, to express an immeasurable, high being, exalted above all else.<-

This word crept into all the Celtic languages; the Latins made from it their <term>Pontifex</term> <note>A member of the highest council of priests in ancient Rome.</note> or High Priest, the origin of which people have never been able to discover. It does not mean, as was previously believed, a **bridge builder** <note>original French: "un faiseur des Ponts"</note>, but rather one who must perform holy, venerable duties.

The French word **Pont** <note>Bridge.</note> flows from this source; but is a bridge not actually an elevated path over water?

Therefore, one must seek the origin of all names formed from this root not in the common French word **Pont**, but in the original meaning of the root itself.

## 2) Nereus.

Much effort has always been spent trying to discover the origin of the word Nereus; (9) but this is an Eastern <note>original: "morgenländisches"—likely referring to Semitic roots, such as the Hebrew "nahar" for river.</note> word which signifies "flowing water," and it serves as a name for a great many rivers and streams, such as the Nera in Italy and the Nairet on Mount Pilat <note>A mountain range in the Massif Central of France.</note> in Lyon. *Naros* and *Nuros* are also Greek words that mean "flowing" or "fluid" in that language.

Hesiod speaks of Nereus in his *Theogony* <note>A classic Greek poem describing the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note> and makes him the eldest son of Pontus; he adds that Nereus was depicted in the form of an old man because he was always just and moderate in his judgments, always truthful, and an enemy of all lies and deception.

> And Pontus begat Nereus, truthful and sincere, <note>original Greek: "Νηρέα τ’ ἀψευδέα καὶ ἀληθέα γείνατο πόντος"</note>
> The eldest of his children; but men call him the Old Man <note>original Greek: "Πρεσβύτατον παίδων· αὐτὰρ καλέουσι γέροντα"</note>
> Because he is unfailing and gentle; nor does he forget the laws, <note>original Greek: "Οὕνεκα νημερτής τε καὶ ἤπιος· οὐδὲ θεμιστέων"</note>
> But knows just and gentle counsels. <note>original Greek: "Λήθεται, ἀλλὰ δίκαια καὶ ἤπια δήνεα οἶδεν."</note>

->Theogony v. 233 and following.<-

A <term>scholiast</term> <note>An ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes in the margins of classical manuscripts.</note> of Hesiod (10) imagined that they meant to say that sailors, through the threat of death ever hovering before their eyes, had learned justice and gentleness. In more recent times, people held... <note>The text ends here; the catchword "billig" (fair/just) suggests the next page continues with a discussion of reasonable or fair interpretations.</note>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Nereus, the Greek sea deity, transitioning from etymological debates to a naturalistic interpretation of his character as "truthful." critics complained justifiably about this well-meaning <term>scholiast</term> <note>An ancient commentator on classical texts.</note>, yet they did no better when they attempted to find the origin of this imagery in the similarity between the name Nereus and Eastern <note>original: "morgenländischen"—referring to Semitic or Middle Eastern languages.</note> words signifying insight and cleverness.

Thus, those who sought to explain the fable solely through intellectual abstraction always went astray in their conjectures, for they completely disregarded the meaning offered to them by nature and necessity—the constant guides of mankind.

Nereus is the water—and was water not always a faithful and true mirror? A judge incapable of any falsehood or pretense? Before this mirror, shepherdesses gazed upon their natural charms; before this mirror, they adorned their heads with flowers as they prepared for a festival or to shine at a dance. The earliest poets knew this; Hesiod, too, knew this well when he composed this beautiful imagery, which only becomes cold and lifeless when viewed from a distorted perspective. Even the critics would have perceived this had they remembered the expression "mirror of the waters" <note>original Latin: *speculum lympharum*</note>, which they might have known from the Latin mythologists since their youth.

### 3) Typhon.

In Egyptian mythology, Typhon plays a major role; he is the enemy of Osiris; the winter; the hostile genius; the storm; the whirlwind; in short, the embodiment of all that is evil and harmful. Here, he represents the sea, because the Egyptians, who hated the sea, called it Typhon; that is, the misfortune-bringing, evil,

### 4) Poseidon or Neptune.

According to the Phoenicians, Neptune was a son of Pontus, or the Sea. Their mythology, therefore, does not entirely agree with the Greek; this is a new proof of the Phoenician origin of this fragment, and that it could not have been forged by Philo <note>Philo of Byblos (c. 64–141 AD), who claimed to translate the writings of the ancient Phoenician priest Sanchuniathon.</note>; for otherwise, he certainly would not have devised a mythology that was neither Greek nor Phoenician. In the Greek language, Neptune is called Poseidon. This name was fashioned from Sidon, which is also pronounced Seidon, and from which the modern name of the city, Saida, is derived. It corresponds with the name of a city located on a lake in Palestine, Bethsaida. This name stems from *Seid*, meaning fish; Sidon consequently signifies "fishery," a place well-situated for fishing. Bethsaida is a "house of fish" <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic roots: *Seid* (fish/hunting) and *Beth* (house).</note>. Therefore, based on its composition from *Pos* and *Said*, Poseidon signifies the "great fishery."

Neptune was also a well-conceived name. It is composed of two root words: first, *Nep*, which signifies a stretch of water. This word has been preserved in the French expression for "a beautiful sheet of water" <note>original French: *une belle Nappe d'eau*</note>, and from this same root comes the Greek second future "I will wash" <note>original: *nipô*</note> and the present tense "I wash" <note>original: *niptô*</note>, which means to wash, as well as the variants "to wash" <note>original: *niphô, neiphô*</note>, "snow" <note>original: *niphas*</note>, and "liquid bitumen" or "Naphtha" <note>original: *napthê*</note>: second, it comes from *Tun* or *Dun*, meaning lofty or deep.

Nereus is water; and was water not always a faithful and true mirror? A judge incapable of all falsehood and disguise? Before this mirror, shepherdesses observed their unadulterated charms; before this mirror, they adorned their heads with flowers when they prepared themselves for a celebration or to shine at a dance. The first poets knew this; Hesiod <note>Ancient Greek poet (c. 700 BC), author of the *Theogony*.</note> also knew this very well when he designed this beautiful image, which became cold and lifeless when viewed from a distorted perspective. Even the critics would have noticed it if they had remembered the expression **mirror of the waters** <note>original Latin: *speculum lympharum*</note>, which they might still have known from the Latin mythographers since their youth.

### 3) Typhon.

In Egyptian mythology <note>original German: *egyptischen Fabellehre*</note>, Typhon plays a major role; in it, he is an enemy of Osiris; he is winter; the hostile genius; the storm; the whirlwind; in short, the epitome of everything evil and harmful. Here he is the sea, because the Egyptians, who hated the sea, called it Typhon—that is to say, the bringer of misfortune, the wicked...

### 4) Poseidon or Neptune.

According to the Phoenicians, Neptune was a son of Pontus, or the Sea. Their mythology <note>original German: *Fabellehre*</note> thus does not entirely agree with the Greek; this is a new proof of the Phoenician origin of this fragment, and that it could not have been fabricated by Philo <note>Philo of Byblos (c. 64–141 AD), a scholar who claimed to translate the ancient history of the Phoenicians from the works of Sanchuniathon.</note>; for otherwise, he certainly would not have designed a mythology that was neither Greek nor Phoenician. In the Greek language, Neptune is called Poseidon. This name is derived from Sidon, which is also pronounced Seidon, and from which the modern name of the city, Saida <note>The ancient port city of Sidon in modern-day Lebanon.</note>, comes. It corresponds with the name of a city located on a lake in Palestine, Bethsaida. This name stems from *Seid*, meaning fish; consequently, Sidon signifies "fishery," a place well-situated for fishing. Bethsaida is a "fish-house." Therefore, according to its composition from *Pot* and *Said*, Poseidon signifies the "great fishery."

Neptune was likewise a well-conceived name. It is composed of two root words: first, from *Nep*, which signifies a stretch of water. This word has been preserved in the French word for "sheet," *nappe*, specifically when one speaks of a "beautiful sheet of water" <note>original French: *une belle Nappe d’eau*</note>, and from this same source arose the Greek second future *nipô* and the present *niptō* <note>original Greek: *νίπτω*</note>, which means "to wash," as well as *niphō* or *neiphō* (to wash), *niphas* (snow), *napthē* (liquid bitumen), and Naphtha. Secondly, it comes from *Tun* or *Dun*, meaning sublime or deep.

### 5) Sidon.

One will no longer be surprised that Sidon was made a daughter of the Sea <note>original: *Pontus*, the Greek personification of the sea</note>. All maritime cities are daughters of the sea, but especially those that owe their greatness solely to the sea, such as Sidon. But why is she attributed with a marvelous voice and the invention of the ode? Perhaps because the ode was actually invented in Sidon; for such flourishing cities are always full of fine minds, poets, and spectacles, and only in their bosom can the fine arts thrive. Furthermore, it is known that the Phoenicians were great patrons of the sciences, which again proves that they must have lived in the enjoyment of all comforts and happiness.

Mount Casius lies between Phoenicia and Egypt; and this place therefore had the most favorable location for the opening of a great trade <note>original: *Handlung*</note> between Phoenicia and Egypt, between Africa and Asia. It therefore also became the main site, the point of union, the center between all these peoples; there was a permanent temple consecrated to the protective deity of the place; there all these peoples gathered every year at a set time—that is, at the time of the celebration of this god's festival—for the sake of trade; here fairs <note>original: *Messe*, referring to the historical intersection of religious feasts and commercial markets</note>, pilgrimages, festivals, and dances were organized at the same time; the merchants traded, the devout visited the temple, the youth danced, all goods could be profitably sold, and everyone departed again happy, spirited, and satisfied.

## Article VIII.

### §. 1.

# Deposition and Mutilation of Uranus.

### 1) Sanchuniathon’s and Hesiod’s Accounts Thereof.

Here we finally come upon the resolution of this long history—to the most unnatural act of Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus</note>, which is far more suited to making him hated, and which one ought only to have recounted with abhorrence; regardless, it is celebrated as an act worthy of eternal fame, through which Saturn becomes like a god. These occurrences are inexplicable if one merely follows the literal sense; but they are true, and in their proper place, as soon as one views this final proof of Saturn’s cruelty from an allegorical perspective. This perspective connects his cruelty with the remaining parts of his history and is the key to all fables that have Saturn as their subject.

In these later stories, the features are much gentler, and Ge <note>Ge is a Greek name for Gaia, the personification of the Earth.</note> no longer allows Uranus to be so severely mistreated by her own son; yet she always remains a goddess who has lost her husband and who, in her grief, wishes to see no one by whom her pain might be renewed.

The Greeks, however, do not wish for a Rhea as unhappy as those of other nations, and they therefore have her husband Saturn mistreated by their son Jupiter. <note>In Greek mythology, Rhea’s husband Cronus (Saturn) is overthrown by his son Zeus (Jupiter), rather than being perpetually mourned as a lost spouse.</note>

These stories were not produced by chance; they did not depict real occurrences, but are rather an allegory repeated everywhere. They are an allegory precisely because they are told sometimes with more, sometimes with fewer details, and under changed names.

One must not be surprised, however, that this allegory was common only to these specific peoples and did not extend further; for since it is essential to Saturn—that is, to agriculture <term>Ackerbau: The cultivation of fields; the author identifies the god Saturn with the invention and practice of farming</term>—it was only adopted by those peoples devoted to farming, and not by others. Only for the nations that enjoy the fruits of this art is a single truth hidden beneath these fables.

### §. 4.
## States which Saturn bestows at his own will.

Our author assures us that Saturn gave Attica to his daughter Athena or Minerva, and Egypt to Mercury.

Here we learn, then, that the Athenians worshipped Minerva, and the Egyptians worshipped Thoth <note>original: "Thot"</note> or Mercury, for reasons relating to agriculture; this was not previously known, and it will confirm all our previously expressed conjectures.

Everyone knows that Minerva is the goddess of the arts and the protectress of the Athenians and the olive tree, while Attica itself was such a barren land that one grew almost nothing there but olive trees.

Likewise, everyone knows that fertile and well-cultivated Egypt derives all its knowledge—especially that which relates to land, its measurement, and its division <note>This refers to the origin of geometry, which literally means "earth-measurement," necessitated by the annual flooding of the Nile.</note>—from Mercury.

Did he truly reign over Attica and Egypt? No, truly not; rather, this is only allegorically true—but in that sense, it is also very true and instructive.

When, at one time, a goddess is the protectress of Athens and a god is the protector of Memphis; when, at the same time, the arts flourish in Athens and agriculture in Egypt; then all of this is an effect of nature. Mankind has contributed nothing of their own other than to adapt themselves to eternal laws and unchangeable institutions.

Flat, fertile Egypt becomes a land of farmers, and these people, in their hard labor, chose a god as their protector.

The mountainous, ungrateful, infertile territory of Attica, by contrast, becomes a land for artists, manufacturers, olive-tree gardeners, and oil merchants. Since these arts—which are quite different from agriculture—require only a sedentary and secluded life, performing nothing outside the house or in the open air, but instead everything within the home, in the women's quarters, in the domain of the mother of the house, they also received only a goddess as their protectress. This goddess was the Moon—the Athena of the Greeks, the Minerva of the Romans <note>original: "Lateiner"</note>.

This very natural division, attributed to Saturn by the Phoenicians, proves how remarkably these peoples distinguished agriculture—the true productive art, the art of Egypt and of every great empire—from the arts that process the materials provided by agriculture. In more recent times, these non-productive arts were rightly called "sterile," <note>This likely refers to the "Physiocrat" school of economic thought popular in the 18th century, which argued that only agriculture produced new wealth, while manufacturing was "sterile" because it only transformed existing materials.</note> and in ancient times they were symbolically called the "Attic arts," because that land was infertile and produced little.

# Article IX.
## Saturn, Uranus, and so forth, depicted by Thoth.

### 1) Various translations of this article.

Sanchuniathon <note>a Phoenician author whose works survive only in fragments cited by later writers; he is often used as a source for ancient mythology</note> informs us that Thoth <note>the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing</note> painted Saturn, Uranus, and Dagon, and that he invented various characters <note>meaning symbols, script, or hieroglyphs</note>. ### 3) How

they reasonably represented **Thoth** as the advisor and **secretary of Saturn**.

The husbandman <note>The German "Ackersmann" refers to a farmer or one who works the soil.</note> can do nothing without observing the stars and the seasons; he must always consult his calendar or **almanac** to arrange all his labors accordingly. But is not **Thoth** or **Mercury**—that is, the "man of signs"—the inventor of this **calendar**, this **almanac**, and these observations?

In short, **Thoth** is the astronomer, just as **Saturn** is the farmer; and for the benefit of the latter, the former literally imitates **Uranus**—or the heavens: that is, he paints the constellations and makes their orbits discernible. Literally, he also paints **Saturn** and **Dagon** <note>Dagon was a major Northwest Semitic deity, often associated with grain and fertility (from the Hebrew word "dagan" for grain)</note>, or rather, he organizes all field and agricultural work according to the seasons and the changes of the year.

**Thoth** and **Saturn** are thus inseparable in the **allegory**, because they are so in reality; the **allegory** would have been incomplete without this union.

These characters drawn by **Thoth** are ultimately sacred because they serve the perfection of agriculture, the sacred and venerable source of all nations and empires;

Because, in the most ancient times, they were engraved upon the walls of temples, which served as the sole meeting points for peoples devoted to agriculture—just as they still are for farmers today;

And because they were always connected with solemn festivals and divine services established for the countryman.

This is the simple and true explanation of an otherwise unintelligible passage; one will be even more convinced of its truth after reading the further development of the **allegory** contained in the history of **Thoth**.

### 3) How Thoth Depicted Saturn.

Our author adds that **Thoth**—or **Mercury**—painted **Saturn** with four eyes and four wings; of these, two were alternately open and two were closed, and in the same manner, he also always had two wings spread wide while letting two hang as if at rest. This was intended to show that he "wakes while sleeping, and sleeps while waking." <note>original: "daß er schlaffend wache, und wachend schlaffe." This paradox illustrates the constant vigilance required in farming.</note> This expresses nothing other than the fact that the husbandman <note>German: "Ackersmann," referring to a farmer or tiller of the earth.</note> must always be on his feet, must never rest, and must utilize every single moment if he desires a successful outcome for his endeavors.

It can also mean that agriculture is a perpetual "mixture of the gods," <note>In this allegorical framework, "gods" often represent natural elements or seasonal forces; the mixture refers to the constant cycle of growth and decay.</note> where at one time some things arise, while others perish.

**Thoth** also painted **Saturn** with two wings on his head to indicate, it is said, his intellect and his capacity for sensation. These qualities must necessarily be possessed by nations devoted to agriculture; for it is precisely through these traits that they rise so far above those nations that disregard the tilling of the fields—if one can even give the name "nations" to small tribes who possess nothing.

Nothing can be more easily proven than what I assert here about antiquity; it is such a self-evident truth that even the Abbot **Banier** <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741), a French clergyman and scholar known for his work interpreting mythology through a historical lens.</note> had to concede it.

Had this scholar always followed such guides—had he stuck merely to facts without trying to explain them away—his work would have been better and mythology less confused. In it, he assumes five different Saturns: Adam, Noah, a Phoenician Saturn, a Carthaginian one, and a Latin one. He could just as well have also counted a Greek, an Egyptian, perhaps even an Indian, and with certainty a Gallic Saturn, etc., etc.

These festivals, with which the year of the farmer—who now saw his labors crowned with the most fortunate success—concluded, were therefore rightfully called *Saturnalia*.

For that same reason, the Greeks called them *Cronian festivals* <note>original: "cronische Feste," referring to festivals of Kronos, the Greek equivalent of Saturn</note>; however, the name always held the same meaning.

The Orient <note>A historical term for the Near East</note>, which knew these festivals in *Babylon* and in *Persia* under the name *Sacaean* <note>original: "Saceische," referring to the Sacaea, an ancient Babylonian festival</note>, had to call them the *Ilian* or the *Festivals of Ilus* in *Phrygia* and *Syria*, because *Saturn* was called by that name in the Eastern language. This name is easily confused with the Ilian or Trojan festivals <note>Because the city of Troy was also known as Ilium</note>, and this has likely already been the case many times.

### 2) As God of Time.

The fact that antiquity held *Saturn* to be the God of Time also proves that it recognized him as the inventor of agriculture; and if this newer way of viewing *Saturn* brought the older one almost entirely into oblivion, it was a consequence of the close connection between these subjects, and of the allegorical spirit that always prefers the literal allegory <note>The author suggests that the physical, "literal" acts of farming became the basis for the more abstract "allegory" of time's passage</note>. Everything that is said about the farmer’s harvests can also be said about time: if time arms itself with the murderous scythe, then the farmer consumes the harvest; if time devours its own children <note>A famous mythological image where Saturn/Kronos eats his children, interpreted here as the earth consuming the seeds it produced</note>, then the farmer likewise nourishes himself from his own fruits; if time serves to calculate the duration of things, then the farmer arranges everything according to his harvests; any other calculation might even be dispensable to him.

All these symbols, through which one intended to figuratively represent the invention of agriculture, thus simultaneously became a portrait of time, and the name of the one also became that of the

### 3) As King of the Golden Age.

As the God of Time, Saturn—and with him the Golden Age so highly praised by the poets and eulogists of bygone eras—was transplanted into the realm of fables.

As for me, I do not consider this era to be a dream; rather, I believe that it truly existed on Earth and occurred during the reign of Saturn. Furthermore, I believe it only depends on humanity to bring it back, and that it would immediately reappear in full splendor as soon as people pay attention to the voice of order and put its lessons into practice.

The Golden Age is the era of the founding of agriculture in the beautiful eastern <note>original: "morgenländischen," referring to the Orient</note> and southern regions, and the transition from powerlessness and misery (this word very well expresses the animalistic state of the people living then) to abundance and prosperity. At that time, the world took on a completely new form—as beautiful, happy, and rich as the previous generations of humanity had been poor and wretched. In every respect, it was the Golden Age, serving both as the source from which goods and the most precious riches flowed, and as the means of promoting a large population and a peaceful, firmly established state constitution. They corrupted the greatest monarchs, suppressed true glory, instilled contempt for agriculture, sank the nations back into their terrifying chaos, and brought the Golden Age, the century of Saturn <note>A mythological era of peace and plenty before Saturn was overthrown by his son Jupiter (Zeus).</note>, into such oblivion that only a mournful memory of it remained, which soon passed into a mere dream.

## 4) Sanchuniathon himself presents this history of Saturn as nothing more than an allegory.

Here is another feature that must not be overlooked, yet one to which no one has paid any attention, despite how important it must seem. Our author <note>Referring to Sanchuniathon, an ancient Phoenician writer whose works survive only in fragments quoted by later authors.</note> assures us that: "The son of Thabion <note>Thabion is traditionally identified as the first priest or hierophant of the Phoenicians.</note> had clothed everything in allegories, combined them with physical and natural phenomena, and handed them down to those who celebrated the *orgies* and to the priests who presided over the mysteries."

Thus, we have not deceived ourselves; the whole thing is an allegory—but an ancient, well-known, and sacred one, because it formed the basis of the hymns in the mysteries and the sacred *orgies* <note>In the ancient world, "orgies" (orgia) referred to secret religious rites or festivals, particularly those of Dionysus or Demeter, rather than the modern sense of the word.</note>.

One should not be surprised by this; it is well known that the mysteries of the ancients, and the hymns sung during them, had agriculture <note>original: "Ackerbau"</note> as their subject. Figures like Osiris, Bacchus, Ceres, Isis, Adonis, Cybele, Saturn, Janus, and so on, were merely repetitions of these same depictions. At Eleusis, people celebrated only the invention of agriculture, and the very same thing occurred on the banks of the Nile and the Orontes.

Even the name of these *orgies*, under which people sang of Saturn—armed with his scythe and known as the devourer of children—proves that his history was only an allegory relating to agriculture.

This name, *orgies*, comes from the Greek word *Orgas* <note>original: "Οργας", a term for a fertile or meadowy tract of land, often one consecrated to the gods.</note>, which originally signifies a field or cultivated land.

An *orgie* was therefore a rural festival; and who else but Saturn—or agriculture itself—and its fortunate

It is true that "orgies" are commonly understood as noisy festivals where unbridled freedom and disorder reigned; however, such a view portrays them only in their degenerate state, rather than as they were originally intended.

Furthermore, the word **Orge** <term>Orgē / Οργη</term> <note>While in later Greek *orgē* came to mean "passion" or "wrath," the author here argues for an older meaning related to vital impulse and activity.</note>, which in later times expressed insolence and frenzy, initially signified only sustained labor, care, toil, and diligence—in short, everything understood by the word **Culture** <note>The author uses "Cultur" in the dual sense of *agriculture* (tilling the soil) and *civilization* (the tilling of the mind).</note>.

This entire word-family is merely an offshoot of the family **Ergon** <term>Ergon / Εργον</term> <note>The Greek word for "work," "deed," or "labor," particularly used by authors like Hesiod in the context of farming.</note>, which expresses field labor, harvesting, and generally every kind of work, toil, and exertion.

This family was produced by the root word **Her** or **Er**, meaning the earth.

**Sanchuniathon** even reveals to us the motivations that moved the ancients to transmit this allegory to posterity; namely, they wished to excite the astonishment and admiration of all nations. No better path could have been taken than this; for the history of **Saturn** has filled all subsequent generations with wonder, and even during those times when it was least understood, it was preserved with the utmost care.

The invention of agriculture, with its beneficial consequences, was bound to elicit admiration from all mortals, even if it had been recounted as a mere history in the simplest possible way. What wonders, then, must it have produced among a people enamored with figures and poetic enthusiasm? From this there arose not only

This took place before the name "Phoenicia" even existed; for among the number of his successors or his initiates (the Greek phrase <note>original: likely referring to the ambiguity between *diadochoi* (successors) and *mystai* (initiates)</note> is capable of this double interpretation), he includes **Chna**, who was the first to be called a Phoenician. This also aligns with what **Moses** says: that Chna, or **Canaan**, became the name of the Canaanites. All this occurred, therefore, before the union of the Canaanites into a national body, in a completely different location than the one inhabited by the ancestors of their founder. When they settled between the banks of the **Orontes**, the **Jordan**, and the **Mediterranean Sea**, they brought nothing with them except what the son of Thabion had taught them, and a growing taste for the allegories that were so common among them.

### 4) Of Ophion and the Ophionids.

Let us pause for a moment at this passage;
it deserves our attention all the more since our
poet, in regards to Ophion—a person
quite unknown to most mythologists—agrees
with Sanchoniathon <note>An ancient Phoenician author whose works are preserved only in fragments; he is often cited as a source on early Phoenician religion.</note>, and the comparison of these two allegorical
writers sheds much light.

We immediately perceive here the philosophical concepts
of the Egyptians, Pythagoreans, and Platonists regarding the
harmony of the universe, which is based on the
seven planets and their relationship—and generally upon
the number seven. Non-
nus <note>Nonnus of Panopolis, the 5th-century Greek poet of the "Dionysiaca."</note> gives the planets here the exact order in which
they stand in the musical system of the Egyptians, where the
Sun also occupies the fourth place or the middle of the
scale, and ends and begins the two quarters <note>original: "zwey Viertel"; likely referring to the two tetrachords that comprise a musical scale.</note> which
make up this system. The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and practitioners of Zoroastrianism.</note> gave them this same arrangement,

<term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and exegete often used as a source for ancient Middle Eastern fragments.</note> adds to this subject that <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>The ancient Persian prophet.</note>, in his definition of the divine, represented God with the head of a hawk; however, one must not understand this as if Zoroaster literally said the deity had a hawk's head. Moreover, we have here a notable example of the way in which the ancient poets grounded their poetic inventions in real facts that were important to humanity; we also see from this that the Orient, and especially **Phoenicia**, was clearly the cradle of allegories, and that foreign poets like **Nonnus** <note>Nonnus of Panopolis, a 5th-century Greek poet who wrote the *Dionysiaca*.</note>, if they wished to follow in the footsteps of their predecessors, had to leave these allegories firmly in their place.

1) **Psamathe** is a Greek word which signifies **coast** or **shore** <note>original: *psamathos*.</note>. This usually separates the domains of the water-god and the wine-god from one another. This nymph was already known in the most ancient times. **Hesiod**, in his *Theogony* (verse 1003), makes her a daughter of **Nereus** and adds that she bore a son named **Phocus** to **Aeacus**. This allegory was very ingeniously explained by **Abbot Bergier** <note>Nicolas-Sylvestre Bergier (1718–1790), a French theologian who argued that pagan myths were corrupted versions of historical truths or natural phenomena.</note> in his remarks on the *Theogony*.

2) This very expressive name is composed of the word *Ar* or *Or*, which signifies **mountain** or **hill** <note>likely referring to the Semitic/Hebrew word *har* (mountain).</note>, and the word *Adne*, meaning delightful or pleasant. Vineyards are indeed delightful hills.

### 6) Etymology of the Name Berytus.

I further add that the characteristic with which Nonnus describes Berytus—namely, that it is filled with the fragrance of cedars—makes it probable to me that the name of this city originates neither from **Bher**, which signifies a **well** <note>original: "Brunnen"</note>, nor from **Bir**, which expresses **strength**; these are etymologies that the **Abbot Barthelemy** <note>Jean-Jacques Barthélemy (1716–1795) was a French archaeologist and writer famous for his work on ancient Phoenician and Greek cultures.</note> has already rendered suspect. Instead, it likely stems from an Oriental word, written in Hebrew as **Beryt** or **Beruth**, which signifies cypresses and cedars, or trees that possess the scent of cedar (3). This is all the more credible because the cedar forests located in the vicinity of Berytus likely extended originally all the way to the sea; the city could not have been populated and cultivated without the clearing of a portion of this cedar forest that stood upon the seashore.

We also recall that the name **Beroe** is also found in the Greek history of Bacchus; so inseparable is this name from this allegory. **Euripides**, in his tragedy titled **Bacchus** <note>Referring to the play commonly known as *The Bacchae*.</note>, and other writers relate that **Juno** <note>The Roman name for the goddess Hera.</note>, when she wished to plunge her rival **Semele** into ruin, assumed the form of Semele's nurse **Beroe** in order to instill in her a suspicion against her lover <note>Semele was the mother of Bacchus/Dionysus; Juno's trickery led to Semele's death when she demanded to see Jupiter in his true, divine form.</note>. We have therefore, with good reason, considered this name to be allegorical.

## Article XII.
### Free Translation of the second Fragment of Sanchuniathon.

**S**ince we have now finished with the explanation of our author, we can now attempt to take up his text once more in order to provide a new translation that aligns more closely with our perspective. This will simultaneously serve as a brief summary of our entire treatise and make it easier to judge whether our thoughts agree with the author, and whether the explanation of the individual parts of this allegory is so natural and appropriate that conviction immediately follows.

At that time, **Elion** <note>A Phoenician deity, often equated with the "Most High"</note> or the **Most High** reigned. He lived in the region of **Byblos**, (in the bosom of light.) From him and **Beruth** <gloss>the Creation</gloss> were produced Heaven and Earth.

The Most High then rested from his labors. His children revered him as God.

As long as the earth brought forth products solely through the assistance of heaven, the latter was considered the husband of the earth and the father of her offspring.

But heaven neglects the earth and her products. At this, she grows angry and demands a redeemer. Her son **Saturn** (the husbandman, he who first cultivated the earth) takes up her cause, upon the advice and with the assistance of **Mercury Trismegistus** (the Sign-Man, the famous inventor of the calendar or almanac) <note>The author interprets Mercury/Thoth not as a god, but as the inventor of the "signs" of the zodiac and the agricultural calendar</note>.

The children of **Saturn** were **Persephone** (the goddess of the sowing season) and **Athena** (the goddess of the arts): the former died as a virgin.

On the advice of **Mercury** and **Athena**, **Saturn** procures a saber (the scythe) and a spear (the plowshare).

His secretary, the Sign-Man, then holds an engaging conversation with **Saturn’s** friends: he persuades them to also undertake the defense of the earth against heaven; thus **Saturn**, or the husbandman, reigns over the earth.

In this struggle, one takes possession of a consort of heaven (the queen of the water); she is given to **Dagon** (the god of the fields) as a husband; from this arises **Demaroon** (the lord of abundance).

**Saturn** surrounds his dwelling with a wall; that is the first city.

When he had conceived some suspicion regarding **Atlas** (the products of the earth), he threw him into a deep pit and buried him <note>This likely refers to the storage of grain or the planting of tubers/seeds in the ground</note>.

**Astarte** wears a bull’s head upon her own as a sign of her royal dignity (representing the crescent moon).

# Introduction.

If the history of <term>Saturn</term> <note>In Roman mythology, Saturn was the god of generation, liberation, and agriculture. The author interprets his myths as a coded history of human progress.</note> which I have just explained is an excellent allegory for the invention of agriculture; if it presents to us the great concepts of the ancients regarding this art; if, in this manner, all the absurdities and crimes contained in this narrative—through which the memory of its hero was defiled—disappear, or are transformed into as many traits as were necessary for the perfection of this allegory, to make it the most apt and truthful; if this way of viewing antiquity sheds the greatest light and interest upon it: then the very same will be the case with the history of <term>Mercury</term> <note>Commonly known as the messenger of the gods, but here identified as the "secret scribe" or counselor to Saturn, often linked to the Egyptian god Thoth, the inventor of writing.</note>, the secret scribe and advisor to Saturn.

The history of the servant was, in appearance, just as confused and inexplicable as that of his master. Why should it have been any clearer? The purpose would then have been entirely lost; for with the clarity of the one, the darkness of the other must also vanish, and the ray of light from the former must necessarily reflect back upon the latter. If Saturn was an allegorical person, his secret scribe had to be no less so; the allegorical traits characterizing the one had to be an extension and completion of those features which designate the other.
