The word **Agriculture** was the foundation of the enigmatic allegory presented by *Saturn* and his fable; likewise, the word *Astronomy* will be the basis for the allegory concerning *Thoth*, or *Mercury*—who is armed with the serpent-staff (<term>caduceus</term> <note>original: "caduceo." The herald's staff carried by Mercury, featuring two entwined snakes; it symbolized negotiation and commerce.</note>), serves as the interpreter of the gods, acts as the advisor to *Saturn* accompanied by a rooster, a dog, and a ram, and is the author of the 36,525 scrolls <note>A reference to the legendary number of books attributed to Hermes Trismegistus/Thoth, containing all the wisdom of the world.</note>.

I do not speak of that sublime *astronomy* through which one is able to measure the heavens; which contains rules by which one can explain the motions of the stars; and which includes discoveries flowing from the excellent *theories* of the moderns concerning the movements of the moon, the *planets*, and *comets*. These are *theories* that we owe to the perfection of our *instruments* and to the critical and creative spirit that distinguishes the moderns—though the ancients also possessed more insight into these matters than has been believed until now, as I shall show elsewhere.

Rather, we are speaking here of that practical *astronomy* which simply observes, which relies on experience, and draws from it sufficient knowledge to organize the course of the year, to design the calendar, to divide the annual cycles of the sun and moon accordingly, and in this way to prevent agricultural work from drifting too far from the course of the sun.

## Article I.

->§. 1.<-

->On the names of Mercury, and how many of them existed in antiquity.<-

Mercury was called Hermes in the Greek language, Thoth, Thaut, Teut, Toyth in the Egyptian, and Teutates among the Celts.

People were quite perplexed regarding both the explanation of these names and the establishment of the concept to be formed from them, as well as the number of Mercuries recognized by antiquity.

Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325 AD), an early Christian author who often cataloged pagan myths to explain or critique them</note> counted four:
> the first was the son of Jupiter and Maia; the second was the son of the Sky and the Day; the third was the son of Bacchus and Proserpina; and the fourth was the son of Jupiter and Cyllene; this one killed Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant of Greek mythology</note>, thereafter fled to Egypt, and brought the knowledge of letters <note>meaning the invention of writing or the alphabet</note> there.

This observation, which was important following an already established identity of all the Mercuries, was on its own far too weak to prove this identity. It is therefore not surprising that Abbot Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741), a French mythologist</note> did not accept the opinion of his fellow brother <note>Likely referring to a fellow member of the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres</note> on this matter.

As for me, having evidence of a completely different strength before me, I start from the principle that in antiquity there was only one Mercury; that the Egyptian, Phoenician, Greek, Gallic, Etruscan, and Roman Mercury, etc., were one and the same allegorical person; that they all represent only one and the same allegory relating to the same objects, connected by the same circumstances and persons, generated by the same needs, and dedicated to the same events.

Let us therefore see in what manner the ancients represented Mercury.

### §. 2.
## Concepts of the Ancients regarding Mercury.

Mercury plays the greatest role in the Phoenician allegory which has come down to us under the name of Sanchuniathon <note>A semi-legendary Phoenician author whose work survived through fragments quoted by Eusebius</note>.

1) He is therein called Trismegistus <note>original: "Trismegist"; from the Greek "Thrice-Greatest," a title later associated with Hermes Trismegistus</note>, the secret scribe and advisor of Saturn.

2) Following his advice, Saturn forges weapons and unites against the Heavens. He himself <note>Mercury</note> delivers an engaging speech to Saturn's friends and persuades them to stand by him.

I believed I had to include this narrative here without any reservation—though it relates to the instruction granted to humanity by Mercury and seems not at all suited to establishing a firm concept of this person—because it will confirm what I intend to present on this subject and provide an irresistible proof. ### §. 4.
### Other Characteristics of Mercury.

I am adding several other traits that serve to characterize him.

1) The first month and the first day of the Egyptian year were sacred to him and bore his name, **Thoth**.

2) **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> say that he was called **Phansnos**.

3) **Plato** calls him in various places in his works (7) the admirable artist, the father of letters. Without doubt, it was difficult to find a thread leading out of this labyrinth that linked these seemingly unconnected facts. Let us therefore not wonder at the divided opinions, and at the presentation of such trivial and non-explanatory things regarding such an important subject; for since the sharp and intelligible characteristics were completely ignored, it was impossible to form any concept of this person, or of the allegory that gave rise to him—an allegory that people do not even look for.

# Article II.

## Opinions of the Learned Regarding Mercury.

The claim of Abbot Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741) was a French mythologist who sought to interpret myths as historical events; he argued that gods were originally deified men.</note> that there were two Mercurys, one Egyptian and one Celtic, has already been mentioned above; however, by this he only doubled the difficulties and explained nothing.

The author of the *History of the Heavens* <note>A reference to Noël-Antoine Pluche (1688–1761) and his influential work *Histoire du ciel* (1739), which argued that mythology arose from misinterpreted agricultural and astronomical signs.</note>, who occasionally puts forward truths, has also said nothing satisfactory about this person. He turns Mercury into a symbol for the Dog Star <note>The star Sirius, the rising of which coincided with the annual flooding of the Nile.</note> and the moment when its rising announces the approaching flood. He adds that Mercury was armed with a staff—which subsequently transformed into a <term>serpent-staff</term> <note>The caduceus, the traditional winged staff entwined with two snakes carried by Mercury/Hermes.</note>—because this sign was used for the public announcement that it was time to retreat to the heights to escape the rising floodwaters.

Johann Nicolai <note>A German historian and antiquarian (1665–1708) who wrote extensively on ancient rituals.</note> in his treatise on Mercury, and the Bishop of Avranches, H. Huet <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a polymath who argued in his *Demonstratio Evangelica* that most pagan myths were corrupted versions of the life of Moses.</note>, believed that Moses was the model according to which the pagans had formed this god.

Cudworth, Mosheim, and Brucker <note>Ralph Cudworth, Johann Lorenz von Mosheim, and Johann Jakob Brucker were prominent 17th and 18th-century philosophers and historians of religion who debated whether mythological figures represented real historical persons.</note> are fully convinced of his real existence; the latter even claims that one would overturn all historical certainty if one wished to deny this.

# First Class of Evidence.

## Mercury's Titles.

### 1) Mercury as Secret Scribe and Advisor to Saturn.

In the most ancient times, he was distinguished by the peoples of the East <note>original: "Morgenländern," referring to the Levant and Mesopotamia</note> with the title of secret scribe <note>original: "geheim Schreiber"</note> and advisor to Cronus or Saturn, and by the Egyptians as the advisor to Isis and a friend of Osiris.

But who is the advisor to farmers? Whose oracular pronouncements do they heed, and whom else do they trust, if not their calendar or almanac? This alone they always consult; it provides them with counsel in all their tasks. Through his almanac, the farmer knows when he must fertilize, plow, or sow his land; when he must harvest, work, and be out in the field; and when he can rest or attend social gatherings. We should therefore not be surprised that "almanac" and "advice" became synonymous terms, and that people used to say, *take your almanacs elsewhere* <note>original French: "portes vos Almanachs à d'autres"; a phrase meaning "keep your advice to yourself"</note>; instead of saying, your advice is worthless, we do not want it.

Simultaneously with the invention of agriculture, the observation and knowledge of time became absolutely necessary. Astronomy thus arose at the same time as agriculture, for one art gives birth to another, and just as a single invention draws the attention of humanity,

The ancients say that of the two dragons <note>The author uses the word "Drachen" (dragons), which in historical heraldic and alchemical contexts often referred to large serpents.</note> which form the serpent-staff <term>Caduceus: the staff carried by Mercury as a messenger of the gods</term>, one was male and the other female, and their point of union was called *Hercules*.

> "It is clear from the Staff that the sun is worshipped in the form of Mercury, which the Egyptians represented in the likeness of joined male and female dragons to be consecrated to Mercury. These dragons are bound to one another in the middle part of their coils by a knot which they call the knot of Hercules; their foreparts, curved back into a circle, meet with a kiss to complete the circle’s circumference; and after the knot, the tails are brought back to the handle of the staff; they are adorned with wings growing from that same part of the handle." <note>original: ”In Mercurio solem coli etiam ex Caduceo claret, quod Aegyptii in specie Draconum maris et foeminae conjunctorum figuraverunt, Mercurio consecrandum. This means: 
> "The serpent-staff proves that Mercury is the sun. The Egyptians dedicated this staff to the most excellent deity in the form of two connected dragons, a male and a female. The point of union is called *Hercules*. Their forebodies form a circle that closes through the meeting of their heads, and their tails likewise meet in a circle above the handle of the serpent-staff, and are decorated by wings which emerge from this very handle."

The serpent-staff with which **Mercury** was armed thus represented a celestial map; and one said with it, quite briefly and emphatically, that he had observed the movements of the **Sun** and the **Moon**, their course through the **equator**—the circle represented by the rod of the serpent-staff—the moment of their union, and the moment of their greatest distance; these are points in time which are the foundation of the year, which circumscribe it and divide it into equal parts. Indeed, one even wanted to imply thereby that he had brought everything relating to the year into order—in short, that he had created the calendar.

To characterize **Mercury**, it would have been impossible to find a more suitable symbol—one which had so much reference to the concept one had to have of him, and which would have belonged to him alone—than this.

It is therefore true; the serpent-staff <term>caduceus|The herald's staff carried by Mercury, consisting of a rod entwined by two serpents, often topped with wings.</term> depicts the year or the annual cycle of the sun and the moon. The rod of the serpent-staff is the equator or the circle which divides the globe into two equal parts, and over which the sun passes twice a year, at the time of the equinoxes.

The male dragon forms the ecliptic <term>ecliptic|The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of a year.</term> or the curved path of the sun during the course of a year. In relation to the equator, it forms a zigzag or an "S," and is presented exactly so on our maps.

The knot of the two dragons, which arises where they meet on the rod of the serpent-staff, is also the moment in which the sun and the moon meet on the equator, at the point where it is intersected by the ecliptic.

This knot, says **Macrobius** <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (fl. c. 400 AD) was a Roman provincial whose works, particularly the *Saturnalia*, were a major source for medieval and Renaissance understandings of ancient mythology.</note>, is called **Hercules**; an important circumstance, for it supports all our claims by proving more and more the kinship between our three allegorical personages: **Saturn**, **Mercury**, and **Hercules**.

These two dragons, of which one is a male and the other a female, and which are the symbol of the two primary causes of all things—the active and the passive—provide the explanation for the two wings which **Mercury** attached to **Saturn's** head, and which he calls **Understanding** and **Sensation**. **Understanding** impresses the action, and **Sensation** receives it; **Saturn** is the active being who sows; the earth is the passive being, which is sown and receives.

The Ram, under whose sign the year began for all peoples where it commenced with the month of March, became a very natural symbol of astronomy.

Finally, the Dog, which—under the name of the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note>—presides over the middle of the month of August, became the true emblem for the Egyptian Mercury <note>The author identifies Mercury with the Egyptian god Thoth or Anubis, who was associated with the star Sirius.</note>, as their year began with the rising of this star.

In the middle of this month, the old year elapsed in Egypt; it was then that the *End* or *Teleute* (1) occurred, and this day was the festival of the goddess Nephte <note>Nephthys, the Egyptian goddess often associated with mourning and the end of life.</note>, who was snatched away from the midst of the number of men. The other day was the festival of *Rosh* (2) or the New Year’s festival; it was the festival of Mercury and his dog, or the festival of the opening of the year by the Dog Star, and of the almanac by the astronomer.

### 3) The Lyre.

But why the lyre with three strings? And what was intended by that harmony of the three tones he invented—the low, middle, and high—which correspond to Winter, Spring, and Summer? Everything is very simple, and relates entirely to the year.

1) *Teleute* <note>original: "Teleute"</note> is a Greek word which means end, death, or expiration; and *Nephte* means exactly this in the Egyptian language, according to the opinion of all connoisseurs of this language, notably Jablonsky <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski (1693–1757), a famous scholar of Coptic and Egyptian mythology.</note>. This harmony, consisting of three strings, is the harmony of celestial movements and of the year composed of the three Egyptian seasons: Winter, Spring, and Summer. For the Egyptians—as we have already observed, and as I shall have further opportunity to prove—counted only three seasons, each consisting of four months <note>Ancient Egyptians typically divided their year into three seasons: Akhet (Inundation), Peret (Emergence/Growth), and Shemu (Harvest/Heat).</note>. At the same time, we will also perceive that the three Greek musical modes—namely the Phrygian, Dorian, and Lydian—of which this people claimed the invention for themselves (a claim never before disputed), are nothing more than an imitation of the three tones that form Mercury’s lyre. These tones took the lead alternately in hymns and poems, depending on whether their content related to one season or another. We shall have the opportunity to observe this more clearly in the future.

## Mercury’s Actions.

### 2) He plays dice with the Moon.

We have already seen above that he played dice with the Moon and won from it the 72nd part—or, as those who prefer round numbers would have it, the 70th part—of all days. From these fractions, he created five whole days, which he placed between the ending year and the new year (which previously consisted of 360 days). In this way, Rhea <note>The author uses the Greek name Rhea for the Egyptian goddess Nut. According to the myth recorded by Plutarch, the Sun (Ra) cursed Nut so she could not give birth on any day of the 360-day calendar. Mercury (Thoth) won these extra days to allow her to give birth to her five children.</note> was able to give birth at a time that was neither part of a month nor part of a year, thereby rendering the curses cast against her by the Sun powerless.

This period belonged to no month because they sought to insert these five days between the last day of the old year and the new year without incorporating them into any specific month.

These days were called <term>Epacts</term> <note>From the Greek 'epaktos,' meaning 'brought in' or 'added'; additional days used to harmonize different calendars.</note> or <term>Epagomenae</term> <note>From the Greek 'epagomenai hemereai,' meaning 'the days added on.' These are the five intercalary days of the Egyptian solar calendar.</note> by the Greeks and in the East, and they are also found among the Romans, though no scholar has yet noticed them among that people. # Fourth Class of Evidence.

## On the Names of Mercury, with which Certain
## Parts of the Year have been Designated.

### 1) Among the Egyptians.

If all the points discussed so far combine to make Mercury the inventor of astronomy or the calendar, this can be said even more so of the contents of this chapter. The first day of the Egyptian year, and the month with which it begins, bear his Egyptian name, Thoth; a point in time which fell in the middle of August when the year was established. The symbol in the calendar for this day was Thoth with a dog's head, or a man with a serpent-staff <term>serpent-staff: The caduceus, a staff entwined with two snakes, which served as the herald's staff of Mercury (Thoth).</term> and a dog at his side. The month preceding the month of Thoth, with which the year ended, was called Misor or Mesori. ### 3) Astronomical characters invented by Thoth.

If the character dedicated to Thoth or Mercury also indicated the first month of the year—which was under his protection—then one must also attribute to him the invention of the characters for the other months and planets.

The astronomical signs for the planets reach back into the grayest antiquity; they are, as I intend to prove elsewhere, a brief outline or sketch of the figures under which the planets or their protecting gods were imagined.

The twelve months were under the protection of the twelve deities known as the "Great Gods." There were six female ones, or six Moons, and six male ones, or six Suns. Each of these Moons and each of these Suns took on different forms according to the different labors performed in each month <note>This likely refers to the "Labors of the Months," a traditional cycle in ancient art where each month is represented by a specific seasonal activity, such as planting or harvesting.</note>. From this arose twelve different paintings, or twelve great gods.

This is the nature of the characters invented by our hero <note>Referring to Thoth/Mercury, the mythical founder of Egyptian wisdom.</note>, all of which correspond to the general concept generated by his various attributes.

<meta>This page continues the linguistic analysis from page 222, specifically how the German word for scrolls (Rollen) was used as a pun or a double-meaning for the "rolling" or passing of years. ...to be taken in the sense of a "book," and from this arises the legendary number of books attributed to him. Modern scholars, who considered such a text to be infallible and could not at all convince themselves that the error lay in the word *books*, considered the number 36,525, which accompanied it, to be mythical. In doing so, they deprived themselves of the only guide through which they could have gained enlightenment. Errors of this kind regarding antiquity are countless. 

But what does the word *scroll* <note>original: "Rolle"</note> mean here, one might ask? This expression had a double meaning, and it was used intentionally to lead astray those who allowed themselves to be seduced—as has happened to all commentators and all who have cited this passage after them. ### 2) Hermes.

The Greeks gave Mercury the name **Hermes**, which signified "interpreter" <note>original: *Dollmetscher*</note>. From this, they formed the verb **hermeneuein** <note>Greek: ἑρμηνεύειν</note>, meaning to interpret or explain. Jablonsky <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski, the 18th-century scholar of Egyptian antiquity mentioned on the previous page</note> suspects that this is the Egyptian name **Armais**. Because Mercury had completed the year by adding five days and supplementing what was missing <note>A reference to the myth where Hermes/Thoth wins five extra days (the epagomenal days) in a game of dice to fix the calendar</note>, Jablonsky was moved to derive the name from the two words **Er** and **Meh**, which mean "to make full" or "to complete." The Etruscans wrote it as **Urms**, sometimes also with the Oriental <note>Used here to mean Middle Eastern or Semitic</note> article, **T-Urms**. It seems that **Terminus** <note>The Roman god of boundaries and landmarks</note>—a goal or boundary—originates from this.

### 3) Mercury.

But what does the name **Mercury**, given to this same god by the Latins, signify? Is it Oriental in origin, or does it stem from the earliest inhabitants of Latium <note>The region of central Italy where Rome was founded</note>? Whichever origin one assumes, it can always be analyzed in very different ways; however, as a reliably compound word, it is very difficult to explain.

Nevertheless, after a precise examination of all possible interpretations of this name, I believe that—even if I have not fully reached the truth—I have come very close to it by perceiving within it a composition of two words, both Celtic and Latin, **Merc** and **Ur**, which mean "sign" and "man"; Mercury would therefore be the "**man of signs**."

In the French language, one says *Marqueur* [Marker], which is an exact translation of the Egyptian name **Thoth**.

No one will dispute the reality of the two root words *Marc* or *Merc* and *Ur* (or *Wr*, *Eur*, *Uir*, from which the Latins derived *Vir* <note>Latin: man</note>); for from the first, they derived the words *mercari* <note>Latin: to trade or bargain</note>, *merces* <note>Latin: trade, wages, or merchandise</note>, and the Oriental <note>A historical term for Middle Eastern or Semitic languages</note> word מהר *Mher* <note>Hebrew: likely a reference to *mahar*, meaning to acquire or to pay a purchase price</note>, which signifies exchange. This was because only such goods were offered for sale that were marked with the seller’s sign. It was exactly as it is today, where all goods and all merchant bales, and all animals sold at markets and fairs, etc.—in short, everything involved in trade—must be marked.

From this also come the words *marché* <note>French: market</note>, *Markt* [market], and *marque* <note>French: brand or mark</note>, a sign or **Mark**.

Every **mark** is a sign, and the **market** is the location or place designated, noted, and assigned for the exchange of marked items, and where the image of Mercury was erected.

The word **Merk**, common to all ancient European languages, still exists in the Nordic languages with this same meaning.

**Merk** signifies everything with which one can mark something, such as a flag, a token, a boundary, a measure, characters, letters, and so on.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the various names of the Egyptian deity Thoth, specifically focusing on his manifestation as the dog-headed god Anubis. The author transitions from discussing the Roman Mercury to the etymological origins of Anubis.</meta>

all mythologists have strayed from the right path. Most derived it from the Hebrew word נבח *Nebach* <note>original: נבח, meaning to bark</note>. Jablonski <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski (1693–1757) was a German theologian and scholar who specialized in Coptic language and Egyptian antiquities</note> derives it from the Coptic word *Anoub*, meaning gold, because—he says—Mercury’s statues were made of gold, and because the dawn and twilight, or the two heavenly gates, were signaled by two gold-colored dogs carried during the solemn processions of Isis.

However, in the Hebrew, Arabic, and even Ethiopian <note>Likely referring to Ge'ez, the classical liturgical language of Ethiopia used in scholarly comparisons at the time</note> languages, there is a word that must necessarily be the root of this name. It is the word נוב *Nub* <note>original: נוב</note>, and its specific, original meaning—which is still preserved in the Arabic language—is *revolution*, *period*, and *sequence*; in short, everything that follows in succession. For this reason, in the Arabic language, it also carries the meaning of a governor <note>likely referring to the term "Na’ib," meaning a deputy or representative who "stands in" for another</note>, while in Hebrew it means to bloom and sprout, as the products of one year always follow the products of another. Finally, in both the Hebrew and Ethiopian languages, it simultaneously signifies speech, phrasing, and eloquence, because one word always follows another.

Consequently, because he organized the annual revolutions and explained the will of the gods or the stars with eloquence, he was depicted in the form of a dog or a man with a dog’s head (whose name is so similar to the name Anubis). Held to be the guardian and gatekeeper of the heavens who opened the seasons or years, he was rightly called Anubis. For this very reason, the constellation with which the Egyptian year began is also called *Canicula* <note>Latin: "Little Dog," the Roman name for the star Sirius</note> or the Great Dog.

### 5) Cyllenius.

He was also given the epithet **Cyllenius**. "Hermes Cyllenius," says Homer, (1) "summoned the souls." This surname placed the commentators in a state of perplexity; at times it was thought he received it because he was born on Mount Cyllenus in Arcadia, other times because he had a temple there, or because a river named Hermes flowed at the foot of this mountain, and finally, because he was a son of the nymph Cyllene.

However, this surname is not Greek; rather, the peoples of the East <note>The author uses "Morgenländer" (Easterners) to refer to Semitic or Near Eastern cultures, a common perspective in 18th-century scholarship seeking the roots of Greek culture in the Levant.</note> gave it to him on account of his lyre. The word perfectly signifies **a lyre player**. It is composed from the Oriental word כלי *Celi*, *Culi*, *Cylli*, etc., which signifies a **tortoise** or a **lyre**, and from which the Greek word χελυς *khelis* <note>original: χελυς, usually transliterated as chelys, meaning tortoise shell or the lyre made from one</note>, meaning lyre, is derived.

...leave its position to another constellation. We also say a year has "gone out" <note>original: *erloschen*; literally extinguished or expired</note> when another begins. These expressions are found in all languages, but they are especially characteristic of mythological fables. This remark was necessary in relation to a fable like that of **Argus**, which has astronomy as its subject.

**Io** is the Moon; **Argus**, covered with eyes, of which one part watches while the other sleeps, is the starry sky, of which we can only ever see one half at a time. His eyes are always open toward **Io**, and **Io** is transformed into a cow because she was depicted in the form of a horned moon, or a cow's head.

**Mercury**, who opens a new year with his caduceus <note>original: *Schlangenstab*; the staff entwined with two snakes carried by the god Mercury</note>, thus ends this revolution <note>original: *Revolution*; here referring to the orbital cycle of the heavens</note> that spies on **Io** or the Moon. He takes only the head from **Argus**, because the calendar <note>original: *Almanach*</note> of the new year appears right at the end of the previous one, or the previous year has disappeared to make room for another year.

For this reason, on the festival of **Mercury** or the renewal, the old year was thrown into the water in the form of a worn-out old man.

And for this reason, at the end of **Carnival**, and when **Easter** brings about the total renewal, in various French provinces they throw the **Carmentran** <note>A traditional folk figure representing Carnival in southern France</note>—or rather the "Entering Lent" <note>original: *carême-entrant*</note>—into the water in the form of a straw man. The customs are identical; only the names are different.

Certainly this also gave rise to the Flemish custom of parading a large number of giant figures, given the names of old kings, on New Year's Day.

**Macrobius** <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius, a 5th-century Roman provincial who wrote the *Saturnalia*, a major source for ancient religious lore</note> also stumbled somewhat upon my explanation of **Argus's** moon; like me, he made the sky out of **Argus**; (2) but in **Io** he saw the Earth, and in **Mercury** the Sun; **Argus** was consequently killed because all his brilliance and all his stars were extinguished with the rising of the sun; <note>original: *veluti enecat, sagt er, vi luminis sui, conspectum earum auferendo mortalibus*; "as if he kills [them], he says, by the force of his light, by taking away the sight of them from mortals"</note>.

One should not be surprised that **Macrobius** missed two of the three characters contained in this riddle, especially the one concerning **Mercury**; this stemmed from the fact that he started from a system whose correct basis was that all pagan gods could be traced back to the Sun and the Moon.

A new touchstone for my explanation is also this: that a few days after the festival of the **Argei** <note>An ancient Roman ritual where straw effigies were thrown into the Tiber River</note> in Rome, the festival of **Janus** was celebrated. This is the new year following the old year, and between the celebrations of both festivals, five days passed in memory of the five **epagomenal days** <term>epagomenal days: extra days added to a calendar to harmonize the lunar or civil year with the solar year, often seen as "days out of time"</term>. In the Roman calendar of **Julius Caesar**, they are therefore present three times, because the beginning of the year was gradually moved to three different points in time, and the old festivals—instead of changing their place along with the altered beginning of the year—were preferred to be repeated, doubled, and tripled with every change of the year's beginning.

Few ancient deities possess such an extensive and diverse domain. But how was it possible for him to be conceived as the central point for so many subjects? This article is intended to answer this question, and it will become clear from it that only a very simple development of the first concepts formed of him, and a gradual application of his name to similar objects, were necessary for this.

### 1) God of Boundaries.

*Thot* was a root word synonymous with the word "sign." Above, we have already seen that the name *Mercury* itself in the Celtic language is composed of the word *Marke* <note>original: "Marke"</note>, which carries the complete concept of a sign or marker.

However, boundaries are signs that separate lands from one another and indicate the rights of the landowners. Every boundary was therefore a *Thot*, a *Mercury*, and all boundaries were naturally subjected to the protection of this god as the time approached when every thing had to be dedicated to a specific deity.

From this source still come the names given to borderlands and territorial divisions in our modern European languages: *Marke*, *Marca*, *Comarka*, *Mark*—from which, in turn, the French words *Marquisats* <note>Marquisates: the territory or dignity of a Marquis</note> and *Marquis* <note>Originally a "Count of the March," or border lord</note> are derived.

It even reached the point that these boundaries were carved into the figure of Mercury. In that case, they were "Herms" or "Mercury" in a double sense. Frequently, the head of Minerva—the faithful companion of Thoth in his labors—was placed atop them, and they were then called *Hermathenae* <note>original: "Herm-Athenen"; these were square stone pillars topped with a bust, often combining the features of Hermes and Athena</note>, a name that Mercury and Minerva shared in the Greek language.

If one adds the article "T" to this very word *Ermes* <note>Greek: Ἑρμῆς (Hermes)</note>, which signifies boundaries, the Latin word *Terminus* <note>meaning: boundary or limit</note> is derived from it. This is much like how the word *Terra* <note>meaning: Earth</note> originated through the combination of the article "T" and the root word *ER*. From the Latin word *Terminus*, in turn, comes the French word *un terme* <note>meaning: a term, limit, or end</note>.

### 2) God of Commerce.

Mercury also had to become the god of commerce and merchants for many reasons; for:

1) Through the organization of the year and the creation of the calendar, he had established the days specifically dedicated to bartering, annual fairs, and markets.

2) Among all nations, his name was used for the signs by which trade is facilitated, and it was even applied to bartering itself and the items intended for exchange. From this come all the French words *Marque* <note>mark</note>, *Marché* <note>market</note>, *Marchandises* <note>merchandise</note>, *Commerce* <note>commerce</note>, and *Commercer* <note>to trade</note>, as well as the words and weights called *Marc* <note>A traditional European unit of weight, especially for precious metals</note>. This was the name given to the marks used to determine the weight of items for sale.

### 3) God of Travelers and Roads.

As soon as Mercury had become the god of boundaries and merchants, he naturally also became the god of roads and travelers. Roads were only built to facilitate trade, for it was only through roads that tribes and nations achieved community. Just as two peoples came into contact with one another, they had to be united by roads so as not to remain separated, but to be able to exchange the goods unique to each land. In this way, they doubled, to a certain extent, the value of their labor, their enjoyment, and their wealth. This principle, derived from nature and always practiced between neighboring peoples, aimed to make the entire earth a single society—one that was divided by its products, yet reunited through barter.

The ancients were also so convinced of the necessity of roads for the happiness of society that they considered it a virtuous act, pleasing to the gods, to work on the maintenance of roads. From this also stems the custom of picking up all stones lying in the path and carrying them to the heaps of stones <note>original: "Steinhausen"; these piles, called *hermaia* in Greek, served both to clear the road and as a tribute to Hermes</note> dedicated to Mercury and erected at certain distances. This was a custom whose original practical reason <note>clearing the path for carts and travelers</note> was eventually forgotten, and which was later believed to have been introduced solely for the worship of Mercury.

### 4) Companion of the Dead.

Even as early as **Homer**, **Mercury** is depicted as the leader of souls into the underworld; he who could lead them there was also able to bring them back again. This privilege of **Mercury**, which seems to have no similarity at all to his other duties, confused mythologists extraordinarily; the reasons cited in their writings on the matter are far too unsatisfying to even deserve being copied here. In the meantime, nothing was simpler.

For must not **Mercury**, to whose protection the paths and journeys on earth had already been subjected, also become the protector of the "great journey"?
<note>The "great journey" is a poetic reference to death and the passage to the afterlife.</note>

It was also nothing more than natural that one would leave the protection of highways and journeys of all kinds to the deity who, through the calendar, had to some extent assigned the sun its path, and through the tropics <note>original: "Wendekreise"; referring to the solstices or the points where the sun "turns" in its annual cycle</note> had determined the points of departure and return of the sun, of death and of life.

As a continuation of this idea, the two tropics were considered the gates of life and death, and

### 5) Protector of Heralds.

Why, finally, were the heralds equipped with the serpent-staff? This symbol, held in common with **Mercury**, also placed critics in great embarrassment, as they did not know the origin of the serpent-staff; it was believed that **Mercury** was only armed with the serpent-staff because he was considered the herald of the gods and their **interpreter** <note>original: "Dollmetscher"; here meaning one who translates divine will into human understanding</note>. While this postponed the answer to the question, it did not resolve it; for one could still rightly ask: why did the heralds carry the serpent-staff? What does it signify in their hands? Why, then, is no satisfying answer given?

**Mercury** does not owe his serpent-staff to the heralds; rather, they borrow this symbol from **Mercury** because, like him, they are the interpreters of another's will. If he carries the serpent-staff—as has already been mentioned above—it is for the reason that in this manner he explains the will of the **astronomical gods**.

Just as he was regarded as an interpreter and herald, and as such carried the serpent-staff as a "speaking symbol" <note>A visual emblem that clearly announces the bearer's office or message</note> of his commission, so too did the heralds have to choose him as their protector, adopt his symbol for themselves, and wear his insignia. ## §. 2.
### What else was understood under the name of Mercury.

When people wished to give names to the days of the month, and for that reason had divided the months into four parts or weeks with reference to the lunar quarters or lunar months, they placed them under the protection of the seven planets. By this means, one immediately obtained two series: one of seven days, and another of seven planets, which bore the same names. The very same thing happened when one wished to give names to the seven metals. These formed a third series, designated by the same names as the previous ones, and since the name Mercury always occupied a part of these series, it followed that Mercury became

->one of the seven planets<-
->one of the seven days, and<-
->one of the seven metals.<- <note>In traditional alchemy and astrology, the "seven metals of antiquity" were linked to the seven celestial bodies: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), Lead (Saturn), and Quicksilver (Mercury).</note>

We will now consider him under these three relationships.

### 1) Mercury as a Planet.

In the most ancient times, the seven planets were regarded as the overseers of time; one therefore began to give them names that referred to the concepts formed about them. — In this regard, it was only fair <note>original: "billig"; here meaning equitable or fitting</note> that the inventor of the calendar should share his name with a planet. Indeed, one of the two planets located between the Moon and the Sun <note>This refers to the ancient geocentric model where Mercury and Venus were situated between the Earth/Moon and the Sun.</note> bears the name Mercury in Egypt, Greece, and Italy, and one can

### 2) Mercury as a day of the week.

The names of the days of the week were arranged in such an order that the **Sun** gave its name to the first day, and the **Moon** to the second day, while **Mercury** shared its name specifically with the middle day of the week. This arrangement was no coincidence; it was believed that the inventor of astronomy must occupy a distinguished place among the days of the week. Since the first day was already possessed by the Sun, and the day of rest <note>Referring to the Sabbath or Saturday, governed by Saturn.</note> by Saturn, Mercury was granted the middle place, or the "heart"—terms that were considered equivalent in those times.

In order for Mercury to take this position, it was done intentionally that he was not counted according to his astronomical rank assigned to him by nature. Since, therefore, the names of the days were not borrowed from the planets according to their physical or natural order—and since, if one takes them four by four <note>This refers to the ancient "planetary hours" system: if you list the planets in order of their orbital speed and assign one to each hour of the day, the planet governing the first hour of each subsequent day follows a pattern of skipping two (or "taking them four by four").</note>, Saturn and the Sun (which give their names to the consecutive Saturday and Sunday) have two planets, Jupiter and Mars, between them, and the same is the case with the Sun and the Moon, etc.—so there really should have been two planets between Mars and Mercury if they were to share their names with the two following days (Tuesday and Wednesday). This, however, is not the case, as the Sun is located between these two planets. The Egyptians and Persians (probably also the ancient peoples devoted to agriculture) also indeed call Mercury

### 3) Mercury as a metal.

When the Egyptians applied themselves to natural history and chemistry, <note>The author uses "Chymie," referring to the early modern transition from alchemy to chemical science.</note> they learned that there were seven metals, which they also named after the seven planets. Thus, the two most precious metals for barter and trade, gold and silver, were dedicated to the Sun and the Moon. One was called gold because it was as yellow as the Sun, and the other silver because it was as white as the Moon. But why did the metal we call **mercury** <note>Also known as quicksilver.</note> fall to the inventor of astronomy, or to the planet from which the middle day of the week takes its name?

## Article V.

->Whether Thoth or Mercury was a real or only an<-
->allegorical being?<-

Having seen that the history of Mercury is merely an allegory relating to the invention of astronomy and the agricultural calendar, there remains only to investigate whether a person named **Thoth** among the Egyptians, **Hermes** among the Greeks, and **Mercury** among the Latins—in short, whether a *man of signs* <note>original: "Zeichen-Mann." This term refers to a personified symbol or a legendary figure who serves as a marker for human progress and the invention of symbolic systems like writing and calendars.</note> lived in every instance, who actually invented everything attributed to him; or whether he himself is merely an allegorical being?

This question is perhaps more difficult to resolve than the allegory itself contained in the story of Thoth. Therefore, *Jablonsky* <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski (1693–1757) was a prominent German scholar of Oriental languages whose work *Pantheon Aegyptiorum* was a standard reference for Egyptian mythology in the 18th century.</note>, so famous for his thorough investigations into Egyptian mythology, has devoted a considerable part of the chapter where he treats *Thoth* (1) to this investigation, and from it the following results emerge:

1) *Thoth* was an allegorical name given to the god of arts and sciences, *Vulcan* or *Ptah* <note>The author equates the Roman Vulcan with the Egyptian Ptah, the demiurge and patron of craftsmen and architects.</note>, and to the columns upon which public instruction was written, and which were placed under the protection of *Vulcan*.

...I hope to be able to shed some light on this subject.

1) He stands in close connection with the history of **Osiris** and **Isis**, of which one can be convinced by the passage from **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote extensively on the mythic origins of Egypt.</note> located at the beginning of this work.

3) He was a contemporary of King **Thamus**, as **Plato** (4) says, who calls him at once a god or divine man, and an inventor of the sciences.

4) **Sanchuniathon** <note>A legendary Phoenician author; his fragments often attempt to provide a rationalized, historical basis for ancient myths.</note> says at the end of the first fragment that he was a son of **Misor**. 5) He continues, saying that he reigned in **Egypt**.

All these combined circumstances seem to indicate a truly existing historical person, and must even, with probability, determine the time in which he lived.

It was reliably at that time when the southern Asian nations—the **Chaldeans**, **Canaanites**, **Egyptians**, etc.—under the leadership of the commanders of their first colonies (namely the **Canaanites** under **Chna** <note>A name often associated in antiquity with Canaan himself.</note>, of whom **Sanchuniathon** speaks, and the **Egyptians** under **Menes** <note>Traditionally considered the first human Pharaoh and the unifier of Egypt.</note>), devoted themselves to agriculture; that is to say, at the time when, after the **Great Flood** <note>original: "Sündfluth"</note> which had devastated these regions, everything began to flourish once more.

4) In his *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue *Phaedrus* contains the famous myth of Thoth presenting the invention of writing to King Thamus.</note>.

He synchronizes Egyptian history with Phoenician and Greek accounts, placing Thoth in the era of the first agricultural colonies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's investigation into the historical identity of Thoth (Mercury), specifically linking him to the genealogical figures found in the writings of Sanchuniathon and Moses (the Pentateuch). The previous page established Thoth as a contemporary of King Thamus and a son of Misor.</meta>

Misor is the **Mizraim** <note>In the Hebrew Bible, Mizraim is the son of Ham and the ancestor of the Egyptians; the name itself is the Hebrew word for Egypt.</note> of **Moses**, the progenitor of the Egyptians, and this very person also seems to be **Menes**, the first king of Thebes or Egypt.

His successor is called **Athotes**. This name very much resembles the name **Thoth**; however, according to **Eratosthenes** <note>A Greek polymath and librarian at Alexandria known for his work in geography and chronology.</note>, it means only a *son of Thoth*; and according to **Jablonski** <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski (1693–1757), a scholar of Coptic and Egyptian antiquity.</note>, a *contemporary of Thoth* or of the *invention of the sciences*.

**Thoth** would thus be the father of **Athotes** and a contemporary of **Menes**, or **Menes** himself, because he is called a king of Egypt.

**Manetho** <note>An Egyptian priest who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek in the 3rd century BCE.</note> says that he presented his works to King **Tham**, a name which means as much as the *Righteous*, and is identical to *Sydyk*.

This [figure], however, is transplanted into the tenth generation of the world: *Sydyk* or *Tham* might therefore well be one and the same as the one whom **Moses** calls *Sadyk-Tham-im* <note>original: "Sadyk-Tham-im." This is a transliteration of the Hebrew words "Zaddik" (Righteous) and "Tamim" (Blameless/Perfect), used in Genesis 6:9 to describe Noah.</note> or the *Righteous of the Righteous*, whom he likewise places in the tenth generation of the world, and who stems from the same family as the leaders of the peoples, *Mizraim* and *Chna* <note>A name for Canaan.</note>.

Since *Sadyk-Tham-im* <note>Noah</note> was the commander of this family, it was very natural that **Thoth** offered or dedicated the works containing his astronomical inventions to him, especially since this ruler of nations is presented by **Moses** himself as the *man of the Adama* <note>original: "Adama," Hebrew for earth or soil.</note>, *the Ge* <note>original: "Ge," Greek for earth.</note>, *or the earth*, that is to say: as the *inventor of agriculture*.

Because **Thoth’s** astronomical works intended the perfection of agriculture, this must have been one more motive for offering them to him.

<summary>The author synchronizes Egyptian and Phoenician mythology with Biblical genealogy, identifying Thoth as a contemporary of the biblical Noah (Sadyk-Tham-im) and the Egyptian Menes, suggesting his astronomical inventions were meant to aid the development of agriculture.</summary>

--- Page 327 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s comparative study of ancient genealogies and mythologies. Following the discussion on page 256 regarding the identities of Thoth and Mizraim, the author now addresses common scholarly errors and proposes a linguistic link between biblical figures and Egyptian deities.</meta>

**Jablonski** <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski (1693–1757), a theologian and scholar of Coptic and Egyptian antiquity.</note> was, as has already occurred, misled by the idea that the arts could only be invented through the "fire of genius," leading him to confuse **Thoth** with **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire and craftsmanship, associated by the Greeks with Hephaestus and by the Egyptians with Ptah.</note>; however, **Vulcan** is called **Ptah** <note>original: "Phta"</note> in the Egyptian language, and this may provide new evidence that **Thoth** is one and the same as **Mizraim** or **Menes**.

When **Moses** lists the children of **Ham** <note>original: "Cham"</note>, among whom **Mizraim** belongs, he seems to count four of them: **Cush**, **Canaan**, **Phut**, and **Mizraim**.

In the meantime, he only speaks of three when he again indicates their children and their places of settlement, and **Phut** is passed over entirely in silence. On the other hand, these names are written in the Samaritan text in such a way that the name **Phut** is not separated from the name **Mizraim**. One might therefore suspect that these two names designated one and the same person, and that the name **Phut** was merely a derivation from the name **Ptah**, which would have been attributed to this person with all the more right since he had introduced the already invented astronomical knowledge into his colony.

The name **Menes** would likewise be suitable for him. This name is identical to the name **Men**, which in all ancient languages signified the sun and the moon <note>likely referring to the Greek "mene" for moon</note>, the leaders and lights of the universe. Thus, it was rightly given to the leaders of colonies, as **Menes** was a leader of the people. In the same way, it also suited **Thoth**, whether he was one person with **Mizraim** or **Menes**, or merely their contemporary, because he had invented or perfected the calendar—the absolutely necessary and luminous guide of a society practicing agriculture.

*Thoth* would therefore be a real being in relation to the invention of *astronomy* and the time of its origin; however, he is an allegorical being in relation to the extension of his name—namely, that it was bestowed upon the deity who presided over the *calendar*. The same applies to the fables invented with regard to *astronomy*, and to all the works subsequently produced on this subject, or those given the form of a *journal* <note>The author refers to the practice of naming periodicals after Mercury, the messenger god, a common practice in 18th-century Europe (e.g., the *Mercure de France* or *Der Teutsche Merkur*).</note>, just as there are still books in *Europe* today published under the name *Mercury*.

Whatever may be the case with this chronological investigation, it remains proven that *Mercury* or *Thoth* was regarded as the inventor of *astronomy* and its characters <note>original: "Charaktere"; here referring to written symbols or astronomical signs</note>; that all the symbols accompanying him consistently referred to this art, and that in this respect he was literally the secret scribe and advisor to *Saturn* <note>Saturn was often associated with Chronos, or Time, in ancient scholarship; Thoth, as the keeper of the calendar, "advised" Time.</note>; establishing this firmly was what I had set out to do.

# Introduction.

Among all mythological stories, the life of Hercules of Thebes <note>The author distinguishes the Greek "Hercules of Thebes" from other figures of the same name, such as the Egyptian or Tyrian versions of the hero.</note> is that from which the allegorical and symbolic spirit of antiquity shines forth most brilliantly and truly. For by encompassing the entire career of a hero from his birth to his death, this symbolic spirit could take on the most interesting form, multiply the scenes infinitely, choose the most opposing disguises, produce the greatest contrast between the individual various parts, pile up symbols, and multiply allusions—and yet always proceed from a **center** of **unity**. Through this, the most apparent inconsistencies and all the fables heaped upon one another form such a pleasant, easily understood whole that the correctness of every single symbol and riddle of which it consists becomes immediately visible.

This new history <note>original: "neue Geschichte"</note> stands in the closest connection with the history of Saturn and Mercury; together with these, it forms three allegories of the same nature relating to the same objects. Through this correspondence and harmony, the explanation of this new history—which is already probable in itself—attains the most irresistible certainty.

But in order to proceed not from an arbitrary point, but rather from one drawn from antiquity and [consistent with] its concepts...

# Part One.

## Diodorus’s Life of Hercules of Thebes.

This is the proper place to speak of the great deeds of Hercules. Writers always find themselves in a great dilemma when they encounter the history of this god; for on the one hand, it is known that through the quantity and magnitude of his deeds, he surpassed everything remarkable that has ever been performed among men. This makes it difficult to worthily recount actions whose reward was immortality <note>original: "Unsterblichkeit." In Greek mythology, Hercules is the quintessential hero who achieves apotheosis—becoming a god—through his "labors" or trials.</note>. On the other hand, because many people place no faith in mythological tales—partly due to their age and partly due to their perceived impossibility—one must either omit most of Hercules’s deeds entirely, thereby stripping him of a great portion of his glory, or, by choosing to tell them all, one becomes committed to an unbelievable story..... However, even if one were to admit that mythology has somewhat overstepped the bounds of punctual truth, is that a reason to justly reject it all? — — It would be unfair to still envy Hercules the well-deserved praise owed to him for his widespread benevolence and the many labors <note>original: "Arbeiten" – likely referring to the Twelve Labors of Hercules, or *Athloi*.</note> he performed in various places across the earth. Let us at least maintain for his memory that reverence and gratitude which our fathers,

## Origin of Hercules.

To begin with the ancestors of Hercules: Perseus was the son of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus.</note> and Danae, the daughter of Acrisius. This prince married Andromeda, the daughter of Cepheus, with whom he had a son named Electryon. From Electryon and Eurymeda, the daughter of Pelops, Alcmene was born. Jupiter paid a visit to Alcmene by night, deceiving her by taking on the appearance of her husband, Amphitryon; it was to this encounter that Hercules owed his life. It is said that at that time, Jupiter wished for the night to last three times longer than usual. Shortly before Alcmene’s delivery, Jupiter—who was always attentive to the birth of Hercules—declared in the presence of all the gods that he intended to grant the kingdom of Perseus to the child who would be born on that day. Juno <note>The queen of the gods, known for her jealousy regarding her husband Jupiter's many affairs.</note>, driven by jealousy, immediately persuaded her daughter Ilythia <note>The goddess of childbirth, also known as Eileithyia.</note> to delay the birth of Hercules and to instead hasten the birth of Eurystheus before the appointed time. Jupiter, though deceived by this trick, did not take back his word, but he simultaneously made provision for the glory of Hercules.

Therefore, in accordance with his promise, he not only gave the kingdom to Eurystheus but also made him the commander over Hercules. However, he persuaded Juno to allow Hercules to be placed among the gods after he had completed the twelve labors <note>original: "Arbeiten." These are the famous heroic tasks Hercules was forced to perform as a penance, which ultimately led to his immortality.</note> commanded of him by Eurystheus.

### Hercules Abandoned and Restored to his Mother.

Out of fear of Juno’s <note>The queen of the gods, who was notoriously jealous of Hercules as he was the son of her husband Jupiter and the mortal Alcmene.</note> jealousy, Alcmene abandoned her child immediately after her labor in the field that is still called the "Field of Hercules" to this day. The beauty of this child caught the attention of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom, also known as Athena.</note> while she was on a walk with Juno. Juno was persuaded by this goddess to allow the child to suckle at her breast; however, quite contrary to what one would expect for his age, he suckled so strongly that the goddess, overcome by the sudden pain, threw him to the ground. Minerva picked him up again, carried him back to his mother, and advised her to raise him.

Who could fail to admire the wonderful hand of fate <note>original: "Fügung des Schicksals." This refers to the providential or destined arrangement of events.</note> here? A mother, whose duty it was to love her child and think of his preservation, abandoned him; and this very child had to find his savior in his enemy, and owe his life to his very enemy.

### First Deeds of Hercules.

Two snakes, which the vengeful Juno then sent to murder this child (who had been given the name Alceus), were strangled by the little one as he squeezed their necks with his hands. Thus, Juno herself was forced to become the author of his fame; for as soon as the Greeks heard of this heroic deed, they no longer called him Alceus, but Hercules <note>The name Hercules, or *Herakles* in Greek, ironically translates to "Glory of Hera" (Juno), signifying that his trials under her persecution led to his eternal renown.</note>. He therefore did not owe his name to his parents, like other children, but solely to his bravery.

With Amphitryon, who fled from Tiryns, he came to Thebes, where he was raised. Here he devoted himself to various physical exercises and soon surpassed all other men in bodily strength and greatness of soul <note>original: "Seelengröße." A classical virtue referring to a noble, courageous, and magnanimous spirit.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the infancy of Hercules to his early adulthood. Upon reaching the age of youth, he freed *Thebes* from the servitude under which it had sighed until then; thus early did he show his fatherland the gratitude it was due.

The *Thebans* were at that time under the dominion of *Erginus*, the king of the *Minyans*. This prince sent deputies to *Thebes* every year to demand tribute. Since these men always performed this task in a manner insulting to the inhabitants, *Hercules*—unconcerned about the unfortunate consequences his plan might bring—undertook an action that will preserve his name forever. For the deputies had already arrived in *Thebes* again to collect the tribute, and had already inflicted every imaginable shame upon the citizens, when *Hercules* chased them out of the city, punishing them by depriving them of their body's extremities. <note>According to myth, Hercules cut off the ears, noses, and hands of the Minyan heralds, tied them around their necks, and told them to take that as their "tribute."</note>

Immediately, *Erginus* demanded the extradition of the culprit, whom King *Creon* of *Thebes* was already willing to hand over out of fear of *Erginus’* power. However, *Hercules* persuaded the youths of his age to liberate their fatherland from servitude. In the absence of other weapons (which the *Minyans* had taken from the *Thebans* to strip them of any thought of rebellion), he gave them the weapons hanging in the temples—those which their ancestors had taken from enemies and dedicated to the gods. Upon receiving news of *Erginus'* approach with an army, Hercules awaited him in a narrow pass. By doing so, *Hercules* rendered the great, superior number of enemies so useless that not only did *Erginus* himself perish, but nearly his entire army with him. Now *Hercules* marched upon the capital of the *Minyans*, *Archo-mene* <note>original: "Archomene." This likely refers to the city of Orchomenus, the capital of the Minyans in Boeotia.</note>...

### The command given to Hercules to perform twelve labors; his rage thereat.

Now Eurystheus, the king of Argos, feared that Hercules might become too powerful. He therefore sent for him to assign the labors he was to perform. Hercules initially gave him a refusal, but Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter"; the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus, who was Hercules's father.</note> commanded him to obey his king, Eurystheus. Nevertheless, he first went to Delphi to consult the oracle, but there too he received the answer that the gods demanded the completion of these twelve labors, after the successful conclusion of which he would attain **immortality**. Hercules fell into the deepest sadness over this; he considered it unworthy of his bravery to serve a man who was far beneath him; yet on the other hand, it seemed dangerous and even impossible to him not to obey his father Jupiter.

While he was dwelling on these reflections, Juno <note>original: "Juno"; the Roman name for Hera, the queen of the gods, who was famously jealous of Hercules as the son of her husband’s mistress.</note> deranged his mind; madness took possession of his ailing intellect, and with each day the fits became more violent, finally turning into a murderous rage. He wanted to kill Iolaus <note>Hercules’s nephew and loyal companion.</note>, but since the latter had fled, he shot his own children, whom he mistook for enemies,

# The Twelve Labors of Hercules.

## First Labor.

->The Lion in the Nemean Forest.<-

Among the labors which Eurystheus now imposed upon him to perform, according to Diodorus <note>original: "Diodor"; referring to Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who recorded various myths.</note>, the slaying of the Nemean lion was the first. This lion of immense size could be wounded neither by iron, nor steel, nor stones; Hercules therefore had to subdue him merely through the strength of his arms. The entire land between Mycenae and Nemea, near a mountain named Tretos <note>Mount Tretos, meaning "the perforated mountain," was famous for the caves that served as the lion's lair.</note>, was frequently devastated by this lion. At the foot of this mountain was a large cave, where this monster usually retreated. Hercules hurried there, blocked the entrance of the cave, fought with the lion at very close range, and finally strangled it with his bare hands by compressing its throat. The immense skin of this animal subsequently served him both as clothing and as a shield in his battles.

# Second Labor.

## The Lernaean Hydra.

Following the slaying of the Nemean lion, the battle with the Lernaean Hydra followed. This monster had a body upon which were 100 necks, each of which ended in a serpent’s head. If a neck was struck off, two other heads immediately grew in its place. In this manner, its strength for defense doubled with every wound, which is why it was also considered invincible. To overcome this difficulty, Hercules employed a cunning ruse: he ordered Iolaus <note>original: "Jolas"; Hercules's nephew and faithful companion who often served as his charioteer.</note> to sear the severed part with a torch to prevent that unfortunate regrowth. Through this stratagem, he finally defeated this beast, after which he dipped his arrows into the animal's bile <note>original: "Galle"; referring here to the Hydra's poisonous venom.</note> so that every shot he would take at other monsters would cause incurable wounds.

The execution of this command appeared exceptionally difficult: for if Hercules wished to follow it precisely, he had to choose his time with great prudence; if he left the animal with too much strength, he ran the risk of being torn to pieces, but through a too-vigorous attack, he might kill it. Nevertheless, through his skill in combat, he succeeded in delivering it truly alive to Eurystheus. When the king saw him, as he [carried] this wild

# Continuation of the Third Labor.
## The Victory over the Centaurs.

Hercules then fought against the Centaurs <note>Mythical beings with the upper body of a human and the lower body of a horse.</note> of his own accord, for which the following event provided the occasion: A Centaur named Pholus had entered into a bond of hospitality with Hercules. This Centaur possessed a cask of wine which, according to legend, the ancient Bacchus <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy.</note> had given to Pholus with the command to preserve it until the arrival of Hercules. When Hercules came into this land four generations later, the Centaur remembered the command received from Bacchus. In his honor, he therefore brought forth the cask that had been hidden underground until then and tapped into it. Immediately, an excellent aroma, arising from the quality and age of the wine, wafted up and spread as far as the nearby dwellings of the other Centaurs. 

These Centaurs, enticed by this pleasant smell, gathered in great numbers around Pholus’s dwelling and fell upon this drink with impetuosity. Pholus, trembling with fear, sought to hide himself, but Hercules defended himself with astonishing courage against the Centaurs, who wanted to carry off the cask by force. Here he had to fight against beings whom the mother of the gods <note>This likely refers to Rhea or Cybele, ancient mother goddesses of the earth and wild nature.</note> had equipped with both the strength and speed of horses as well as the reason and experience of humans. In this attack, some of the Centaurs were armed with fir trees that still had their full roots, others with large stones, and still others with firebrands,

# Fourth Labor.

## The Hind with Golden Horns.

Thereupon Eurystheus commanded Hercules to deliver to him the exceptionally fast-running hind with golden horns <note>This creature is traditionally known as the Ceryneian Hind, a beast sacred to Diana (Artemis) that was said to outrun arrows.</note>. In order to achieve his goal in this undertaking, he made use of his cunning more than his strength; for some say he captured her in nets, others that he set snares for her, and still others that he hunted her until she was exhausted and thus took possession of her. This much is certain: he completed this labor without running the slightest risk of danger.

# Fifth Labor.

## The Birds of Prey of the Stymphalian Lake.

Now he received the command to hunt the birds of prey of the Stymphalian Lake, for the execution of which he likewise employed his wit. An unbelievable multitude of these birds lived around the aforementioned lake, and they devastated all the crops in the neighboring regions. Had he wished to kill them one by one, it would have been impossible to exterminate them completely. For this reason, Hercules invented a <term>brazen drum</term> <note>original: "eherne Trommel"; while this text mentions a drum, other traditions specify bronze castanets or rattles fashioned by the god Hephaestus.</note>, and through its constant and loud noise, he drove them all away. This method completely cleared the lake of these birds of prey.

This hero remained the victor in all the games without ever having fought; for no one dared to compete with him because of his extraordinary strength. ### The Gifts which *Hercules* Received from the Gods.

We must not pass over in silence the gifts that the gods gave to *Hercules* to honor his bravery. For when he allowed his warlike labors to rest for a while to recover at festivals, social gatherings, and games, all the gods presented him with gifts, each in a very unique way. *Minerva* <note>The Roman name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom and crafts.</note> brought him a veil <note>original: 'Schleier'; in mythology, Athena is often said to have woven a magnificent robe or cloak for Hercules.</note>, while *Vulcan* <note>The god of fire and blacksmithing, also known as Hephaestus.</note> gave him a club and a breastplate.

Between these two deities, a great rivalry existed because of the similarity of their activities. *Minerva* devoted herself to the arts of peace, which aim for the utility and pleasure of life, whereas *Vulcan* worked only for the arts intended for war.

From the other gods, he received the following gifts: *Neptune* gave him a horse; *Mercury* a sword; *Apollo* a bow, the use of which he also taught to *Hercules*; and *Ceres* <note>The goddess of agriculture, known as Demeter to the Greeks.</note> established the Lesser Mysteries <note>The Lesser Mysteries of Eleusis were held at Agrae; tradition states they were founded to allow Hercules to be initiated and purified.</note> in his honor as an atonement for the killing of the *Centaurs* <note>original: 'Centauern'; refers to the accidental or incidental killing of the half-horse, half-human creatures during his labors.</note>.

Among the women whom *Jupiter* loved, the first was *Niobe*, a daughter of *Phoroneus*, and the last was *Alcmene*. Mythologists count sixteen generations between the first and the last. *Jupiter* thus began to father humans with a mortal woman—a lineage that *Alcmene* counted among her own ancestors. ## The Battle of *Hercules* Against the Giants.

Meanwhile, the Giants undertook to wage war against the gods at *Pallene* <note>A peninsula in Chalcidice, Greece, which according to myth was the site of the Gigantomachy, the great battle between the Olympian gods and the Giants.</note>. *Hercules* rushed to the gods' aid, slew several of these "children of the Earth," and received very great honors in return. *Jupiter* granted the title "Olympians" only to those gods who had provided him with assistance, as a mark of distinction between the brave and the cowardly. Even though *Bacchus* <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy.</note> and *Hercules* had only mortal mothers, they were nonetheless honored with this glorious title—not simply because they were sons of *Jupiter*, but because they shared similar inclinations with their father and had softened the coarseness of humanity through their good deeds <note>original: 'Wohlthaten'; referring to the civilizing influence and benefits they brought to human society.</note>.

## *Hercules* Slew the Eagle of *Prometheus*.

During this time, *Jupiter* held *Prometheus*—who had shared the heavenly fire with mankind—not only captive in chains and bonds, but an eagle was also forced to gnaw at his liver. *Hercules* shot this eagle, for he saw that *Prometheus* was only being punished because he had spread blessings upon the human race. Subsequently, he completely appeased the wrath of *Jupiter* and, in this way, became the savior of a benefactor of mankind.

# Eighth Labor.

## The Mares of Diomedes.

He then received the order to fetch the mares of Diomedes from Thrace <note>A region in Southeast Europe, north of Greece, known in myth for its fierce warriors and wild horses.</note>. They were so fierce that they had to be given bronze mangers, and so strong that they could only be bound with iron chains. They were not fed grain to eat, but rather the limbs of unfortunate strangers who, upon arriving in Thrace, were hacked into pieces. Intending to steal these mares, Hercules first seized their master; he then made them completely docile by feeding them the flesh of the very man who had accustomed them to eating human flesh. Immediately after they were delivered, Eurystheus <note>The king of Tiryns who assigned the labors to Hercules.</note> dedicated them to Juno <note>The Roman name for Hera, the queen of the gods.</note>. Their lineage continued until the reign of the Macedonian King Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note>.

# Tenth Labor.

## The Cattle of Geryon.

---

->On this occasion, the island of Crete is cleared of wild beasts, and Africa is made fertile.<-

As his tenth labor, Eurystheus ordered Hercules to fetch the cattle of Geryon, which grazed on the coasts of Iberia <note>The ancient name for the peninsula comprising modern-day Spain and Portugal.</note>. Hercules realized that he could carry out this command only with great effort and preparation; he therefore equipped a very fine fleet, which he manned with soldiers worthy of such an undertaking. # Twelfth Labor.

## The Golden Apples of the Hesperides.

The final labor of Hercules, which consisted of fetching the golden apples of the **Hesperides** <note>Nymphs of the evening and the golden light of sunset, who tended a blessed garden in the far west of the world.</note> from Africa, required him to make a second sea voyage to that land. The opinions of mythologists are quite divided regarding these apples; for some say that in certain gardens belonging to the Hesperides, actual golden apples were grown, but were guarded by a terrifying dragon who watched over them incessantly. Others claim that the Hesperides possessed such beautiful flocks of sheep that, by way of poetic license, they were given the epithet "golden," just as the name is given to **Venus** <note>The Roman goddess of love (Aphrodite in Greek), often called "Golden Venus" in classical poetry due to her beauty and radiance.</note> because of her beauty. Finally, some report that these sheep had a very peculiar color that closely resembled gold. These latter writers even add that one must understand the "dragon" to be the guardian of these sheep—a very strong and courageous man who had the habit of killing all those who dared to steal any members of his flock. . . . This much is certain: after slaying the guardian of the sheep or apples, Hercules brought them to **Eurystheus**, and now, having completed his twelve labors, he felt assured of the immortality promised to him as a reward, just as the oracle of **Apollo** <note>The Delphic Oracle, which originally told Hercules he would become immortal if he successfully served Eurystheus for twelve years.</note> had foretold.

## The Rescue of the Hesperides and the Slaying of Busiris and Emathion.

Meanwhile, we must also include here what the mythologists relate concerning **Atlas** and the **Hesperides**. In the land of Hesperis, they say, there once lived two very famous brothers, Atlas and **Hesperus**; Hesperus became the father of a daughter named **Hesperis**, whom he gave in marriage to his brother Atlas, and from whom the land received its name. Atlas sired seven daughters with Hesperis, who were called either **Atlantides** after their father, or **Hesperides** after their mother. Since they possessed extraordinary beauty and uncommon wisdom, it is said that upon hearing this rumor, the Egyptian King **Busiris** <note>A mythical king of Egypt who, according to legend, sacrificed foreigners to the gods to end a famine; Hercules eventually slew him.</note> formed the resolution to seize them. He commanded pirates to invade their land, abduct them, and then bring them to him. These pirates ambushed the daughters of Atlas just at the time when they were enjoying themselves in their gardens, seized them immediately, hurried with them to their ships, and had already embarked with them when **Hercules** unexpectedly came upon them during their meal near the shore. After he had learned from these young girls of the misfortune that had befallen them, he killed all the abductors and brought the Atlantides themselves back to their father.

This grateful prince then not only presented Hercules with the apples for which he had come, but also taught him **Astronomy** <note>The study of the stars and celestial bodies; the text suggests Hercules brought this scientific knowledge back to the Greeks.</note> from the ground up. Atlas had learned this science through his own great diligence and reflection, and had progressed very far in it. He had even, with much skill, manufactured a **celestial sphere** <note>A model representing the stars and constellations as they appear in the night sky; the "heavens" that Atlas was said to support.</note>; therefore, it was subsequently believed that he carried the world on his shoulders. ## Hercules yields his wife Megara to Iolaus; he seeks Iole; consequences of this event.

## The sacrifices offered to him.

His friend Menoetius <note>The father of Patroclus, the companion of Achilles.</note> sacrificed a bull, a wild boar, and a ram to him, and ordered that these same sacrifices be offered to him every year in the city of the Opuntians. The Thebans also followed this example.

In the meantime, the Athenians were the first people to pay him divine honors, and the example of this piety soon caused all the peoples of Greece, and subsequently all nations of the earth, to recognize him as a god.
