# Part Two

->Hercules is not a real person; he is only a symbolic figure, concerning a real and physical object.<-

---

## First Article
### Preliminary Remarks

->§. 1.<-
->The story of Hercules is an allegory.<-

For nearly as long as the story has been told, the preceding lengthy narrative has been considered the history of a truly existing hero, whose truth was merely distorted through oral traditions and the addition of several fictions <note>original: "Fictionen" — refers here to the mythical embellishments and supernatural elements added to historical accounts over time.</note>. Whenever certain scholars <note>original: "Gelehrte" — referring to Enlightenment-era mythologists and historians.</note> were unwilling to rest easy with this judgment and wished to see in it nothing but an allegory, they always gained only a few followers. This, however, did not stem at all from their opinions being groundless; the time had simply not yet arrived when these subjects were to be fully developed through more rigorous examination and prior discoveries.

One must even concede that the very manner in which these allegorical explanations were provided had so little to recommend them that they were rather a

<vocab>Hercules, Allegory, Fictions, Scholars, Mythology</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces a scholarly shift in the text, moving from the myth of Hercules to a critical argument that he is a symbolic representation of physical phenomena rather than a historical figure.</summary>
<keywords>Hercules, allegory, mythology, historical criticism, symbolism, Enlightenment scholarship</keywords>

--- Page 372 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from a narrative account of Hercules to a systematic allegorical analysis. The previous page concluded by suggesting that earlier attempts to explain these myths as allegories failed because they were incomplete, leading to "prejudice" or skepticism from readers. The author now proposes a comprehensive "system" where every detail of the Hercules myth—from birth to death—is part of a unified symbolic structure.</meta>

...apt to arouse prejudice against themselves. The clarifiers <note>original: "Klärer" — referring to earlier scholars or rationalist mythologists who attempted to explain myths as metaphors.</note> of this history well realized that the subjects contained therein could be interpreted allegorically, but they did not yet oversee the entire structure; they therefore gave explanations concerning only individual parts, and what they did not explain seemed to be an irrefutable objection against their system.

To avoid this error, I will strive—just as I sought to show a perfect agreement of all individual parts in the allegorical sense in the history of Saturn and that of Mercury—to also explain all the components of the history of Hercules. I want to demonstrate that, from the birth to the death of this hero, it contains only allegorical features; that all persons and labors <note>original: "Arbeiten" — a reference to the famous Twelve Labors of Hercules.</note> occurring in the account of his labors, down to the very order and sequence of these labors, were absolutely necessary for the beauty and perfection of this allegory lying hidden beneath the history of Hercules. I want to show that one cannot move any labor from its place without simultaneously harming the harmony of the whole and missing the allegorical meaning.

In this way, one will become aware that the history of Hercules is only an allegory; yes, even more, one will find it well-founded that he is called the general of Osiris or Saturn, and the companion of Thoth or Mercury <note>The author connects Hercules to Egyptian figures (Osiris/Thoth) and other Roman/Greek gods (Saturn/Mercury), suggesting they all belong to a single, unified symbolic system of nature or physics.</note>. In short, all these allegories flow from one source, or rather, to put it better, form but a single allegory.

### §. 2.
### Why this story has been considered a real one for so long.

It is not surprising that the meaning of these allegories has been lost, and that people have even forgotten

<meta>This page continues the argument that Hercules’s story is a systematic allegory. The text begins mid-sentence, completing a thought from the previous page about how the historical narrative grew out of a symbolic core.</meta>

[on,] that purely allegorical subjects lie at the foundation. They had to imperceptibly become entirely historical; the memory of their first origin had to disappear, since they had arisen in the Orient <note>In this context, "the Orient" refers generally to the ancient Near East, including Phoenicia and Egypt.</note> in the grayest antiquity, were presented under the guise of an actual history, and were composed in a language that is now less understandable.

The Hercules who arose far earlier than the Greeks—the Hercules who, at the time of his origin, was the leader of the gods of Sabeism <note>original: "Sabeismus" — a term historically used to describe ancient star-worship or the religions of the Near East that preceded Greek mythology.</note>, the symbol of the Almighty, the soul of growth, and for whom temples were first erected among the Phoenicians—this Hercules appeared to the Greeks as if through a degradation. Just as Saturn became a prince far too famous for his cruelties, Hercules appeared only as the son of Alcmene, as the last among the gods and the first among the heroes.

As long as one viewed Hercules, as has happened until now, only through the eyes of our predecessors and teachers, the Greeks, it was also impossible for Hercules to regain his former dignity in our midst.

To discover the origin of all these things, one therefore had to take refuge in the Orient; yet the Orient seems so dark, and people have so often already misused the Eastern languages to see in them whatever they wished to see, and so few traces of the ancient wisdom remain, that one did not seem to expect the discovery of these matters at all. —

## Ideas which various modern scholars formed of Hercules and his labors.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Hercules as an astronomical allegory, specifically detailing the scholars who interpreted his twelve labors as the movement of the sun through the twelve signs of the zodiac.</meta>

Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar and theologian.</note> dedicated an entire chapter in his learned work on Heathenism (1) to the proof that Hercules was the sun, and that his twelve labors arose through the division of the zodiac into twelve signs.

Cuper (2) <note>Gisbert Cuper (1644–1716), a Dutch philologist and politician.</note> held this same view. According to him, Hercules is the sun; his club represents the oblique direction of the ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the sun across the sky; the "oblique" path refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis.</note>; the lion's skin represents the strength of this celestial body when it is located in the sign of Leo; the stolen golden apples are the stars, which disappear because of the sunshine, and the twelve labors are the twelve signs.

Both of them thus adopted the opinions of the commentator on Hesiod, as well as those of Macrobius, Porphyry, etc., who all agreed on this and saw in these fables very ingenious allegories invented with great shrewdness.

Aleander the Younger expressed these same concepts in his explanation of the Sun Table (3).

However, since none of them expressed themselves in detail on this matter, everything they said about it seemed more like a clever invention than a well-founded fact.

The learned Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Swiss theologian and scholar known for his critical approach to history.</note> did not believe in it either, but rejected all these allegories as baseless; in order to [besse...] <note>The catchword at the bottom of the page suggests the next page continues with a word like "besser" (better) or "bessern" (to improve/refine).</note>

---

1) *Of the Origin and Progress of Heathenism*, Vol. 2, Ch. 15, p. 380 ff. <note>original: "De theologia gentili et physiologia christiana; sive de origine ac progressu idololatriae" by Vossius.</note>
2) *Treatise on Harpocrates*. <note>original: "Harpocrates, sive Explicatio figuratæ & graphicæ" by Cuper, concerning the Egyptian god of silence.</note>
3) Pages 25-30 of the 2nd edition of the *Explanation of the Sun Table*. Paris 1617, 4to. The first edition is said to have appeared in Rome in 1616. <note>original: "Explicatio Heliae Tabulae" by Girolamo Aleandro.</note>

<meta>This page continues the critique of various scholars' interpretations of the Hercules myth. It follows from the previous page's discussion of Jean Le Clerc, who rejected astronomical allegories in favor of a more grounded, though perhaps equally flawed, historical perspective.</meta>

...to prove it better, he published a treatise (4) in which he turned Hercules into a Phoenician merchant who performed great deeds, founded major settlements, undertook extensive journeys, and conducted a vast trade.

This treatise, although quite extensive (5), is worthy neither of its author nor of its content. Lacking critical rigor, taste, or interest, it serves only to excite a great aversion toward the entire study of fables <note>Fabellehre: A historical term for mythology or the systematic interpretation of myths.</note>. We should not be surprised by this; for by considering each fable in complete isolation and individually, rather than grouping them together, it was impossible to gain a complete overview or to rise to the allegorical meaning, which is as complex as it is manifold. Only the consistency of the entire system of fables could lead to a single meaning; but where would one have suspected less harmony than in mythological fables?

Abbé Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741), a French clergyman and member of the Académie des Inscriptions, famous for his "Euhemeristic" approach—interpreting myths as distorted historical facts.</note>, the zealous defender of the historical sense, considered Hercules to be a hero actually born in Thebes (6) who, through his heroic deeds, performed the most useful services for the Greeks. He accepts everything and does not even suspect that much could be fabulous; yet he distinguishes five or six heroes who all bear the name Hercules—such as an Egyptian, a Phoenician, and an Indian Hercules, and so forth—and admits that all their deeds could have been united into a single person.

6) *Mythology*, Book 3, Chapter 6, Vol. 7, pp. 1–88. <note>original Latin abbreviation: "Mythol."</note>

### §. 4.

## Observations Proving that the Allegory of Hercules Refers to Agriculture.

One will certainly wonder that I relate the history of Hercules—a hero held to be the vanquisher of monsters, the avenger of innocence, and the conqueror of giants—to agriculture, and that I see in his heroic deeds only field labors, which seem to bear no resemblance to them at all.

But if one considers that the life of Hercules cannot possibly be a real history; that no hero could have done as much as is attributed to him; that nevertheless all parts of this history are in too good a connection for one to consider them corrupted or to claim they are no longer what they were at the beginning; if one further considers that Hercules has been identified with **Saturn** <note>The Roman god of agriculture and time.</note> or **Osiris** <note>The Egyptian god often credited with bringing the knowledge of farming to humanity.</note>; that the entire outline of his life, presented in such a unique way, must have been modeled after a specific pattern in nature which offered all the allusions contained in this history; if one pays particular attention to the number twelve—the number of Labors established—and how this number corresponds with the number of months in the year and the seasonal cycle of field work; and finally, if one reflects that none of the explanations previously given for this history have endured; then one might perhaps suspect that I could be right, and become inclined to follow my reasoning.

All my explanations shall flow from the very nature of this matter; they shall follow in the exact order in which the heroic deeds were presented to me. My interpretations, therefore, will contain nothing arbitrary and will, I flatter myself, be secured against every significant objection.

### § 2.
### Hercules was, in the Orient, the protective sun of agriculture.

Why, then, are the labors by which the earth was forced into submission credited to Hercules? Why is he—if he is an allegorical being—presented as one born in Thebes, as a son of Jove <note>original: "Jov," referring to Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, and as a descendant of the family of Cadmus?

All of this belongs to the important facts that must be synthesized if the full splendor and beauty of this allegory is to reveal itself to our eyes.

Hercules was already the name used by the people of the Orient <note>original: "Morgenländer," a historical term for the peoples of the Near East or Levant.</note> for the sun, which these peoples—devoted to Sabianism <term>Sabianism: also called Sabeism; the ancient worship of celestial bodies (sun, moon, and stars) as deities</term> or the veneration of the stars—regarded as the deity protecting agriculture, the primary cause of all growth, and the soul of nature.

<summary>The author explains the symbolism of Hercules’ club as the first scepter of civilization and argues that European monarchy owes its existence to the foundations of agriculture. He begins a mythological deconstruction of Hercules as an ancient solar deity associated with star worship.</summary>
<keywords>Hercules, agriculture, monarchy, Sabianism, solar myth, allegory, civilization, Cadmus, Thebes</keywords>

--- Page 389 ---
<meta>This page continues the explanation of Hercules as an allegorical figure representing the sun and its role in agriculture. The previous page discussed how Hercules’s club symbolizes his rule over the earth through cultivation and how modern monarchs owe their civilization to these agricultural roots.</meta>

It is indeed the sun which, through its beneficial warmth, brings the entire world back to life, dries the flooded fields, and draws the vapors from the earth which then dissolve back into rain—the means of all fertilization <note>original: "Befruchtung." In this context, it refers to the fecundity or productivity of the soil.</note>—and accelerates the harvests. Without this celestial body, our globe would be plunged into darkness and remain eternally barren. All living beings yearn for the sun; they are joyful in its light and revive at its approach. Now the earth clothes itself again in its most beautiful finery; it breathes out the most pleasant fragrances; the winged singers once again let their harmonious songs resound in the air; all of nature renews itself; it appears more beautiful than ever; man himself rejoices at the sight of the foodstuffs sprouting up on all sides.

One need not wonder, then, that the name of this celestial body became the foundation of the allegory relating to the reclamation and cultivation of the earth, since without it, none of this could take place at all. Furthermore, it is no surprise that its name was bestowed upon heroes who performed deeds whose success depended on the active power of that celestial body; and that these deeds have been reduced to the number twelve, because the sun’s orbit is divided into the twelve heavenly signs <note>These are the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>, which form the farmer’s calendar and guide all his labors.

->§. 3.<-

### Why is he called the Theban?

But why is he said to have been born in Thebes in Boeotia <note>A region in ancient Greece; Thebes was its primary city-state.</note>, as a member of the Cadmian family <note>The royal lineage of Thebes, descended from its legendary founder, Cadmus.</note>? Nothing is more natural or simple.

--- Page 390 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Hercules’s origins. The previous page established that Hercules is an allegorical representation of the sun, and his "twelve labors" correspond to the twelve signs of the Zodiac used by farmers to track the seasons for cultivation. This page explains why Hercules is specifically associated with the city of Thebes.</meta>

Thebes was one of the Phoenician colonies through which the customs, sciences, allegories, and even the language of this ancient people were brought to Greece. From there, the wondrous tales of the first Eastern <note>original: "morgenländischen." In this era, "morgenländisch" or "Oriental" referred primarily to the civilizations of the Near East, such as Phoenicia, Egypt, and Mesopotamia.</note> institutions spread throughout the rest of Greece. These tales thus originated from Thebes, and it was therefore believed that this hero <note>Hercules</note> himself had been born in Thebes.

Furthermore, the names of this city and its founder, Cadmus, were among those Eastern names created to attract attention, to be used as allegorical characters for the most important subjects, and to provide a fertile source for wondrous tales.

*Theba* <note>תבה; tebah</note> was, for example, an Eastern word that signified an ark or a ship. However, the Eastern peoples imagined the sun traveling in a ship, with the sun itself as the helmsman. The sun, or Hercules, was thus rightly called "the Theban" in this sense—that is, "the sailor"—by the Easterners.

Imperceptibly, the Greeks came to understand this name as referring to an inhabitant of Thebes, a person born there.

We must also note that the Phoenicians established schools or famous academies in Thebes at an early date, which is why the Greek youth flocked there in great numbers to be instructed in Eastern wisdom and in the Phoenician arts, which had already reached a high level of perfection.

The Greek fables that have come down to us, whose setting is in Thebes and within the family of Cadmus—

<meta>This page follows a critical analysis of Cicero’s "De Natura Deorum," where the author discussed the various historical figures named Hercules mentioned by classical scholars. The text transitions from debating the number of these figures to identifying their singular origin.</meta>

Until now, no one has dared to decide whether these different versions of Hercules referred to a single being or to several; but by means of our thread <note>The author likely refers to his "thread of reasoning" or thematic consistency throughout the work.</note>, no more doubt remains on this matter. All of these versions of Hercules, honored in so many places and especially by the Phoenicians—who regarded him as their supreme god and introduced his worship wherever they established a settlement or trading post—are one and the same deity. He was a god revered for his benefactions and granted the most sacred divine honors. One may read about the ceremonies with which he was honored in the works of *Silius Italicus* <note>Silius Italicus (c. 26–101 AD) was a Roman poet whose epic "Punica" contains descriptions of the temple of Hercules in Gades (modern Cádiz).</note>.

A different age was attributed to these various Hercules figures, depending on whether the colonies in which this god was worshiped under this name were founded earlier or later. Thus, the Hercules of Thebes is considered younger in relation to the Hercules of Tyre, because his name and divine worship were brought to Thebes by a Phoenician colony. Consequently, he was worshiped in Thebes much later than in Tyre, where he first received divine honors.

## Article III.
### Proofs that Hercules originally represented the Sun.

### §. 1.
### Testimony of the Ancients.

This first and universal deity among the Phoenicians, whom they called Hercules, was the Sun, and from the very beginning, he was the symbol of the Creator of fire and light.

**Nicolaus of Damascus** <note>A historian and philosopher from the 1st century BCE, known for his universal history and his friendship with Herod the Great.</note> says: "that the **Sun** is **Cronos** <note>Though distinct in early Greek myth, later Hellenistic philosophy often conflated Cronus (the Titan) with Chronos (Time).</note> or the time that never grows old, and is one and the same as **Hercules**," which is to say: always strong and courageous.

This Egyptian figure of speech led **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Swiss theologian and scholar known for his rationalistic interpretations of ancient myths.</note> astray; for by deviating from its true meaning, he believed he saw in it an excellent proof for his system, according to which **Hercules** was merely a merchant who made voyages in the "Bowl of the Sun" because his ship was named *Sun* or his tent displayed this image.

How could he possibly overlook the correspondence of this passage with Egyptian theology, which places the **Sun** and the **Moon** in vessels as the helmsmen of the universe and has them row upon the upper waters?

How can one person be both mortal and im-
mortal at the same time? Why did the Greeks act rationally
by honoring him from these two perspectives, and
building double temples for him? This behavior is in-
comprehensible if he is merely a human; but if he is the sun,
then everything becomes clear.

The one Hercules is the summer sun in its full
strength, shining very brightly, and like the gods,
gives life to all beings.

The other is the winter sun, without strength, without
power; it casts almost no ray of light; nature beneath it
is as if dead and dormant; it is only the shadow of
what it once was.

Moreover, the one stands high in the heavens, while
the other seems to be hidden in the bowels of the
earth.

This distinction, taken from nature itself,
was therefore very sound. It did not escape the Greeks
at all, and in what follows we will become aware of
various fables which they constructed on this foundation,
and to which, for example, the story of the Dioscuri <note>original: "Dioscuren" — the "Sons of Zeus," divine twin brothers in Greek mythology</note>,

mortal for six months and immortal for the same number of months,
must be counted.

They did not stop there; rather, they made
as many persons out of the sun as there were seasons;
this happened especially in Egypt, and everything was a
consequence of those first steps taken.

<meta>This page continues the argument that various mythological figures are actually personifications of the sun at different stages of the solar year. The previous page concluded by noting that the Egyptians created different deities for each season.</meta>

The reviving **Osiris**, the powerless and weak **Harpocrates** <note>The Greek adaptation of the Egyptian Har-pa-khered ("Horus the Child"), often depicted with a finger to his lips</note>, the young and shining **Ammon**, the old bearded **Pluto** or **Serapis**, crowned with a grain measure <note>original: "Getraidemaaße" — specifically the *modius*, a basket-like crown symbolizing fertility and the underworld's riches</note>, are all one and the same object, viewed from different successive points of view; they are the sun at all its ages, which revives at the time of the **winter solstice**, is thereafter powerless and weak, until it appears again in the spring in its full splendor and shining youth, and in the autumn, laden with fruits, dies and breathes its last, satiated with life.

Sometimes all these considerations were also combined into a single figure, though one can well feel that it had to turn out too artificial or monstrous. Thus there was a figure with three heads: a **lion's**, a **wolf's**, and a **dog's** head; a true emblem of time. The wolf's head to the left signified past time, which devours everything; the lion's head in the middle was the emblem for the present time, which moves forward with speed, as the lion runs, and flees just as quickly; and finally the dog's head located to the right designated that flattering hope of the future, which has so many charms and is such a great refuge in misfortune. <note>This three-headed figure is famously described by the Roman writer Macrobius in his *Saturnalia* as an accompaniment to the statue of Serapis.</note>

This strange [title], for a hero,

<meta>This page continues the argument that Hercules, often viewed merely as a hero of strength, was originally a solar deity similar to Apollo. It specifically addresses his title as "Leader of the Muses" (Mussagetes) mentioned at the end of the previous page.</meta>

—from whom one could not have suspected any association with the **Muses**—the titles bestowed upon him, which the **Thebans** had granted to **Hercules** long before the **Romans**, prove how much people were mistaken in the concepts previously held of him. It shows that among the **Phoenicians**, he occupied the position that **Apollo** subsequently took among the **Greeks**.

The same holds true for the fable in which **Hercules** contested **Apollo** for possession of the **tripod**. This tripod, over which Apollo presided, is no ordinary tripod. According to the people of the East <note>original: "Morgenländern" — a term used historically to refer to Near Eastern cultures such as the Persians or Babylonians</note>, it represents the year divided into three seasons, which thus walked on "three feet." People manufactured calendars with three legs that emerged from a common center, forming a sort of wheel. <note>This description closely resembles a "triskelion," a motif of three interlocking legs or spirals used in various ancient cultures to represent cycles or progress.</note> On each leg was a description of a season, or of four months of the year. This same thing can also be seen on **Runic** monuments. (1)

This also proves that the **Greeks** substituted their **Apollo** for the **Phoenician Hercules**, and that they imperceptibly forgot the original concept of this figure.

This last circumstance was used to establish the proposition that this hero was more famous for his learning than for his bravery, and to turn him into a great philosopher. However, given the darkness surrounding this hero's origins, this was a very pardonable mistake. In order not to overburden this article with an irrelevant digression, I will address this in the third note.

### §. 5.
### Concerning the Names of Hercules and Their Relation to the Sun.

Hercules was called *Chon* <note>original: "Chon" — likely a reference to the Egyptian lunar-solar deity Khonsu, though the author connects it here to "strength."</note> by the Egyptians, as can be seen from the great *Etymologicon* <note>The *Etymologicum Magnum*, a significant Greek lexical encyclopedia compiled in Constantinople around 1150 AD.</note>. This word in the Coptic language means **strength, power, or effective force**. Such is the concept one has of **Hercules**, and this is exactly how the **sun** acts.

*Macrobius* <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (5th century AD), a Roman provincial whose works explored mythology through solar symbolism.</note> knew the significance of this name; he asserts that **Hercules** means the "power of the gods" <note>original Latin: "virtus deorum"</note>, or the "strength of a ruling deity" <note>original Latin: "Dei Regentis"</note>. (3)

**Pythagoras**, who was well-versed in the Egyptian sciences, likewise explained the name **Hercules** (according to the testimony of **Iamblichus** <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the life and teachings of Pythagoras.</note>) as the **force** or **power of nature**. One could call him the "physical dynast" <term>physical dynast: a ruler or sovereign power over the material, natural world</term>, or the **king of nature**.

(2) <note>original: "Fast. L. VI. p. 213. u. f. w." — refers to Ovid's *Fasti*, Book VI, page 213 and following, which describes the Roman religious calendar.</note>
(3) <note>original: "Saturn. L. I. C. 20." — refers to Macrobius's *Saturnalia*, Book I, Chapter 20, where he argues that most pagan gods are actually different aspects of the Sun.</note>

The passage by Nicolaus of Damascus <note>Nicolaus of Damascus (born c. 64 BC) was a Greek historian and philosopher who served as a tutor to the children of Antony and Cleopatra and was a friend to Herod the Great.</note> cited earlier also fits here, in which he states that the sun is the "ever strong and brave Hercules."

Holy Scripture also finds pleasure in presenting the sun under the image of a young and powerful hero who pursues his course with indestructible courage. <note>This is a likely reference to Psalm 19:5, which describes the sun "like a champion rejoicing to run his course."</note>

This name **Chon** did not vanish with the ancient Egyptians. The Copts, the remnants of this ancient people, still call the season in which the sun rules—when it stands at its highest and manifests its full strength—**Som**. The Swedish Goths, the Danes, and the English—peoples who received their calendar from the Orient—call the **Summer** by this very name; for among the first people it is called *Somm-ar*, and among the latter two *Somm-er*.

In the same way, the Anglo-Saxons, the Dutch, the Germans, and others call the sun by the Egyptian names **Son** and **Sun**, and the Swedish Goths call midday—the moment when the sun expresses its strength most greatly—**Sunn-an**. (†)

The root of this word is likely the stem-word **Sum**, which signifies everything high, sublime, or ruling, and which has given rise to so many derivatives in all our languages. <note>The author is likely connecting this to the Latin *summus*, meaning "highest."</note>

The first syllable is the French article **le** (the); **Al-cides** is thus the same as the Spanish word **Le-Cid**, which signifies a hero, and has become so famous through **Corneille**. <note>Pierre Corneille (1606–1684) was a French tragedian whose play *Le Cid* immortalized the legendary Spanish hero Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar.</note> One should therefore not be surprised by the expression, "as brave as the heavens."

The Greeks call him **Herakles**, from the words *Hera* (Juno, or the air) and *Kles* (glory or fame). <note>The author refers to a common ancient etymological theory, often attributed to the Stoics, that the name of the goddess Hera was an anagram of the Greek word for air, *aer*.</note> They explained him, therefore, as the "ornament of Juno" or "of the air."

But were they the inventors of this name? Did they receive it from the Orient, or did they form it as an imitation or parody of a similar name which he bore among the Oriental peoples, and particularly among the Phoenicians?

This may be difficult to decide. It is true that in the records of antiquity one sees an **Arcles** <note>A reference to "Archles" or "Arcles," names sometimes found in lists of Phoenician kings or associated with the god Melqart, whom the Greeks identified with Hercules.</note> among the Oriental kings, and that this name has much in common with the name **Hercules**; yet this alone cannot possibly be sufficient to decide that **Hercules** is an Oriental name.

Moreover, the Latins pronounced *Hera-Kles* as **Hercules**, which might lead to entirely different roots, between which it may be impossible to decide with certainty.

### §. 6.
### Regarding the Tithe Which Was Sacrificed to Hercules.

The divine worship paid to Hercules, which consisted in dedicating to him the firstfruits of the harvest and the tithe <note>A "tithe" refers to a tenth part of one's goods or earnings offered as a religious sacrifice.</note> of all the goods of the earth, serves as irrefutable proof that he was considered the author and protector of these goods—the god who, through his beneficial warmth, promoted their growth and ripening.

This divine worship, initially offered only to the deity in general, soon became the specific cult of Hercules or the Sun, after this celestial body—the soul of agriculture—had been personified or elevated to divinity.

### Symbols of Hercules; the final proof that he was the Sun.

**Hercules** was depicted clothed in a **lion skin** and armed with a **club**, sometimes even with a **bow**; the **poplar tree** was also a tree held sacred to him.

The **Thasians** <note>The inhabitants of the Greek island of Thasos, who famously maintained a dual cult of Hercules as both an Olympian god and a hero.</note> had erected a statue of him ten cubits high <note>The original German uses "Arme" (arms), likely referring to the cubit, an ancient unit of length based on the forearm.</note>, which held a club in the right hand and a bow in the left.

The Sun also bore these very same symbols. Thus, on the beautiful "Sun Tablet"—or the image of the Sun that **Alexander** <note>Likely referring to Alexander the Great; ancient sources often mention his interest in solar symbolism and his association with the god Helios-Ammon.</note> exhibited publicly—it was depicted with a bow, quiver, and arrows; meanwhile, two clubs serve as the "shield-bearers" <note>The figures or objects flanking a central image, similar to supporters in heraldry.</note> of the painting.

The ancients were fully convinced that this entire array of weaponry referred to the Sun. "**Probus** says," (1) "the poplar tree was dedicated to Hercules because its two-colored leaf (which is white on top but dark green underneath) is very well suited to represent day and night." <note>The white poplar (*Populus alba*) was said to have been turned white on one side by the sweat of Hercules during his labors in the underworld.</note>

**Porphyry** said (2) that the uneven and knotted club of Hercules signifies the inequality of the days <note>Referring to the varying lengths of days throughout the changing seasons.</note>, and the lion skin signifies that the Sun exerts its greatest strength when it is in the zodiac sign of **Leo** <note>The constellation of the Lion, where the sun resides during the height of summer.</note>.

The ancients called this sign the "Lion" because, like the lion, it was entirely fire, and they designated it as the seat of the Sun. (3)

# Article IV.
## The Parents, Wives, and Children of Hercules.

### §. I.
### His Father and His Mother.

His father is Jove <note>Jove is another name for Jupiter (the Greek Zeus), the king of the gods.</note>, the highest god, and this is not disputed; however, the name of his mother varies.

<margin>4) Photius, *Bibliotheca*, Codex 190. The *New History* of Ptolemy Hephaestion, Book VII. <note>Photius was a 9th-century Byzantine scholar whose *Bibliotheca* preserved summaries of many lost ancient works, including the *New History* by Ptolemy Chennus (Hephaestion).</note></margin>

A hymn of praise from the Thebans <note>The inhabitants of the Greek city of Thebes, Hercules' traditional birthplace.</note> dedicated to him began with these words: *Son of Zeus and Hera* <note>original Greek: "Διος και Ἥρας υἱος"</note>, or Jupiter and Juno. (4) This aligns perfectly with what Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> reports to us at the conclusion of his biography of the Hercules of Thebes: that Juno finally consented to adopt Hercules as her child. His supposed mother is therefore merely an allegorical being, just as his entire history is allegorical. According to others, his mother was Asteria; however, this name signifies "Queen of the Stars" and can be viewed as an epithet <note>A descriptive title or name.</note> for Juno.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of Hercules' parentage, specifically the hymn identifying him as the son of Zeus and Hera, this page explores the linguistic and solar symbolism behind the name of his mother, Alcmene, and his adversary, Eurystheus.</meta>

The allegorical mother of the **Hercules** of **Thebes** was called *Alcmene*. This name must be of Oriental <note>In the 18th and 19th centuries, "Oriental" was a broad term for the cultures and languages of the Near East, particularly Semitic languages like Hebrew and Aramaic.</note> origin, as it begins with the Oriental article *Al*; it is perhaps the feminine form of *Alcman*. It must belong to the Oriental family of the word <note>original Hebrew: חמה (Chamah)</note> *Rhme* <note>The author uses a phonetic transcription of the Hebrew root for heat or the sun.</note>, which means heat or warmth; perhaps it even arose from a union with the word *Ain* or *En*, which means a source or spring. Thus, *Alc-me-ene* would express the "Source of Warmth."

He was born during a triple-length night—that is, in a night of indefinite duration. This expression can be an allusion to two different subjects: first, it can refer to the moment when the sun first became visible in the universe after an indefinite night; furthermore, it can also relate to the winter solstice, when the sun rises again after the longest night of the entire year.

He is bound to obey *Eurystheus*—that *Eurystheus* of whom *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was a historian of the early Christian church who often analyzed pagan myths.</note> confesses that he does not see at all how one could explain him in an allegorical sense. Yet he could not have been better described: *Euryst* <note>original Hebrew: עריץ (Aritz)</note> signifies "the Strong" or "the Irresistible" in the Oriental language. Such a one is he who forces the sun to run around the world and perform twelve labors in the year.

### §. 2.
## Of the Fifty Sons of Hercules.

**Hercules** fathered fifty sons with fifty sisters. This trait, which completely misled the mythologists, flows perfectly from the truth and agrees entirely with the allegorical spirit of antiquity.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of Hercules as a solar deity and the etymological origins of his mother Alcmene and his master Eurystheus, this page explores how ancient mythology used numerical allegories to represent the passage of time.</meta>

This antiquity personified the various parts of time. From this arise the series of successive allegorical numbers. Thus, we have seen in the history of **Saturn** that the seven sons sired with **Rhea** signified the seven days of the week, and the seven daughters sired with **Astarte** signified the seven nights.

If we proceed from the principle that **Hercules** is the sun, then it is not at all difficult to find an explanation for the fifty sons of **Hercules**. They are the weeks of which the year is composed <note>While a solar year has 52 weeks, many ancient lunar-solar systems used 50 weeks as a rounded allegorical number for a "great year" or specific ritual cycles.</note>, and these are indeed the children of **Hercules**, or the sun.

For this reason, fifty boys and fifty daughters are also given to **Ilus**, the builder of **Troy**, as a consequence of his labors.

From this source come the fifty sons of **Aegyptus** and the fifty daughters of **Danaus**, who can never fill the perforated barrels. In reality, the weeks also accumulate in vain; time is never full and always begins anew <note>The myth of the Danaides—condemned to pour water into leaky vessels—is interpreted here as a metaphor for the endless, repetitive nature of time.</note>.

Allegories were also invented with regard to the days of which the year is composed.

Hence come the 360 jugs which were seen in the temple of **Osiris**, and of which **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus was a 1st-century BC Greek historian who described Egyptian customs and myths in his *Library of History*.</note> speaks.

From this also derive the 360 Libyan priests of whom this same writer treats, and whose perpetual occupation consisted of drawing water from the **Nile** into a perforated barrel.

A fable which completely corresponds with that of the **Danaides**.

### §. 3.
## Iolas, a relative of Hercules.

Iolas, a relative <note>Iolas, or Iolaus, was the nephew of Hercules, being the son of Hercules’ half-brother Iphicles.</note> of Hercules, plays a very important role in the history of this hero. He accompanies him in his labors; he is at the head of the colony that Hercules sends to Sardinia <note>original: "Sarde." Mythology states Iolaus led the Thespiades (the fifty sons of Hercules) to settle in Sardinia.</note>, which consists of his fifty sons; to him, his uncle entrusts his wife Megara at the end of his career; Hercules consecrates a grove to him in Sicily; and finally, Iolas restores life to this hero.

Iolas is therefore also an allegorical name, worthy of accompanying Hercules, whose character must harmonize with all those in the story of Hercules. It will cost us little effort to discover its meaning.

**Iol**—pronounced as **Hiol**, **Jul**, **Yule**, **Giul**, **Zweol**, **Wheel**, **Wiol**, **Vol**, and so on—is a root word which carries with it the entire concept of revolution and the wheel.

**Jul-Iom** <note>A combination of the root *Jul* and the Arabic *Yawm* (day).</note> signifies in the Arabic language the first day of the year; it literally means the day of return or arrival.

**Giul-ous** <note>Likely referring to the Persian *Julus*, meaning a royal accession or "sitting," which the author connects to the turning of a cycle.</note> signifies in the Persian language the change of the year; it is also used to denote a royal coronation.

**Hiul** signifies "wheel" in the Danish and Swedish languages.

In Flanders this is expressed by **Wiel**, and in England by the word **Wheel**.

Among the Germans, the verb **wel-zen** means to roll or turn.

"Wel" signifies waves or floods, in that they constantly follow one another.

The French word *houle* <note>A sea swell or surge.</note> refers to a sea wave. From this also stems the *vol-vo* <note>original: "vol-vo," the Latin verb meaning to roll, turn, or tumble.</note> of the Romans.

Since the **solstices** are the time in which the sun returns to its path, they also received their names from this. From this comes the Greek name **Tropicus** <note>original: "Tropicus," from the Greek *tropikos*, meaning "of a turning."</note>, which means return.

This same thing occurred among the **Celts**. They gave the **solstices** and the months that take their beginning during the **solstices** the name **Jul**, which likewise expresses return.

**Stiernhielm** <note>Georg Stiernhielm (1598–1672), a Swedish linguist and historian.</note>, who was experienced in Nordic languages and antiquities, reports (1) that the ancient inhabitants of **Sweden** celebrated a festival named **Jul** at the time of the **winter solstice** or around Christmas; that this word signifies **revolution** or **wheel**; that the month of December is therefore called **Jul-month**, the month of the return; and finally, that this word is also written as **Hiule** and **Giule**.

The inhabitants of the county of **Lincoln** in England also call the log which one burns on Christmas Day, and which must last throughout the holidays, the **Jule-Block**, **log** or **trunk of Jul**.

One should therefore not be surprised if our month of **July** <note>original: "Julius."</note>, which follows the **summer solstice**, received its name from this. It is true that the Romans tell us this month took its name from **Julius Caesar**; but could this etymology not also be one of the flatteries with which they were accustomed to overload their emperors? ## §. 4.
### Iole and the other Wives of Hercules.

After performing his labors, Hercules hands over to Iolaus not only his sons but also his wife, Megara. He then wishes to take Iole as his wife, but instead becomes a slave to Omphale and later marries Deianira.

It has never before been suspected that these names might be allegorical; however, they must be so, since the entire history of Hercules is nothing but an allegory <note>A story where characters and events symbolize deeper meanings—here, the movement of the stars and seasons.</note>. But what could these names mean?

<meta>This page continues the allegorical analysis of Hercules as a solar figure. Having established Iolaus as a symbol for the "new revolution" or the start of a new solar cycle at the winter solstice, the author now interprets Hercules's successive wives—Iole, Omphale, Megara, and Dejanira—as representations of different phases of the astronomical year and the moon.</meta>

In consequence of what I have said regarding the *Iol* <note>Referring to the wild goat or "Ihwl" discussed on the previous page as a symbol for the winter solstice.</note>, the name of the person whom *Hercules* wishes to marry after completing his labors can cause no difficulty. Since she is called *Iole*, her name is allegorical and refers to the new revolution <note>In this context, an astronomical "revolution" refers to the completion of one full cycle and the beginning of the next.</note>.

Now *Hercules* becomes a slave to *Omphale*, the queen of the *Maeonians*. However, עון *On* <note>original Hebrew: 'On'</note> signifies the times; פלא *Phala* <note>original Hebrew: 'Phala'</note> means to divide or distinguish.

She is thus the Moon, the celestial body which divides time and produces the months, which are here called *Maeonians* from *Mene* or *Man*, *Moon* <note>The author links the Greek *mene* (moon/month) and the German *Mond* to the name of the Maeonian people to support the lunar allegory.</note>. (†)

If *Hercules* becomes her slave after completing his labors, it happens because he is truly united with her at the time of the solstice <note>The point in the year where the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky; here likely referring to the sun's position relative to lunar cycles.</note>.

The first wife of *Hercules*—that is, the preceding year—is therefore abandoned; he no longer has need of her; she is a stranger to him, or *Megara*; for this is what that name signifies in the Eastern language <note>The author likely connects the name to a Semitic root such as the Hebrew 'magar', interpreting it here as 'stranger' or 'one cast off'.</note>.

In *Dejanira* one cannot fail to recognize the Eastern word *Nur* or נור *Nyr* <note>original Hebrew: 'Nur', meaning light or fire</note>, which means light, and the word *Dei*, meaning abundance; for after the winter solstice, the sun appears in new splendor, or rather the year is completed and has reached its goal.

# Part Three

## Explanation of the Life and the Twelve Labors of Hercules

### §. 1.

These labors were painted on the walls of temples in ancient times. But why was this done?

It has already been mentioned above that the twelve labors of **Hercules** were painted on the sacred walls of his temple at **Cadiz** <note>original: "Cadix"; an ancient Phoenician port city in modern-day Spain, home to a famous temple of Melqart, whom the Greeks identified as Hercules</note>.

This circumstance provides a great deal of clarity; first, it follows from this that the labors of **Hercules** were not a Greek invention, as the **Phoenicians** had already painted them on the walls of a temple far older than that of the Greek **Hercules**.

Secondly, because they were painted on the temple walls, events of great importance must lie hidden beneath these labors—events closely connected both with religion and with the best organization of society.

These paintings actually represented the twelve signs <note>A reference to the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>, and the human labors corresponding to those signs, or to the part of the year which they governed according to the thinking of that time.

One must not be astonished by this. In those remote times, one had only stone and marble with which to instruct the people. Everything by which nations

should be enlightened, was engraved upon monuments of this kind and publicly displayed for the benefit of all members of society.

However, no monuments were better suited to achieve this purpose than the walls of temples. Besides providing people of talent with the opportunity to develop themselves in the most excellent and noble manner, one could choose no better means to spread instruction quickly and universally.

For peoples devoted to agriculture <note>original: "Ackerbau"; refers to the transition from nomadic lifestyles to settled farming societies</note> and scattered across the countryside, temples served as the true point of unification. By gathering here from all directions to thank the Deity for its blessings, they simultaneously learned the proper application of the days that followed. Thus, the fulfillment of the venerable duties of religion was joined with instruction in those matters most vital to them—matters without which no civilized or flourishing society could exist.

Here they were instructed in everything regarding the various days of the year: its beginning and end, the new moons, months, and seasons, the days of labor and the days of rest, and the rising and setting of the stars that presided over their work.

It was truly the priests who provided the people with information on all these matters; for it was their duty to organize the calendar and everything relating to public worship. They therefore always had the new moons and the new year publicly proclaimed, and we see this custom in ancient Rome, as well as among the Hebrews, Greeks, and so on.

At the head of all these paintings, Mercury, equipped with his caduceus <note>original: "Schlangenstab"; a staff entwined with two snakes, the symbol of Mercury</note>, led the procession of these important tasks.

But just as religion loses nothing when it surrenders that which is not God and truth, so too history can lose nothing by giving up purely allegorical persons; rather, it gains by it. Through this, it rids itself of facts which are entirely contrary to reason <note>The author writes from an Enlightenment perspective, where "Reason" is the primary tool for determining truth.</note>, which therefore cannot be accepted at all, and are only capable of producing a powerful prejudice against history.

Reason likewise gains by it, partly through the interest it takes in narratives which acquire a completely different value in its eyes, and partly through the pleasure afforded by the thought that objects which have always delighted us are not foolish and tasteless stories, but rather ingenious lessons founded upon the needs of mankind.

In this way, true history enriches and expands itself—the history of human knowledge <note>original: "Geschichte der menschlichen Kenntnisse"</note>, which is far more sublime than the history of peoples and heroes.

# First Image.
## The Two Snakes Strangled by Hercules in the Cradle.

**N**o story seems more foolish on the surface than that of the two snakes sent by Juno <note>The Roman Queen of the Gods, known for her jealousy toward Hercules, who was the son of her husband Jupiter and a mortal woman.</note> to murder Hercules in his cradle; the child bravely strangled them with his hands, and in this way, even in his infancy, gave striking signs of what he would one day become.

Mythologists have ignored this event entirely, as they considered it a mere fable which had no relation to the Labors of Hercules.

As for myself, being convinced that everything in mythological narratives has a meaning and a purpose, I see in this fact an ingenious allusion to the event by which the ancient calendar begins. Before I develop this, however, I wish to add two circumstances which Theocritus <note>A Greek poet from the 3rd century BCE, famous for his "Idylls" or short poems.</note> (1) preserved for us in his idyll in honor of Hercules; for these are too remarkable, and prove everything I have yet to say so well, that I could not pass them over in silence.

<meta>This page transitions from the literal description of Hercules strangling the snakes (as told by Theocritus) to an astronomical and allegorical interpretation of the myth, specifically linking it to the Caduceus and the solar calendar.</meta>

<page-num>354</page-num>

Here we have, then, an allegory, which is very precisely characterized by the following traits:

1. Hercules strangles two dragons;
2. At the age of ten months;
3. At midnight;
4. They are thrown into the fire with rituals of atonement. Given these characteristics, one cannot fail to find the answer to the riddle.

Without doubt, one will remember that the caduceus <note>The winged staff carried by Mercury, often shown with two serpents coiled around it.</note>, the symbol of **Mercury** <note>The Roman messenger god, known as Hermes in Greek mythology, often associated with wisdom and the invention of science.</note>, consisted of two dragons pressed together in the middle, a male and a female; that their point of union was called **Hercules**, and that Mercury was the inventor of astronomy or the calendar.

The strangling of the two dragons by Hercules is therefore probably only an allegory relating to the caduceus, or to the object which it represented, and is closely connected with the **Year of the Husbandman** <term>Year of the Husbandman: original German "Jahre des Ackermannes." This refers to an ancient agricultural or seasonal calendar used to guide farming cycles.</term>, of which it marked the beginning.

With which day of the year, with which moment, does the caduceus stand in connection? The ancients tell us, in that they call the solstices the "head" and "tail" of the dragon.

The "Year of the Husbandman," presented in the story of Hercules through allegorical imagery, thus opens with a solstice. However, there are two of these: one in the summer on **St. John’s Day** <note>Midsummer, June 24th, historically associated with the summer solstice.</note>, and one in the winter at **Christmas** <note>Midwinter, December 25th, historically associated with the winter solstice.</note>; which of the two is intended here? More depends on the decision of this question than one might believe; the entire series of the **Labors of Hercules** <note>The famous twelve tasks performed by the hero, which the author is likely preparing to map onto the zodiac or the calendar year.</note> depends upon it.

It will not be difficult to find the beginning; it is distinguished by two unmistakable characteristics:

1) It occurs earlier than the victory that Hercules achieves over the lion <note>The "Victory over the Lion" refers to the first labor of Hercules, which the author interprets as the sun entering the zodiac sign of Leo.</note>;

2) Hercules was only ten months old at that time.

The overcoming of the lion refers to the month of July, which is marked by the Lion; the two dragons were thus strangled in the month that precedes July—that is, according to our way of counting, at the time of the solstice in June, on the twentieth of this month, which among the ancients was the eve of the first day of summer.

Hercules was ten months old at that time because the beginning of the year for the Egyptians—among whom Theocritus <note>Theocritus was a 3rd-century BCE Greek poet who spent much of his life in Alexandria, Egypt; his Idyll 24 describes the infant Hercules strangling snakes.</note> resided when he composed the idyll of Hercules in the cradle—fell in the tenth month <note>The author is likely referring to the Egyptian civil calendar and how its start date shifted through the seasons over long periods of time.</note>.

Finally, as this poet has informed us, he ceases to prove himself victorious through the fire of atonement, in which the two dragons were burned at midnight.

### §. 2.
## St. John’s Fire.

Can one fail to recognize here the fires of Saint John—those holy fires lit at midnight at the time of the solstice by most ancient and modern peoples? This religious solemnity thus dates back to the remotest antiquity, and it was observed in order to promote the prosperity of states and nations and to ward off all misfortunes.

The origin of this fire, which so many nations still retain and which in antiquity entirely

From this also stems the name of this month, *Junior* <note>original: "Iunior," the younger</note>, the one who renews himself; whereas the preceding month, the month of May or *Major* <note>original: "Major," the older</note>, is called the elder. These bonfires were at the same time accompanied by vows and by sacrifices for the well-being of the people and the fruits of the earth. People danced around this fire; for is there indeed a festival without dance? and the most agile among them leaped over it. On the way back, everyone took a burning brand <note>original: "Brandt," a piece of burning wood</note> with them—some larger, some smaller—and the remainder was thrown into the air so that the wind might carry away all misfortune, just like these ashes.

After a long series of years, the year no longer began at the time of the solstice <term>solstice: the time when the sun reaches its highest point in the sky, marking the longest day of the year</term>; yet, out of habit and the superstitious ideas linked to it, the custom of the fire was still maintained at that same time. In general, it is a sad thing to completely abolish a day of joy during a season when there are so few of them; therefore, this custom has been preserved even up to our own times.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of solar symbolism, specifically moving from the sun’s association with the constellation Leo to the allegorical connection between the lion and the "civilizing" work of agriculture. For this very reason, the ancients, when they assigned a sign to each planet, chose the sign of the Lion for the Sun. But this is not the only similarity the lion has with *Hercules*; there is an even closer relationship relating to agriculture <term>agriculture: original "Ackerbau", meaning the cultivation of the fields</term>.

The tamed lion was the symbol of the cultivated earth, corresponding entirely to the care of the farmer. The ancients themselves tell us this:

> "The tamed lions that follow *Rhea*," says *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and writer often cited for his works on agriculture and religion</note> in a remarkable passage I have already cited, "teach men that there is no land which cannot be conquered and put into good condition."

For this same reason, the chariot of *Rhea* or *Cybele* <note>Rhea and Cybele were ancient Mother Goddesses associated with the fertility of the earth; they were often depicted in chariots pulled by lions</note> is drawn by lions. It is true that tigers also sometimes draw it; however, this is done to represent the variety of colors that shimmer upon the earth, which is more "striped" than any tiger skin.

This first labor <note>The author refers to the First Labor of Hercules: the slaying of the Nemean Lion</note> thus refers to the first labors of the farmer—those coarse and arduous tasks which alone are capable of promoting the culture of a land, and to which only those are committed who, in order to make their land arable, clear forests, drain stagnant waters, keep rivers within their banks, clear stones from the path, etc.; in short, they combat all the obstacles that previously made this land an infertile and desolate wilderness. These are true "giant-like" and "lion-like" works which, since they require significant progress and the greatest knowledge, presuppose in the leaders of the first societies, and of the colonies devoted to agriculture, an ability and a courage...

This heat was essential for completely drying the newly cleared earth, developing its fertile germs, warming it, and making it ready to receive and fertilize the seeds in its womb.

If this lion is called the Lion of the Nemean forest, or simply the Nemean, it is because in the Greek language, *Nemea* <note>The author likely refers to the Greek word *nemos* (νέμος), meaning a wooded pasture or glade</note> means a forest. "Nemean Lion" thus simply means "Lion of the Forest." Therefore, this lion does not belong to any specific forest; instead, it represents every forest that has been cleared and made arable.

## Third Painting.
### The Vanquished Lernean Hydra.

### Second Labor.

This Hydra was a fearsome monster; for it had only one body, but this was, says Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, known for his monumental universal history.</note>, provided with a hundred necks and a hundred heads, the latter of which, according to one mythologist, were even made of gold.

Hercules is condemned to slay this monster. He strikes off its heads, and so that they cannot grow back in their place, he burns the body of the Hydra with fire.

I will not dwell on repeating the various explanations of this "blue fairy tale," <note>original: "blauen Märchens"; a German idiom referring to a tall tale or a fantastical, unbelievable story.</note> I only wish to state that it is an allegory, a true riddle, for which nature itself and the labors of Hercules must provide the solution in the most satisfying way.

For our advantage in explaining these labors is that two illuminating points of comparison shine and guide us: on one hand, the order of the labors of Hercules, and on the other, the sequence of agricultural field work.

If we proceed from this principle, the story of the Hydra presents no difficulty at all; rather, the subject of the allegory lies plainly before our eyes.

This labor falls in the month of August, the sign of which is the Virgin <note>The zodiac sign Virgo.</note>, the Sibyl, or the beautiful reaper, with ears of grain in her hands.

# Third Painting.
## The Vanquished Lernaean Hydra.
### Second Labor.

This Hydra was a terrifying monster; for it had only one body, yet this was—says Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note>—provided with a hundred necks and a hundred heads, which the latter, according to one mythologist, were made of gold.

Hercules is condemned to destroy this monster. He strikes off its heads, and so that they cannot grow back in their place, he burns the body of the Hydra with fire.

I do not wish to dwell on the repetition of the various explanations of this fanciful fable <note>original: "blauen Mährchens"; a German idiom literally meaning "blue fairy tale," used to describe a tall tale or an unlikely story.</note>, I only wish to state that it is an allegory, a true riddle, for which nature itself and the labors of Hercules must provide the solution in the most satisfying way.

For our advantage in explaining these labors is that two luminous points of comparison shine upon and guide us: namely, on one side, the order of the labors of Hercules, and on the other, the sequence of agricultural field work.

If we proceed from this principle, the story of the Hydra presents no difficulty at all; rather, the subject of the allegory lies completely before our eyes.

This labor falls in the month of August, the sign of which is the Virgin <note>The zodiac sign Virgo.</note>, the Sibyl, or the beautiful reaper, with ears of grain <note>original: "Kornähren"; in this period, "Korn" referred to the primary cereal crop of a region, such as wheat or rye, rather than American maize.</note> in her hands.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the agricultural and zodiacal interpretation of Hercules' second labor, the Hydra, linking it specifically to the grain harvest in the month of August (Virgo) as established on the preceding page.</meta>

Do harvests not truly conclude in this month? At that time, does the farmer not truly gather the fruit of his cares, and does he not—armed with the murderous scythe—cut off the golden ears of grain from their stalks? These are the true Hydras with a hundred necks and a hundred heads on one body, since in the fertile regions of the Orient <note>The "Orient" here likely refers to the Levant or Egypt, known for high agricultural yields in antiquity.</note>, many other stalks grow from the stalk of a single grain, whose proud head is supported by a marvelous neck.

Hercules then burns the body of the Hydra, just as the farmer did then—and as is still done today in various regions—burning his stubble to fertilize the earth with its ashes.

Moreover, one should not be astonished to see the ears of grain transformed into a Hydra. In antiquity, serpents were always the symbol of grain <note>In many ancient Mediterranean cultures, snakes were associated with the earth (chthonic deities) and fertility; for instance, the goddess Ceres/Demeter was often depicted with serpents.</note>, whose allegorical name, as we shall soon have the opportunity to see, was not poorly chosen.

One should not object to the explanation of this second labor by claiming it is unnatural to let the harvest follow immediately upon the work performed to promote the cultivation of the earth. We are not speaking here of the work performed on a single field, but of the labor of an entire countryside; if one has cultivated one part of it in the month of July, one is already harvesting in the next month from another part of it, which was cultivated and sown in the previous year.

At the end of my explanations of the labors of Hercules, one will become aware of yet another interpretation of this one, in relation to the third and twelfth labors.

# Fourth Painting.

## The Captured Wild Boar Sacrificed to the Gods; the Conflict with the Centaurs.

### Third Labor.

First, *H e r c u l e s* takes possession of a wild boar, which he sacrifices to the gods; afterwards, on the occasion of a wine cask <note>This refers to the jar of wine owned by the Centaur Pholus, the opening of which attracted the other, more aggressive Centaurs.</note>, all the Centaurs fall upon him, but he remains their conqueror.

These events refer to the month of December, the labors of which are depicted through them. Immediately after the harvest, people showed their gratitude to the gods by sacrificing a pig. Their choice fell on this animal because it was harmful to the farmer through the devastation of his lands. The pig plays a prominent role in antiquity under this dual relationship <note>The pig is both a sacred offering and a practical pest.</note>. It is a pig by which Adonis is wounded; by a pig Attys is killed; a pig devastates the Calydonian territory; and it was a pig that the peoples devoted to agriculture sacrificed to the gods.

In the *Fasti* of Ovid, this is often spoken of:

> ” First CERES rejoiced in the blood of the greedy sow,
> ” Having avenged her wealth <note>Meaning her crops or grain.</note> by the deserved slaughter of the guilty one:
> ” For when the crops were milky in the tender furrows of the new Spring,
> ” She found them rooted up by the snout of the bristly swine.
> ” The sow paid the penalty. . . . (1)

Originally, the Centaurs were similar to the Satyrs and Pans; they were monsters who combined a human body with the feet and horns of a bull. In the following period, they were depicted in a more noble way; from the waist down, they were given the body of a bull with four feet.

In their first representation, they resembled the ancient Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy, often associated with bull imagery in earlier cults.</note>, who was called *Tauri formis* <note>original: "Tauri formis", meaning "bull-formed"</note> (3). It remained inexplicable only for lack of a firm standpoint from which one could begin.

By means of our standpoint—our "guiding thread"—this riddle will be explained just as easily as the others.

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of Hercules’s "Third Labor" as an allegory for agricultural cycles. In the subsequent period, the Greeks depicted him with more decorum but no less truth. They presented him as a handsome youth on a triumphal chariot drawn by Centaurs; the other Centaurs, however, played on various instruments, such as flutes, brass drums, lyres, and so on.

This symbol will gain a new degree of certainty by being placed alongside the preceding Egyptian one, regarding whose meaning everyone agrees. The months of July and August were painted on the banks of the Nile under the figure of a Sphinx, which represented half a woman and half a lion. This nation, so fond of agriculture, wanted thereby to depict the time of year designated by a Virgin <note>Referring to the zodiac sign Virgo.</note>, in which Hercules—who here represents the sun or human strength—designated by the Lion <note>Referring to the zodiac sign Leo.</note>, was merely devoted to inactivity and pleasures; this is at the same time the period of the Egyptian Carnival <term>Egyptian Carnival: A historical term for the festivals held during the Nile’s annual inundation, when the fields were underwater and agricultural labor was impossible.</term>, because the land, flooded by water, allows Hercules no work.

Here, however, he is now placed upon a bull, because the time for field work has approached; this is no longer the time of rest or of gentle and easy tasks, but rather the time of harder labor and toil, during which he must draw furrows with a strong plow and powerful bulls and till the fields.

If one sees wine barrels, which have been kept for this time, at the side of the Centaurs, this is an allusion to the wine that one must drink to restore one’s strength, and to the custom by which the master of the field work has vessels of wine brought to the field so that the workers can drink to quench their thirst.

# Fifth Painting.
## The Hunt for the Hind.
### Fourth Labor.

Here one sees *Hercules* as he masters a hind after a long pursuit. This hind ran with extraordinary speed, [had] golden horns, and *Hercules* seized her [with] nets.

A hind with golden horns is a fabulous <note>meaning "of fable" or "mythological"</note> creature; however, this is only an error of the observer. In the Phoenician gallery, this animal captured by *Hercules* was a *Gais* <note>original: *Gais*; likely referring to a mountain goat or a species of antelope/deer like the *dorcas* gazelle.</note>, a stag of a [particular] species which resembles a hind. [Thus], a hind with golden horns was created.

# Sixth Painting.
## The Birds of the Stymphalian Lake.

---

### Fifth Labor.

Hercules now receives the command to drive away the birds of the Stymphalian Lake, which were devastating the neighboring regions; he invents a bronze drum, which made a hideous and perpetual noise.

This painting, too, is taken from nature; one could not better depict the month of *November*, and the state of the fields associated with it. At that time, immense swarms of migratory birds, driven by the cold of the North, cover the land, which would devastate everything if one did not find means to be rid of them.

This explanation of these last two paintings, which already accords so well with nature, agrees no less with the calendar of pagan Rome; Rome had consecrated these two months to the gods corresponding to them, namely *Mars* <note>The Roman god of war, who also had ancient associations with agricultural protection.</note> (God of War) and *Diana* <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon.</note> (Goddess of the Hunt). These deities were thus so many symbols relating to the labors of these two months.

# Seventh Painting.
## The Cleansed Stables of Augeas.

### Sixth Labor.

Here one sees Hercules cleansing the stables of Augeas by means of a water stream. This labor refers to the month of December. Thus, we likely have here a depiction of the rainy weather of this season. They called the rainy season **Winter** <note>original: "Hyems"</note>, which literally expresses the "time of water," as this word is composed of two root words: **Hu**, **Hou**, or **Hy**, meaning **water**, and **Ems**, meaning **time**. For this very reason, the signs that appear at this time have been given the names **Aquarius** <note>German: "Wassermann," literally "Water-man"</note> and **Pisces** <note>German: "Fische," literally "Fish"</note>.

One can also say that the farmer <term>husbandman: a farmer or tiller of the soil</term> uses this season—which is a time of rest for the fields—to repair and clean his stables. He now carries out all internal tasks on his estates intended for the benefit of agriculture, which his previous pressing labors had prevented him from performing.

## Eighth Painting.

### The Subdued Bull; the Institution of the Olympic Games.

### Seventh Labor.

We encounter here a labor that had a preeminent influence on the most important events in Greece, namely the introduction of the games, particularly the Olympic Games. But what connection exists between the games and Hercules? What link do they have with the perspective from which we are considering him? What similarity is found between agricultural field-work and these games, which the whole of Greece was so enamored with, and which, it is said, were intended to maintain among its inhabitants the martial spirit <note>The "martial spirit" refers to the *arete* or excellence in combat that the Greeks believed was fostered by athletic competition.</note> through which they so greatly distinguished themselves in antiquity? It will be easy to discover all of this.

<margin>1) Strabo, *Geography*, Book VIII.</margin>
The origin of these games is lost in the darkness of the centuries; all arose during mythological times. The Nemean games, established in memory of the conquered lion, as well as the Olympic games, are attributed to Hercules; they are said to have been introduced by Hercules, though deciding exactly *which* Hercules this was presents a difficulty. Some say it was the Theban <note>The "Theban Hercules" refers to the famous son of Zeus and Alcmene.</note>, while others maintain (1) it was the Idaean <note>The "Idaean Hercules" refers to one of the Dactyls, mythical beings associated with Mount Ida who were sometimes credited with the earliest Olympic games.</note>. However, since one is as legendary as the other, one can only attribute the introduction of these games to him in an allegorical sense.

<meta>catchword: As soon as</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Seventh Labor of Hercules—the Subdued Bull—and its connection to the historical and agricultural origins of the Olympic Games.</meta>

As soon as Greece became a state devoted to agriculture, it also established fixed games; the same was true for the island of Crete, to which the Idaean Hercules <note>original: "Idäische Herkules." The Idaean Hercules refers to one of the Dactyls, mythical figures from Mount Ida in Crete who were often credited with establishing the first games, distinct from the later, more famous Theban Hercules.</note> was transplanted. Due to its trade with Egypt and Phoenicia and its fertile soil, Crete appears to have reached a state of prosperity much earlier than Greece.

However, these games did not originate in Crete or Greece; rather, they had already been introduced in the Eastern <note>original: "morgenländischen." Literally "morning-lands," referring to the Orient or the Near East.</note> kingdoms founded upon agriculture. For as soon as there were even just two farmers who had finished their harvests and tilled their fields, they surely took each other by the hand and performed a dance around their fields, expressing their joy and gratitude toward the Author <note>The "Urheber" or "Author" here refers to the divine creator or the source of nature's bounty.</note> of so many blessings. They also had their assistants dance and even crowned the animals—the faithful companions of their labor—with flowers. It was only right that everyone was moved by such happy results.

In Greece, these games merely received a more perfect, stable, and diverse organization, as they became the games of the entire nation, or of all the united Greek republics; among other peoples, however, they never achieved this level of universality.

It was not without reason that Hercules was honored with these games; they were placed under his protection and connected with the history of the Erymanthian Bull <note>The original text specifies the "erymantischen Stier" (Erymanthian Bull). In standard mythology, the Erymanthian beast is a boar, while the bull is Cretan. The author appears to be conflating these or following a specific variant of the legend.</note>.

All these subjects are very closely linked. The bull overcome by Hercules represents the bullfights—originating in the East and still so famous in southern countries today.

These games are assigned to the Seventh Labor, which falls in winter; for this is the time when—after the field work is completed and with full granaries and well-stocked cellars—people think only of pleasures in anticipation of the time when labor begins again. For all nations living with us under the same latitude, this is the season of festivals and public games. Such festivals in former times were the **Saturnalia**, of which the Feast of Kings <note>original: "Fest der Könige." This likely refers to Epiphany (Three Kings Day), which was often celebrated with "King of the Bean" festivities that echoed the social inversions of the Roman Saturnalia.</note> is but a shadow; another such festival is the modern **Carnival**.

They are an invention of **Hercules** or the **Sun**, because they were arranged according to the solar path and represented its course and labors. Therefore, at the entrances of the public places where these games were celebrated—such as at the entrance to the arenas—there were usually lions <note>The lion is a common solar symbol, often associated with the constellation Leo where the sun is strongest.</note>, while the arenas themselves were circular, like the orbit of the sun.

For this reason, the games of the **Circus** were also called **Sabine**; however, this was not intended to indicate that they were invented by the Sabines, but rather only that they were an imitation of the Sun, which, as we know from the history of Saturn, was called **Sab** or **Sab-us** <note>The author links the name "Sabine" to a solar deity name "Sab," following a tradition of interpretive mythology that looks for solar roots in tribal names.</note>.

The Olympic Games were celebrated only every four years, partly because it was too expensive to celebrate them every year, and also because they were organized according to the **leap-year solar cycle**, which encompasses four years, the fourth year of which is always one day longer than the other three.

This period of time was called an **Olympiad**. This method of counting the years only became common in Greece when **Iphitus** <note>Iphitus of Elis is the legendary figure credited with restoring the Olympic Games and establishing the "Olympic Truce" in the 8th century BCE.</note> [restored] the Olympic games, eight

# Ninth Painting.
## The Mares of Diomedes.
### Eighth Labor.

In the middle of the month of February, Hercules takes possession of the mares of Diomedes. They were so terrible that they were given bronze mangers, and so strong that they had to be bound with iron chains. They were not fed with the fruits of the earth; rather, they ate only the strangers who, to their misfortune, had arrived in Thrace. To tame them, Hercules satiated them with the flesh of the man who had accustomed them to human flesh; thereafter, he presented them to Eurystheus, who in turn made a gift of them to Juno.
