This is a bronze and iron allegory, and we should not be surprised that it has provoked so many explanations, of which each is more ridiculous than the last.

At approximately this same time, the Egyptians offered cakes to the gods upon which bound hippopotamuses were painted. This enigmatic image seems to have been the model for the mares of Diomedes, which were likewise bound with iron chains; for among the Egyptians, the hippopotamus represented Typhon <note>In Egyptian mythology, Typhon was the name often given by Greeks to Set, the god of chaos and storms, who was the rival of Osiris and Horus.</note>—overcome by Horus <note>original: "Orus"</note> and his horse—or the winter.

The Egyptians said that when Horus wished to avenge the death of Osiris (who had been killed by Typhon, or winter), he achieved his goal not with a lion, but on horseback. The underlying basis is shared; only the secondary circumstances differ slightly from one another.

Winter is indeed a terrible season, during which the earth produces nothing, and its womb is a bronze and iron womb, closed to all the labors of the husbandman; it forces the farmer to nourish himself from his previous labors, to consume his harvests, and to empty his cellars and granaries.

Hercules takes command of the month of February; he causes the winter to cease; he gives the horses their master to eat, for from that moment on, he <note>Referring to Diomedes, who personifies the winter.</note> does not appear again.

Hercules has overcome Diomedes; for here, Diomedes and Typhon are one and the same. His name—composed of <term>Dio</term> <note>Meaning Jupiter or Heaven.</note> and the word <term>mad</term> <note>Meaning moist or wet.</note>—clearly designates the winter or the rainy season.

# Tenth Picture.

## The War with the Amazons.

### Ninth Labor.

If there is any Labor of Hercules for which one can be excused for interpreting it historically, it is certainly this one. The narrative of it is so detailed, so simple, and so natural that one can harbor no suspicion toward it—all the less so because no monsters appear in it, unlike in the other labors. Consequently, everyone considered this war with the Amazons to be an actual historical event.

To be sure, one should have doubted the truth of such a bloody war fought merely over a belt <note>This refers to the Girdle of Hippolyta, the Queen of the Amazons, which Hercules was tasked to retrieve for Eurystheus's daughter.</note>; but so many wars have been incited over trivial things, so many nations brought to ruin, so many cities destroyed, and so many atrocities committed, that oppressed humanity is no longer surprised by anything. Thus, it is not found unbelievable when a wandering hero—as Hercules is depicted—lets streams of blood flow for the sake of a belt.

Admittedly, one should also have relegated such a strange nation as that of the Amazons to the realm of fabulous beings; but antiquity speaks of them so often, and did we not ourselves believe for a long time that Amazons existed? One has such a great inclination for the marvelous and the extraordinary that, I repeat, one is very much [inclined...]

### Interpretation of these ten characters.

Until the month of March, the nights contested the heavenly girdle with Hercules—or the Sun; until then, the nights lasted longer than the days, and the dominion of the heavens belonged to them. Finally, Hercules gains the upper hand; he wrests the girdle from them, the days become much longer, and the shamed, dismayed Night seeks to hide herself in Scythia. <note>In the ancient world, Scythia represented the cold, dark, and remote northern regions—a fitting place for the retreating "winter" nights to flee.</note>

To obtain the girdle, Hercules sails across the Black Sea and the land of the Cimmerians; yet both terms denote the darkness of the night. The latter was derived from the Oriental <note>The author uses "Oriental" to refer to Semitic languages, specifically Hebrew.</note> word *Camar* <note>original: כמר (*kamar*); in Hebrew, this root can refer to being scorched or darkened, which the author interprets here as the blackness of night.</note>, which means black, dark, or the terrors of the night. From this comes the proverb "Cimmerian darkness," by which one intends to indicate the thickest gloom.

The queen, the owner of the girdle, bears the name **Melanippe**, a word that signifies the queen of the black horses; but who can fail to recognize the Night in this mournful and lamentable team? <note>The name Melanippe is derived from the Greek *melas* (black) and *hippos* (horse), often associated in myth with the chariots of the underworld or the night.</note>

Her subjects are called **Amazons**, and they could bear no more appropriate name. It is derived from the root word *Am* or *Ama*—meaning "reunion" or "gathering"—and the word *Zone*, meaning "girdle"; thus, they are the nights which all together rule over one zone. <note>This is a speculative historical etymology. While modern scholars debate the origin of the word "Amazon," the author here links it to the Hebrew *am* (people/gathering) and the Greek *zone* (belt/region) to fit the astronomical allegory.</note>

This etymology is so fortunate that, even if one had intended to devise it specifically for this purpose, one could not have made it any better; moreover, it is also perfectly consistent with the spirit of antiquity. In this—

...the name **Azonoi** <note>original: ΑΖΩΝΟΙ; from the Greek 'a-' (without) and 'zone'</note> was given to those gods who had no specific territory or their own zone in the heavens. The name **Themiscyra** finally concludes the explanation of this allegory, of which it is the resolving word.

...retreat further back behind **Scythia** <note>A vast region of northern Eurasia, often used in classical texts to represent the cold, dark, and "barbaric" North</note>, and do not appear again.

This is also literally true. **Minerva**, or in the Greek language **Athene**, reliably signifies the Moon. The **Athene** in question here is therefore not the city of Athens, but the goddess of that name. She completes the victory over the Amazons because the New Moon follows immediately upon the Spring Equinox in March, shortening the nights even further and forcing them to leave Scythia.

If one possesses even a little mythological and Oriental linguistic knowledge, one will not be surprised that **Minerva** or **Athene** is the Moon, and even less so that the Moon was called **Athene**. The Moon was the Queen of the Stars, and this is precisely what **Athene** signifies: "the Ruler." **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer (c. 46 – 120 AD)</note> even states in his treatise *On Isis and Osiris* that the Moon is called *Athenais* in the East. This word is the feminine form of the name for the Sun, **Adonis**, "the Lord" or "the King." <note>The author is connecting the Semitic root *Adon* (Lord) to the lunar deity to support his astronomical interpretation.</note>

The story of Orpheus, which seems to be the episode of a chatterer <note>original: "Schwätzers"; likely referring to a digressive or overly descriptive narrator</note>, is quite appropriate here; it is also likely that the story of the Voyage of the Argonauts, mentioned only as if by chance, has a greater connection to these subjects than one might believe.

The Eleusinian Mysteries, as well as the initiations into them, were closely linked with the views of the ancients regarding the <term>Elysian Fields</term> <note>The final resting place of the souls of the heroic and the virtuous</note> and <term>Tartarus</term> <note>The deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment and suffering for the wicked</note>. Orpheus, who sang of them, composed a poem titled *Descent into the Underworld*; it was therefore claimed that he had traveled down into the netherworld.

Since Virgil <note>The Roman poet, author of the Aeneid</note> felt compelled to have his pious hero <note>Aeneas</note> initiated, he likewise had him make a journey to the Underworld. Theseus is also said to have gone there; with this intention, he sat down upon the stone of sorrow <note>original: "traurigen Stein"; likely the Agelastos Petra, or "Mirthless Stone"</note>, upon which Ceres <note>The Roman name for Demeter, goddess of the harvest</note> had also sat when she was completely exhausted from searching for her daughter.

The "descent into hell" and Cerberus <note>The multi-headed hound guarding the gates of the Underworld</note> thus became the symbols for the mysteries and initiations. In this passage regarding the Labors of Hercules, Cerberus likewise stands in place of all the mysteries and initiation; a ceremony which was described with magnificent expressions as a real journey into the kingdom of the dead, and of which Apuleius <note>Author of the 2nd-century Roman novel "The Golden Ass"</note> said:

> ” I have approached the boundaries of death, and
> ” have returned from my journey through the realm of Proserpina <note>The Roman name for Persephone, Queen of the Underworld</note>,
> ” carried by the elements. In the middle of the
> ” night, I saw the sun in extraordinary brilliance...

But what should one understand by this Garden of the Hesperides, and by the apples plucked by Hercules? It is in vain that one consults antiquity and modern scholars here; of all the conjectures expressed on this subject, none is satisfactory.

Some said these golden apples were sheep, with which *Atlas* wished to repay Hercules for the services rendered to him; these sheep were supposedly most famous at that time for their beautiful wool. That one truly understood "sheep" by these "apples" is proven, they say, by the Greek word *Melon*, or *Malon* in the Doric dialect, which means both **sheep** and **apple**. The Latins also derived their word *malum* <note>original: *malun*—the Latin word for apple</note> from this.

Others, among whom **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French scholar who sought to explain Greek myths through Phoenician etymology.</note> is numbered, saw in these apples the riches of **Atlas**; because **Malon**, which in the Phoenician language means "apple" just as it does in Greek, also signifies "wealth" in this Eastern tongue.

Still others saw in them actual apples—golden apples or bitter oranges <note>original: *Pomeranzen*</note>—which were therefore called **Aurantia** <note>Latin: "golden things"</note> or gold-fruits in the Latin language, or **Orange** in the French language.

Regarding the pillars erected by **Hercules** as his "nothing further beyond" <note>original: *non plus ultra*, a Latin phrase marking the limit of the known world</note>, the boundary of his wanderings, there is just as little agreement. Some believed one should understand them as actual pillars erected on both coasts of the Strait of **Gibraltar**, as this strait was for a long time considered the end of the world. Others saw in them the mountains **Calpe** and **Avyla** <note>Now known as the Rock of Gibraltar in Europe and Monte Hacho or Jebel Musa in Africa.</note> which border this Strait of **Gibraltar**, one of which is located in **Europe** and the other in **Africa**; they supported their opinion through etymology, as **Avyla** signifies a "pillar" in the Eastern languages.

According to still others, they are two pillars erected in the Temple of **Hercules** at **Cadiz** <note>original: *Cadix*</note> as two talismans against the fury of the water. **Hercules** had engraved magical words upon these in the Palace of the Fates <note>original: *Parzen*, the deities of destiny</note> in order to secure the land and the **Ocean** forever.

This month is **June** <note>original: *Junius*</note>; but does **Hercules**—or the sun—not truly reach the end of his labors at the entry into the sign of **Cancer**, as the highest point of his course? Is this sign not truly the "nothing further beyond" <note>original: *non plus ultra*, a Latin phrase signifying a limit that cannot be passed</note>? These two famous pillars, beyond which he can never pass, are thus the two **Tropics** <note>original: *Wendekreise*; the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note>; they are the pillars or boundaries which **Eurystheus** <note>In myth, the king who assigned Hercules his twelve labors</note> or the Almighty assigned to him; they are the barriers which he never crosses, which circumscribe the immense circle destined for his path, and between which he performs all his labors.

**Calpe** and **Avyla** <note>The mountains flanking the Strait of Gibraltar</note> are nothing in comparison with these pillars; to the first **Phoenicians** they may well have served as the goal of their journeys, but for our heavenly fighter <note>i.e., the Sun</note> they were not the boundary.

But how then is he found in the Garden of the **Hesperides**? Nothing is simpler. The word **Hesper**, from which the **Latins** made ***Vesperus*** <note>Latin: "evening" or "the evening star"</note>, constantly signifies the evening or the sunset. This word, however, is not a root word; it is rather made from the Oriental word ***Sper***, which means day, light, or morning, and which, when the negation ***He***, ***Que***, or ***Ve*** precedes it, expresses evening, sunset, or darkness.

Figurative expressions are also linked with these peculiar terms. Thus, the expression **morning** or **day** is used for **life**, just as the setting of the sun, darkness, and night are associated with the concept of **death** and the **end**.

As soon as **Hercules** reaches the month of **June** <note>original: *Junius*</note> or one of his **pillars**, and has finished his course, he is already truly in the **Garden of the Hesperides**.

**Evenus** <note>original: *Evene*</note> literally means the **river of the sun**. This word is composed of the two root words <term>Ev</term> or <term>Av</term> (meaning water) and <term>Ew</term> or <term>Oen</term> (meaning sun). **Nessus**, on the other hand, is the Oriental word נצה <note>original: *Nesshe*</note>, which means **victory**; it is a name given to the last day of the year.

If these words are transformed—one into a hero or centaur, and the other into a heroine or the wife of Hercules—then they are truly the authors of his end. For if the number of his days had not become full, and if he had not achieved **victory** by arriving at the end of his career, he would still be continuing his course; he would still be wrestling in the **circus** <note>The author uses "circus" here to refer to the celestial arena or the circular path of the sun through the zodiac</note>.

# Fourteenth Painting.

## Death of Hercules and his Deification.

Now that Hercules has brought his labors to an end, entrusted his first wife and his fifty sons to Iolaus <note>original: *Jolas*; in Greek mythology, Iolaus was the nephew and charioteer of Hercules</note>, married Omphale and Deianira, and taken possession of Iole, he has himself carried to Mount Oeta. There, he casts himself upon a great funeral pyre and, after his sudden disappearance, is placed among the gods.

Here we behold again the ancient allegories of all the peoples of the East—the dead Osiris mourned by the Egyptians, as well as Thamuz and Adonis, who share a similar fate in Phoenicia and Syria, and so forth.

Osiris, Adonis, Thamuz, and Hercules on Mount Oeta, etc., are all one and the same allegory referring to the end of the year and to the sun—to the sun which moves away, which dies, until it returns from the interior of Africa as radiant as ever, spreading cheerfulness and joy everywhere.

The name of Mount Oeta is derived from the Eastern word for fire, which also signifies the sun: **Esch** or **Oet** <note>original: **Esch**, **Oet**; these likely refer to the Hebrew word *esh* (fire) and related Semitic roots for heat or light</note>. Hercules burns himself on Mount Oeta just as the Phoenix does upon the altar at Heliopolis <note>Heliopolis is Greek for "City of the Sun," an ancient Egyptian city where the mythical Phoenix was said to be reborn</note>. This revolution <note>In this context, the author uses "revolution" to mean a completed cycle or orbit of time</note> has thus concluded to make room for another, and the spectator has been dismissed with a beautiful display of fireworks.

<meta>This page continues the astronomical and allegorical interpretation of the life of Hercules. ### Hercules refuses to be placed among the twelve great gods.

Hercules, having finally been introduced into heaven as a reward for his labors, refuses to take his place among the twelve great gods <note>original: *die zwölf grossen Götter*; likely referring to the *Dii Consentes*, the twelve major deities of the Greco-Roman pantheon such as Jupiter, Juno, and Apollo</note> in order, as he says, not to offend anyone. This circumstance, told as if by chance <note>original: *wie von Ohngefähr*</note>, completes this allegory. The twelve great gods were, as we shall see in the following, merely the symbolic representations of the sun and the moon for each month, from which people subsequently created just as many deities to protect those months.

Since Hercules was the sun itself, which presided over all these months, he could not—without self-degradation <note>original: *Selbsterniedrigung*</note> and without the allegory becoming false and forever obscure—accept a place among the twelve months.

### Marriage of Hercules to Hebe.

Even if Hercules refuses the position among the twelve great gods, he does not do so in regard to Hebe; he accepts her offered hand and thus becomes the husband of the goddess of youth. But is the husband of the goddess of youth not himself the god of youth? Here we have yet another allegory which, if Hercules is considered merely a man, has no basis; however, it becomes very fitting and entirely appropriate to nature as soon as Hercules is understood as the sun, the leader of agricultural labors. For every year the sun reappears with all the charms of youth, with its former strength, and with it all of nature revives, adorned with the full splendor of spring and the bloom of life.

This allegorical marriage alone should be sufficient to prove in the clearest possible way that the entire history of Hercules is merely an allegory, which has the sun and agricultural labors as its subject.

Would it not have been the greatest folly to have made a mortal the husband of Youth, when one could have chosen from among so many other deities?

# Part Four.

## The remaining deeds of Hercules; a general overview thereof.

---

If the birth of Hercules, his worship, his names, his symbols, all his labors, his deification, and his marriages prove that he represents the sun—specifically in regards to the reclamation of land and agricultural works during the course of a year—then the majority of his remaining deeds prove this just as well. These include his victories achieved over Antaeus <note>a giant wrestler who drew strength from touching the Earth</note>, Emathion <note>a king of Ethiopia slain by Hercules</note>, Busiris <note>an Egyptian king who sacrificed travelers until he was stopped by Hercules</note>, and so forth; his works performed on the island of Crete, in Africa, in Greece, and in the Alps; his battles against the giants; his arrival at the Palatine Hill <note>the central hill of Rome, where Hercules was said to have stopped while driving the cattle of Geryon</note>; the foundations attributed to him under the name of the Idaean Hercules <note>a distinct, older figure associated with Mount Ida, often considered one of the Dactyls or divine craftsmen</note>; the twelve altars he erected for the twelve great gods; the spread of his worship; and the divine honors paid to him in so many places, and so on.

All these heroic deeds are in too natural a connection with the immortal hero, and are too poorly suited for a human being, for them not to prove once again that everything in the life of Hercules is allegorical. If a hero of this name ever actually lived in Greece, none of his real actions have reached us, because they have been merged with the solar allegory that constitutes the history of Hercules.

### §. 1.
## Victories of Hercules over Antaeus, Emathion, Busiris, etc.

Various mythologists place these victories within the twelfth labor of Hercules; they are therefore allegorical, just as that labor is. To prove this, the names of these tyrants alone are sufficient.

Antaeus is the son of the Earth; one cannot seize him except by lifting him up high above the earth. <note>In mythology, the giant Antaeus remained invincible as long as he touched his mother, Gaia (the Earth). Hercules defeated him by holding him aloft and crushing him.</note>

Emathion is the son of the Dawn <note>original: "Morgenröthe"; Emathion was the son of Tithonus and Eos, the goddess of the dawn</note>.

Busiris kidnaps the daughters of Atlas, and so forth. These are nothing but fables or allegories; one will never be able to take these persons for real beings. Nonetheless, I feel too inadequate to give a satisfactory explanation of the allegory they offer, which is perhaps too little developed for us to grasp it properly. In the meantime, I will venture an attempt.

Busiris kidnaps the daughters of Atlas, who carries the heavens on his shoulders; Hercules, angered by this, comes to the aid of Atlas and returns his daughters to him. All of this is true <note>i.e., "true" in the sense of having a consistent symbolic meaning</note>.

Atlas, who carries the heavens on his shoulders, designates the mountains; specifically, cultivated mountains, for his name leads to the concept of culture and labor <note>The author likely connects Atlas to the Greek *tlao* (to endure or bear), relating the "burden" of the mountain to the heavy labor of terrace farming or mountain agriculture</note>.

The daughters of the mountains are the grapevines, which are always planted on high ground.

### §. 2.
### *Melampyges*, an Epithet of *Hercules*.

When **Hercules** had captured two robbers <note>The Cercopes, mischievous forest creatures or gnomes in Greek myth.</note> and was carrying them by their feet upon his back, he suddenly heard them break out into laughter and call him **Melampyges**, which means **the man with the black b . . . .** <note>original German: "Mann mit dem schwarzen H . . . ."; a reference to *Hintern* (buttocks). The epithet *Melampygos* literally means "black-bottomed." According to legend, the robbers laughed because Hercules' backside, exposed by his lion skin, was tanned dark or hairy.</note>. He found their good humor and frankness so amusing that he granted them their freedom and let them go. This story and this epithet are likewise an allegory referring to the **sun**; for just as the setting **sun** turns its back, everything immediately becomes dark and black.

### §. 3.
### The Altars Erected by Him to the Twelve Great Gods.

**Hercules** is said to have erected an altar to each of the twelve gods. This truly accords with the **sun**, whose path—divided into twelve months—gave occasion for twelve sacrifices. On the first day of each month, one would sacrifice in honor of each deity on as many different altars as there were gods protecting the months. This custom, observable in ancient **Rome** regarding the twelve altars (one for each month), continues even today in **China**.

## §. 4.

### Hercules’ Residence on the Island of Crete and in Africa; the Labors He Performed There.

The manner in which Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, famous for writing a massive "Universal History."</note> recounts the beneficial effects of Hercules’ stay on the island of Crete and in Africa—while he waited there for the favorable time to undertake his tenth labor <note>The tenth labor was the capture of the cattle of the giant Geryon.</note>—provides us with even more striking evidence that the story of Hercules is merely an allegory for the reclamation of the earth and for agricultural labor.

> ” the wild beasts that had previously devastated it.

> ” This hero subsequently also freed Africa from a great multitude of wild

### §. 5.
## The Drainage Accomplished in Greece.

The farmer, however, does not restrict himself merely to dry soil; rather, he seizes as much land flooded by water as he possibly can. He does this, partly to expand his territory, and partly to make the waters themselves more useful through the advantages he knows how to draw from them, ever since he has enclosed them in a narrower space. This occurred in Greece as well as in all other regions where agriculture is practiced, and one could rightly attribute all these labors to *Hercules*, that is, to the allegorized farmer. It is this *Hercules* who, as *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, the 1st-century BCE historian mentioned on the previous page.</note> relates, by digging a deep trench in the form of a canal, created a riverbed for the river *Peneus*, into which all the waters—by which a significant district of *Thessaly* had been flooded—flowed away, thereby transforming a desolate region into a charming landscape known by the name of the fertile valley of *Tempe*.

For this very reason, the story of his struggle with the river *Achelous*—who was transformed into a bull—was devised; he tore a horn from the river, from which the horn of *Amalthea* <note>Commonly known as the *cornucopia* or "horn of plenty," symbolizing abundance.</note> originated.

This too is an allegory referring to the drainage of marshy lands; it is all the more attractive because *Diodorus* explains it himself, and his explanation perfectly agrees with our principles. The battle against

### §. 6.
## Hercules’s Labors in the Alps.

The farmer is not content with the mere production of precious riches; he also wants to have them transported to all places where they are needed, where he can exchange them for other useful things. To achieve this goal, he must be able to send them everywhere by water and by land with the greatest possible ease. The farmer therefore paves ways for himself in all directions; in low-lying lands, he constructs elevated stone roads, he makes the mountains lower, over the rivers he builds bridges, and so forth. We must therefore not wonder when our author has Hercules cross the Alps, and has him make all the paths of this land so level and so convenient that an army, with all its baggage, could march across it with little effort.

Hercules, or the farmer, is the only one capable of carrying out such works; for he alone derives benefit from them, and he alone possesses the means to do so in the immeasurable resources offered by his art and its success, which are constantly renewed.

All the festivals of Sicily relating to agriculture were presented as if Hercules were their originator, or as if they had some reference to him. These latter festivals remind us of the **Saturnalia** <note>A Roman winter festival in honor of Saturn, characterized by role reversals and social freedom, rooted in ancient harvest traditions</note> celebrated in other regions, where the solemnities are likewise derived from agriculture. The former festivals in honor of Proserpina <note>The Roman name for Persephone, whose return from the underworld symbolizes the growth of grain</note> also arose from a devotion to farming and, as I have already demonstrated in the *History of Saturn* under the entry for Proserpina, refer to the sowing season.

### 2) Sacrifices, and the divine worship paid to him in various places.

The same situation applies to the sacrifices offered to him in Greece and the divine honors paid there, all of which related to agriculture. Among these were the sacrifices organized in his honor by the Opuntians <note>Inhabitants of Opus, a city in ancient Greece</note> and the Thebans. These consisted—very much like the sacrifices called **Suovetaurilia** <note>original: "Suovetaurilia" — a traditional Roman sacrifice involving a pig (sus), a sheep (ovis), and a bull (taurus)</note> by the Romans—of a bull, a pig, and a ram <note>The original German "Bocke" refers to a male goat or ram; in the context of the Suovetaurilia, it typically refers to a ram</note>. These rituals were introduced for the preservation and promotion of the successful growth of the crops in the fields.

### 3) The tithe introduced in his honor.

Upon his arrival at the Palatine Hill, Hercules was very well received by the local inhabitants, and a tithe <note>A "Zehnde" or tithe is a one-tenth part of something, usually crops, paid as a tax or religious offering</note> was introduced in his honor.

The tithe can only exist in a land suited for farming. One should not be surprised, however, to see his festival celebrated by the inhabitants of the Palatine Hill—an Arcadian colony—long before the time of the Romans. ### §. 9.
## The Idaean Hercules and his Dactyls.

Regarding the Hercules who bore the epithet of the **Idaean**, who was the leader of the **Dactyls** <note>In Greek mythology, these were archaic chthonic beings (dwarves or magicians) associated with the Great Mother goddess and metalworking</note>, and to whom is attributed the introduction of the Olympic Games, the art of forging metals, and the invention of dancing to the sound of instruments—intended, so it is said, to prevent Saturn <note>The Roman equivalent of the Titan Cronus, who attempted to swallow his children</note> from hearing the cries of the infant Jove <note>original: "Jovs"; Jove or Jupiter, the king of the gods, hidden from his father Saturn on Mount Ida</note> entrusted to him by Jove’s mother—I must necessarily be somewhat more detailed.

This elaborate story—this Hercules along with his people, these metals, these dances, these noisy instruments, and this guarding of the infant Jove—utterly confused all mythologists who wished to see in it nothing more than historical events; consequently, they cast over it a darkness that has remained impenetrable until now.

However, since Jove was the supreme God and Saturn was Time, their story could only be an allegory; thus, the Dactyls—the guardians of the former—must also represent only allegorical beings. It will not be difficult to rediscover their true meaning. They were called **Dactyls**, that is, the fingers, because their number amounted to five; the Idaean Hercules was their leader.

But Hercules is, as I have shown, the Sun; he was given the epithet of the Idaean not because he inhabited Mount Ida on the island of Crete <note>original: "Creta"</note>, but because the Sun illuminates and oversees the entire world. It was from this very concept that Mount Ida also received its name <note>The author likely refers to the Greek verb "idein," meaning "to see," suggesting Ida is the "mountain of seeing" or the "lookout"</note>, in that one...

...from its peak, since it was a very high mountain, one could look out far and wide.

This name comes from the root word **Eid** <note>The author is likely referring to the Proto-Indo-European root *weid-*, meaning "to see" or "to know"</note>, which means **to recognize** and also **to see**; it has produced many words in the Greek and Latin languages. The Greek words include **to know** <note>original: "Eid-no", likely *eidô* or *oida*</note>—to become aware—and **behold** <note>original: "Id-e", likely the imperative *ide*</note>, and so forth. Among the Latin words belonging here are **see** <note>original: "Vid-e"</note>, **I see** <note>original: "Vid-eo"</note>, and **that** <note>original: "Id"</note>—precisely that which you see. The Oriental word **hand** <note>Hebrew: י יד (*Yad*)</note> is also certainly related to this; for in order to precisely recognize an object and its form, one reaches for it with the hand, and one only sees quite exactly what one holds in one's hand. From this also stems the well-known word **Idea**, the origin of which so few knew.

These five **Dactyls** <note>From the Greek *daktyloi*, meaning "fingers"</note>, of whom he [Hercules] is the leader, are therefore—and indeed quite certainly—the five **planets** subordinate to the Sun and the Moon, which were called the **bodyguards of the King and Queen of the Heavens**; they are also all in the service of **Rhea** or the Great Goddess, and are the guardians of **Jove** <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods</note>.

It has already been mentioned above in what sense the introduction of the Olympic Games must be attributed to their leader, namely in the very same sense in which they are considered the inventors of metals. Everyone knows that in antiquity, metals and planets bore the same names—a custom of which we still discover traces today in the name **Mercury**, which denotes both a planet and a metal.

**Saturn** signifies **Lead**; **Jupiter** signifies **Tin**; **Mars** signifies **Iron** <note>original: "le fer" (French for iron)</note>; both words [Mars and Iron] come from **Har**, which was pronounced as **Mar** and **Fer**. **Venus** designated **Copper**, from which comes her name **Cupris** or **Cypris** <note>referring to the island of Cyprus, famous for its copper mines and association with Venus/Aphrodite</note>, and the

The name of the island of Cyprus, which is sacred to Venus or Cypris, comes from the copper mines located there. <note>The English word "copper" is derived from the Latin *cuprum*, which itself comes from *Cyprium aes*, meaning "metal from Cyprus."</note> Mercury still meant, as it does now, *Mercurius* (quicksilver). The Idaean Hercules, or gold—the most excellent metal—was called *Sol* <note>Latin: "Sun"</note>, and *Luna* <note>Latin: "Moon"</note> designated silver.

Gold and silver became more distinguished than other metals; they became the "colors and metals" of the coat of arms <note>original: "des Emaux," referring to heraldic enamels or tinctures</note>; a distinction preserved in heraldry, whose language and symbols stem from hoary antiquity.

The colors and metals in the coat of arms <note>original: "les Emaux"</note> do not unite with one another because the Moon and the Sun do not travel in company; however, the [other] metals go with the colors and metals in the coat of arms because they represent the planets, the bodyguards of the Sun and the Moon. <note>The author is providing a mythological explanation for the heraldic "Rule of Tincture," which generally forbids placing a metal on a metal (gold on silver) or a color on a color.</note>

The similarity of Hercules to the Olympic Games leads us to the explanation of an Egyptian symbol, which seems to be one of the strangest; namely, they are said to have represented the year by a quarter of a field.

This was very well conceived; the entire field was the Olympiad, or the cycle composed of four years; a quarter of it is the year.

The field is the farmer's ground and soil divided into four parts, of which he tills one part every year. Through this division into four parts, it became the "field" of the coat of arms <note>The "field" in heraldry refers to the background of the shield.</note>, which, by its division into four fields, provided the opportunity to demand four quarters for the proof of ancestry <term>Ahnenprobe: A formal requirement in noble society to prove one's lineage by displaying the coats of arms of one's ancestors.</term>, or for the strictest proof, four times four, or sixteen quarters.

This was the deciding reason for this choice, which could also have fallen on completely different sacred numbers adopted for other subjects, such as three and five.

->§. 10.<-

### Hercules among the Argonauts; his heroic deeds before Troy.

Among all the events in the life of Hercules, his voyage with the Argonauts—who found themselves forced to leave him behind because he was starving them out <note>original: "ihn zu verlassen, gezwungen sahen, weil er sie aushungerte." This refers to the mythological tradition where Hercules' immense appetite or his great weight made him a liability to the ship's provisions or the rowing capacity of the crew.</note>—and his heroic deeds before Troy seem truly historical, and it seems almost impossible to take them in any other sense. The latter consisted first in the rescue of Hesione, who was condemned to be the prey of a sea monster; afterward in the vengeance taken upon Laomedon, the King of Troy, who broke his word and withheld from him the reward promised for saving his daughter Hesione; and finally in the rebuilding of Troy.

But even assuming it could not be proven that these occurrences could be taken in an allegorical sense, they still cannot nullify the preceding circumstances which encompass the entire life of Hercules.

In the meantime, I intend to achieve even more; when I come to the voyage of the Argonauts, whose number initially amounted to only 52 <note>In allegorical interpretations of the time, the number 52 was often linked to the number of weeks in a solar year.</note>, I will show that this is an allegory, in the same style as all other mythological fables.

The story of Hesione itself is an absurd fable in a historical sense; if it has an underlying meaning, then this can only be an allegorical one. However, since it primarily belongs to the history of Troy, I will save its development for my treatise concerning Troy.

### First Note.

#### Ancient Monuments Relating to the Labors of Hercules.

From various monuments of antiquity, one can see that the labors of Hercules frequently provided the subject matter upon which artists practiced; they were painted and engraved sometimes together, sometimes individually, as the intended use required.

Individually, they are struck on very many commemorative medals <note>The original term "Schaumünzen" refers to medals or coins produced for display or to commemorate specific events rather than for general currency.</note>; one sees many of these in the collections of medals and antiquities.

The Emperor **Commodus** liked to compare himself to this god <note>The Roman Emperor Commodus (reigned 180–192 AD) was famously obsessed with Hercules, often appearing in the arena as a gladiator and ordering statues of himself depicted with the god's lion skin and club.</note>.

On one of his medals, one therefore sees a Hercules depicted with a club, bow, and quiver (1).

On another, this hero holds the handles of a plow, with the inscription: *Hercules the Founder* <note>original Latin: "Hercules Fundator." This refers to the tradition of a hero or ruler plowing a ritual furrow to mark the boundaries of a newly founded city.</note>.

On the medals of **Postumus** <note>original: "Posthumius." This likely refers to Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, the 3rd-century ruler of the Gallic Empire, who frequently used Herculean imagery to legitimize his rule.</note> one sees his battles against the bull (2), the boar, the dog **Cerberus**, and against **Antaeus**, and so forth.

1) Vaillant, *Roman Imperial Medals*, Volume III, page 147.
2) Ibid., page 4.

One also sees them on a square altar in the *Giustiniani Gallery* in *Rome*, an illustration of which can be found in the works of *Father de Montfaucon* (16) <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) was a French monk whose massive illustrated volumes helped popularize the study of ancient art and archaeology.</note>. It is quite correct that one of the sides is missing, on which three of the labors—the seventh, eighth, and ninth—were presented.

There are also historical monuments of these works.

## Second Note.

### Similarities between Hercules and Samson.

The names Hercules and Samson have such a great similarity through their relationship to the sun, and because they both designate individuals of quite extraordinary strength, that it would not be surprising if the deeds of one had been credited to the account of the other. I myself believe I discover in the Greek Hercules some of the important deeds of the Hebrew hero, which should not, however, be considered a new thought, as various scholars—including Fabricius (*) among others—have already expressed it.

---

*) Fabricius <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a celebrated German classical scholar and bibliographer.</note> says in his notes on the work of Philastrius <note>Saint Philastrius, the 4th-century Bishop of Brescia who wrote a famous catalog of heresies titled *Libre de Haeresibus*.</note> concerning heresies: that the pagans confused Samson with Hercules and believed that he was one and the same as the sun.

My opinion is based on the following circumstances:

I. In the *Antiquity Explained* <note>Original: *L'antiquité expliquée et représentée en figures* by Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741), a massive 15-volume work that laid the foundations of modern archaeology.</note> by Father Montfaucon, (1) one sees a very strange copper engraving made from an engraved gem. On this, Hercules carries two pillars on his shoulders, which were called the Gates of Cadiz; this hero is depicted, however—and this deserves to be noted—without his lion's skin.

Can one fail to recognize Samson here, who carries away on his shoulders and without a lion's skin the gates of Gaza—a Phoenician city like Cadiz?

II. Herodotus <note>The 5th-century BCE Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note> tells a fable about Hercules which seems so absurd to him that he cannot believe it at all. Here is this short narrative: "According to the
" Greeks," he says, (2) "Hercules came to Egypt, where he was
" taken prisoner by the Egyptians. They immediately decided
" to sacrifice him to Jupiter <note>Original: *Jupiter*, the Roman name for the king of the gods, whom the Greeks called Zeus and the Egyptians associated with Amun.</note>; they had already led
" him to the foot of the altar, and the sacrificial
" words had already been spoken over him, when Hercules suddenly
" gathered his strength and killed them all.

This story, transplanted to Egypt, necessarily seemed absurd to Herodotus: "The Egyptians,"
" he says, "sacrifice only animals; would they then
" have sacrificed a human." Meanwhile, this story was so widely affirmed that he did not dare to reject it entirely; he even asks the gods and heroes for forgiveness for his disbelief.

Who, however, does not recognize here the story of Samson, the Hebrew Hercules, as he, by the Philistines, a—

[...of] an Egyptian colony, captured in the neighborhood of Egypt? These Philistines were very easily confused with the Egyptians by the Greeks.

### III. 

In the fourth book of Ovid's *Fasti* <note>Ovid’s *Fasti* is a famous Latin poem that explains the origins of Roman festivals and customs throughout the year.</note>, there is another detail very similar to the story of Samson; it concerns Carseolum, a city of the Peligni in Magna Graecia <note>Latin for "Great Greece," the coastal areas of Southern Italy that were heavily colonized by Greek settlers in antiquity.</note>. As is well known, all cities there grew out of Oriental—and especially Phoenician—colonies; also, learned men, among others **Mazocchi** <note>Alessio Simmaco Mazzocchi (1684–1771) was an Italian antiquarian and priest known for his work on ancient inscriptions.</note>, famous for his precious works, have proven that most cities there bore Oriental names. This case applies perfectly to Carseolum. This name is a combination of two Hebrew or Oriental words which mean **Fox-town**; an etymology that completely agrees with Ovid's narrative of this city. This poet says:

> "At Carseolum, it is forbidden by law to boast of having captured a fox."

He adds that every year there, with great solemnity, foxes are burned by means of straw bundles tied to their backs. (3)

Filled with astonishment at a prohibition and such a strange custom—which he certainly would have wondered at even more had he known the meaning of the name of this city—he asks the inhabitants for an explanation: they reply to him that this was done in memory of their grain being burned by a fox; for a young man had tied straw bundles to a fox, set them on fire, and let it run into the field. <note>This bears a striking resemblance to Judges 15:4–5, where Samson ties torches to the tails of 300 foxes and releases them into the Philistines' grain fields.</note>

3) *Fasti* Book IV. 681 : 712. <note>original: "Fast. L. IV. 681 : 712."</note>

IV. Those who search for sacred history within secular history—specifically within mythology—will surely find the similarity between **Hercules** and **Moses** quite striking. Hercules was abandoned by his true mother and raised by his persecutor, **Juno** <note>In Greek myth, Hercules was the son of Alcmene, but the goddess Juno (Hera) hated him and tried to destroy him, though she unwittingly nursed him at one point.</note>; similarly, Moses was abandoned by his mother but rescued by an Egyptian woman, the daughter of his oppressor.

<meta>This page continues the author’s effort to show how Greek myths often originated from misunderstood Hebrew names or biblical accounts. However, the word **Ain** also signifies **vigorous** <note>original: "Geil"; in this archaic context, it likely refers to a lush, bubbling, or fertile spring.</note>, and **Kore** is the participle of the verb **to cry out** <note>original: "Kre".</note>. In the history of **Hercules**, there is also a feature in which people believed they perceived the event that happened to **Jonah**. **Lycophron**, a Greek poet living at the court of the Egyptian kings after the time of the Translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, says right at the beginning of his **Cassandra** <note>Also known as the *Alexandra*, a notoriously difficult and obscure poem.</note>; that **Hercules**, who was conceived in **three nights** <note>Referring to the myth where Zeus extended the night of Hercules' conception to the length of three nights.</note>, was swallowed by the sea monster that was supposed to devour **Hesione**, and was then spat out again.

Since **Lycophron** is the only one to report this circumstance, and he could have been informed of the story of **Jonah**—which occurred long before his time—it is quite possible that he intended to imitate it in his poem, which is already overloaded with foreign and peculiar expressions. As for me, I am much more inclined to believe that he intended to provide a reason for the epithet given to **Hercules**, the **one born in three nights**. Similarly, I believe even more that this epithet is merely an allusion to the length of the night preceding the winter solstice, during which the sun is swallowed by the monsters of the water in which it hides.

## Third Note.

### Whether Hercules distinguished himself in the sciences? The origin of the Muses and Graces.

The title **Musagetes** <note>original: "Musagettes"; from the Greek *Mousagetes*, meaning "Leader of the Muses."</note> or Leader of the Muses attributed to Hercules (1) actually persuaded some scholars that Hercules distinguished himself just as much through his excellent intellect and extensive knowledge as through his strength and skill.

Among those who maintain this, one can place the **Abbé de Fontenu** <note>Louis-François-Claude de Fontenu (1667–1759), a French historian and member of the Academy of Inscriptions.</note> at the top of the list. In a treatise found in the **Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions** (2) <note>original: "Memoires de l’ Academie des Inscriptions"</note>, he appeals to **Diodorus**, **Isocrates**, **Pausanias**, **Aristotle**, and **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**; he turns Hercules into a true **polyhistor** <note>A "polyhistor" is a person of great and varied learning; a universal scholar.</note>, and into a man very experienced in **theology**, **philosophy**, **medicine**, **botany**, **geometry**, **hydraulics**, **astronomy**, in the **fine arts**, **poetry**, and the **art of divination**.

Unfortunately, these are merely overly extended conclusions drawn from some symbolic concepts of the ancients.

For example, the fact that Hercules determined the points of the **equinoxes** and the **solstices** in the **Zodiac** arose solely because he represented the Sun, whose path indicates these points.

He is the leader of the Muses because the Muses were originally the nine months of the year during which the earth could be cultivated; the three remaining months were called **Graces**; they were depicted dancing because they represented the three months dedicated to rest and pleasure. <note>In this allegorical interpretation, the "nine Muses" represent the nine months of the agricultural labor cycle, while the "three Graces" represent the winter months of rest.</note>

When he was identified with **Apollo**, tripods were dedicated to him, as occurred in the beautiful monument I just described, "Hercules at Rest"; was this not simply a result of the symbolic meaning of the tripod, which designated the seasons, of which there were originally only three? <note>Ancient Greek traditions often recognized only three seasons: Spring, Summer, and Winter.</note>

The learned **Fulvius Nobilior**, the conqueror of **Aetolia**, built the first temple in **Rome** to Hercules as Leader of the Muses <note>The Temple of Hercules Musarum.</note> after his return from that campaign. In this temple, he installed new bronze statues of rare beauty, which represented the nine Muses sharing in the spoils of war.

This temple was later restored by **Philippus**, the father-in-law of **Augustus**; it became a gathering place for great minds and scholars; one could see masterpieces there, both in painting and architecture.

## Fourth Note.

### Allegorical Legend of the Scythians regarding Hercules, and its Explanation.

Allegorical fables were not only rooted among the Phoenicians, Egyptians, and Greeks; they also flourished among various other peoples. However, because these fables became blended with local historical legends, they became inexplicable to all those who sought to interpret them. In the flattering hope of perhaps bringing them back under the correct perspective, I wish to attempt an explanation of one such legend, in which **Hercules** is likewise the subject. In this tale, he becomes the father of the **Scythians** <note>The Scythians were nomadic people of ancient Central Eurasia, often viewed by the Greeks as exotic and powerful warriors.</note>—a story upon which some writers have relied to suggest this people truly descended from this hero. These Phoenicians, who called one of these parts of the world *Asia*—that is, the Orient <note>Literally the "Morning Land."</note>, the region of light—but another *Africa*, or the sun in its strength: these very people gave the name *Europa* to the third part of the world, which expresses the Occident <note>Literally the "Evening Land."</note>, the land situated on the side of night; for the word ערב <note>Original: ערב (*Ereb*). This name is likewise suitable for the Moon; one sees it only in the evening; at the time of the new moon, one beholds it only toward the setting of the sun. Is it not, moreover, the queen of night? Is it not, therefore, rightly called *Europa*?

## Sixth Note.

### Explanation of the phrase "to die as a virgin," and the story of Xipheus.

In the symbolic writing of the ancients, the phrase *to die as a virgin* expresses nothing more than *to be the last in a series of the same kind*. Thus, the last month or the last day of the year dies without offspring and as a virgin because they are the last of their family. Upon this was founded the allegory of the twelfth *Amazon* killed last by *Hercules*, which refers to the last of the twelve nightly months, who, in accordance with her vow, truly dies as a virgin <note>The author suggests that myths of "slaying" characters at the end of a cycle represent the natural conclusion of a month or year.</note>.

On this very point is also founded the previously inexplicable allegory of *Janus*, who was adopted in place of a child by *Xipheus*.

The daughter of *Erechtheus*, King of *Athens*, named *Creusa*, a girl of extraordinary beauty, was, as they say, (1) assaulted by *Apollo*; she thereafter brought a son into the world, who in *Delphi*

### The Fable of Hippomenes and Atalanta, who were both transformed into lions.

Every riddle can be presented from different perspectives, and in the same way, one and the same allegory took different forms among the ancients.

Even with only a slight knowledge of mythology <term>mythology: The author uses "Fabellehre," or the study of fables and myths, reflecting the 18th-century view of myths as coded lessons.</term>, surely everyone knows the story of Hippomenes and Atalanta; how the former defeated the latter in a footrace by throwing apples in her path, and how both were transformed into a lion and a lioness through the vengeance of Cybele <note>A Phrygian mother goddess often depicted in a chariot drawn by lions.</note>. # Conclusion.

Finally, by linking symbol to symbol and trait to trait, comparing and dissecting the entire structure upon which I labored and choosing it as my guide, I have reached my goal of explaining these three Eastern <note>original: "morgenländische," referring to the Orient or the ancient Near East</note> allegories. Throughout the entire path I have traveled since then, and through all subsequent discoveries, I have never been forced to revise my principles <term>Grundsätze: the fundamental rules or theoretical foundations of a study</term>. What is this, one might ask, other than the effect of a "spirit of systems" <term>System-Geist: the tendency to force all facts into a preconceived theory, often blinding the researcher to the truth</term>, which sees exactly what it wishes to see everywhere and knows how to interpret everything to its own advantage?

Most certainly, the spirit of systems is extremely dangerous because it colors everything it touches; however, it ceases to be dangerous as soon as it follows the analytical method <term>analytische Methode: a process of breaking down a complex topic into smaller parts to better understand its nature</term>, sticking strictly to the facts, encompassing everything contained within the subject, and drawing conclusions only from their comparison—

## Note.

Despite the translator’s efforts to avoid frequent printing errors in this work, many have crept in, as can be seen from the following list. Apart from the fact that the content of this work itself may contribute somewhat to their excuse, they were primarily caused, partly by the considerable distance of the place of printing, and partly by the fact that the corrector <term>Korrektor: a proofreader at the printing house</term> improved the Hebrew words according to the Masoretic reading <term>masoretische Lesart: the traditional system of pronunciation and notation of the Hebrew Bible established between the 7th and 10th centuries</term>, quite contrary to the intention of the author, who bases his etymologies <term>Etymologien: the study of the origins and historical development of words</term> on his own pronunciation.

<image-desc>Small ornamental horizontal divider with scrolling ends and a central leaf motif.</image-desc>
